# A Real Pathway to a Trade

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/a-real-pathway-to-a-trade> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

## A Real Pathway to a Trade

Too many young New Zealanders are pushed towards university without being given a proper chance to try a trade. For a bright, ambitious young person, an apprenticeship can mean earning while they learn and building skills that could one day lead to running a business of their own.

ACT will end the university-first mindset and put trades on an equal footing. We’ll build a proper national pathway so choosing a trade is just as straightforward and respected as choosing university.

Read ACT's full policy here.

#### ACT will:

- Remove funding caps on approved trades subjects at school, with funding following students and schools keeping their base and equity funding when students learn off-site.
- Create Industry Awards alongside University Entrance, showing employers that students have completed relevant learning and are ready for their next step.
- Give employers a stronger voice in what students learn, with Industry Skills Boards developing new subjects as technology and workforce needs change.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT List Candidate Paul Henry says:

"Trades are not a second-best option. For a bright, ambitious young person, becoming an electrician, builder, or mechanic can be the most intelligent decision they ever make. They can earn while they learn, build valuable skills, avoid taking on a large student loan, and potentially go on to run their own business and employ others.

“ACT will end the university-first mindset and put trades on an equal footing."

---

# A Starship for Cancer

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/a-starship-for-cancer> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Health

## A Starship for Cancer

Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year, and around 1,000 more die from cancer each year than would if our cancer mortality rate matched Australia’s.

New Zealanders should not have to accept second-rate cancer care. Starship showed what can happen when we bring our best people, technology, research and generosity together. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

ACT will support a world-class National Cancer Centre with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch. It will bring complex treatment, research, clinical trials and specialist expertise together in one institution. We want New Zealand to have cancer care that stands alongside the best in the world.

Read ACT's full policy, Beyond Tomorrow – A Starship for Cancer, here.

#### ACT will:

- Build National Cancer Centre campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.
- Bring cancer treatment, research, clinical trials, and specialist expertise together in world-class centres.
- Establish an independent National Cancer Centre Foundation to attract major philanthropic investment.
- Use public-private partnerships, philanthropy, existing health investment, and private capital to fund the centres.
- Locate Health New Zealand’s relevant Auckland and Christchurch cancer services at the new centres.
- Remove the $33,333 cap on tax benefits for charitable donations.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:

"I’ve joined politics because I am ambitious for New Zealand and think it has endless potential. We should not accept being second-rate at treating a disease that touches almost every family.

"Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

"This is an investment in New Zealand’s future. It is the type of project that makes New Zealand the envy of the world and attracts private healthcare investment, new technologies and therapies, teaching, medical research, and international clinical trials."

documents/abolish-labours-rental-tax.md.text:
# Abolish Labour’s Rental Tax

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/abolish-labours-rental-tax> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Abolish Labour’s Rental Tax

Labour claimed to help renters, then made the homes they live in more expensive to provide. ACT will reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by ending loss ring-fencing. This will ease pressure on rents, freeing up money for repairs and investment in more homes, and ultimately give renters more choice and market power.

#### ACT will:

- End loss ring-fencing for future rental losses. Allow residential rental losses incurred from the day the policy takes effect to be offset against other taxable income.
- Cover existing homes and new builds. Improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes.
- Retain the current treatment of earlier losses. Losses already ring-fenced will remain subject to the existing rules.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“There’s no such thing as a tax on landlords that renters can safely ignore. When Labour made rental housing more expensive to provide, tenants faced the consequences through pressure on rents, fewer homes, less choice, and poorer quality.

“Removing ring-fencing will improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes. Alongside ACT’s resource management reforms and opening up access to new building materials, it will encourage supply and give renters more choice.”

# Abundant and Affordable Electricity

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/abundant-and-affordable-electricity> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Infrastructure

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Abundant and Affordable Electricity

Cheaper power puts more money in your pocket and gives businesses room to grow. New Zealand needs much more electricity, and people are ready to invest their own money in producing it.

Building and connecting new generation has been made unnecessarily difficult and slow. Households putting solar panels on their roofs face barriers to selling the power they make. Around a quarter of a typical power bill goes to a local lines monopoly you cannot switch away from.

ACT has already secured the repeal of Labour’s oil and gas ban. We need to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand’s potential by backing the people ready to build more power.

Read our full policy, Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity, here.

#### ACT will:

- Let you choose who buys your power. Households could sell to a different provider from the one they buy electricity from, or through local businesses and community energy schemes, with proper metering, network charges and consumer protections.
- Lift unnecessary limits on your solar. Allow households to export more power where the network has room. Make lines companies explain and justify restrictions.
- Get new power connected faster. Let private investors build and operate their own transmission lines connected to the National Grid, meeting common technical and reliability standards. The generators and customers using those lines would pay through voluntary agreements.
- Let you shop around for a connection. Open eligible work on new or upgraded connections to competing accredited contractors. Lines companies would still set the safety and technical standards.
- Make lines companies prove an upgrade is worth it. Require them to test major upgrades against competing options, such as batteries or ways to reduce demand at peak times, before putting the cost on your bill.
- Keep investment in more power coming. Oppose forced break-ups of the major companies that generate and sell electricity. Strengthen enforcement when companies misuse market power to shut out competitors or block fair access to electricity markets and infrastructure.
- Cut red tape for solar power by implementing the recommendations of the Ministry for Regulation's Solar Regulatory Review, including legalising plug in solar.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Energy and Resources Spokesperson Simon Court says:

“New Zealand became a prosperous country in part because we were blessed with abundant energy. But you cannot maintain a first-world standard of living without reliable, affordable power. When energy becomes scarce and expensive, households feel it in their power bills, businesses face higher costs, investment becomes harder, and ultimately New Zealanders’ standard of living suffers.

“The answer is not for politicians to go looking for successful businesses to blame or promising to pull the electricity market apart. We’ve seen that before with the oil and gas ban. We need to make it easier for people to invest, generate more electricity, build the networks needed to move it, and compete for customers. That is how New Zealand gets abundant electricity and lower costs.”

---

documents/affordable-government.md.title: A Smaller, More Affordable Government
documents/affordable-government.md.text:
# A Smaller, More Affordable Government

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/affordable-government> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Democracy & Equal Rights

## A Smaller, More Affordable Government

Making New Zealand affordable again must start at the top.

New Zealand has 78 ministerial portfolios, 28 ministers, and 43 departments. Norway has a similar population and runs with 20 ministers across 17 ministries. New Zealand’s oversized Government isn’t intentional, it’s like a hedge that stopped being trimmed years ago.

#### Under ACT’s plan:

- The 43 departments would be consolidated into 19 coherent departments.
- The 78 overlapping portfolios with 28 ministers would be collapsed into just 18 ministers.
- Each department would report to one minister for its budget and outcomes.*
- Ministers would be allowed to appoint chief executives for a fixed term, renewable once, with clear protections for officials.
- Chief executives could be removed by Ministers for specified reasons such as non-performance or policy misalignment, but they would retain public service protections and the right to return to a lower classified role.
- Operational independence would be protected by law for agencies that need it, such as Police, NZSIS, and NZDF.

ACT’s full proposal, ' ACT’s plan for a consolidated bureaucracy', can be found here.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential.

“The Government is too tangled to act. Housing, infrastructure, welfare dependency, crime, and health all cut across multiple agencies. When seven departments share a problem, it can stop being anyone’s job to solve it. Kiwis are left frustrated, bouncing between departments or denied straight answers.

“Sprawling, tangled bureaucracy is expensive. It costs money that can’t be returned to taxpayers, can’t pay down debt, can’t reach the nurse, teacher or police officer on the frontline, and can’t build the infrastructure we need.

“Overseas research shows more ministers with spending power means bigger deficits. When many ministers each control part of the budget, but the cost falls on the whole tax base, each has an incentive to grow their own spending while bearing only a fraction of the cost.

“ACT’s plan won’t affect frontline services like nurses, teachers, or police. If anything, it will make them more effective with clear lines of responsibility and a focus on their core role.

“The Coalition Government has accepted the argument for a smaller Government, but current changes are tinkering around the edges. Kiwis are tired of piecemeal change that takes forever, so ACT is proposing a thought-out plan for the whole government, that we can start rolling out immediately in the next term.

“ACT would also fix the broken accountability line between ministers and departmental chief executives. At the moment, ministers are held responsible for delivery, but they do not appoint the person leading the department responsible for that delivery. ACT would remove the Public Service Commission and allow ministers to appoint chief executives, and chief executives could be removed for specified reasons.

“That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential. A government with clear structure and limits, not the tangled result of accidental growth. Small enough to be accountable, simple enough to act, and focused on results for New Zealanders instead of managing itself.”

---

# Affordable School Uniforms

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/affordable-uniforms> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Affordable School Uniforms

A school uniform should identify a school, not lock families into buying every basic item from one supplier.

Many families spend well over $1,000 per child once they buy several shirts, socks, shorts or skirts, PE gear and replacements. In 2025, 38,000 WINZ hardship loans worth $11 million were issued to help families meet the cost.

Some state schools require everyday items to be bought from one approved supplier, even when an equivalent item is available at an ordinary retailer for much less. There is no educational reason for a logo to make a pair of navy socks cost several times more.

#### ACT will:

- Amend the Education and Training Act to limit state schools to a maximum of three compulsory branded uniform items.
- Require schools to offer generic alternatives for high-use items such as shorts, pants, skirts, skorts and socks.
- Let families buy those generic items from standard clothing retailers.
- Keep room for schools to choose a small number of branded items that preserve their identity and traditions.
- Exclude sports uniforms, team strips, kapa haka uniforms and tracksuits from the new rules.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Education spokesperson Laura McClure says:

“Many families are spending well over $1,000 per child once they buy several shirts, socks, shorts or skirts, PE gear, and replacements. Last year the Government issued 38,000 WINZ hardship loans worth $11 million for school uniforms. Parents should not have to go into debt for clothing that costs far more than it needs to.

“There is no educational reason for a pair of navy socks to cost three times as much because it has to come from one supplier. More competition and choice could put hundreds of dollars back in parents’ pockets without changing what children wear to school.”

documents/an-easier-end-to-dead-end-empl.text:
# An Easier End to Dead-End Employment

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/an-easier-end-to-dead-end-employment> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## An Easier End to Dead-End Employment

Small businesses shouldn’t need a lawyer just to have a difficult conversation about someone’s employment.

Sometimes an employment relationship is no longer working. An employer may be willing to pay the employee to leave, and the employee may be happy to accept. Under today’s law, simply raising that possibility can expose the business to a personal grievance.

ACT’s Golden Handshake policy would let both sides discuss a voluntary exit. The employee is free to say no. If they agree, the deal goes in writing and both sides can move on. ACT trusts adults to make their own decisions.

#### ACT will:

- Allow an employer to offer an employee a specified payment to end their employment by mutual agreement, whether or not a dispute has already arisen.
- Protect the employee’s right to reject the offer.
- Stop the offer itself from becoming grounds for a personal grievance.
- Generally keep the offer and resulting negotiations out of later Employment Relations Authority proceedings.
- Require every agreement to be written and signed by both sides.
- Require the employer to advise the employee to seek independent advice and give them a reasonable opportunity to do so.
- Make an accepted agreement a full and final settlement of claims arising from the employment relationship.

### In our team’s words:

ACT Small Business spokesperson Laura McClure says:

“In some cases, an employer would happily offer an employee compensation to leave, and the employee would happily accept. But current law makes it unnecessarily risky to even start that conversation.

“Small businesses shouldn’t need a lawyer just to have a difficult conversation.

“There is no reason our laws cannot treat people like adults and provide the opportunity to reach a fair agreement, shake hands, and move on before a difficult employment relationship turns into an expensive legal dispute.”

# Back the Volunteers

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/back-the-volunteers> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Hunters and Firearms

## Back the Volunteers

DOC is responsible for more than 950 huts and 15,000 kilometres of tracks. It faces a 30 per cent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021.

Hunting, tramping and conservation groups already restore huts, maintain tracks and run trap lines at a fraction of the cost. Too often they survive on annual discretionary grants, with no certainty that they can keep the work going.

ACT would fund capable community groups to deliver the work and let accredited hunting groups earn nature credits for conservation results that can be independently verified

Read the full policy

#### ACT will:

- Require DOC to give community groups the first opportunity for funding when they can offer a competitive option for backcountry upkeep.
- Allow multi-year contracts so volunteer organisations can plan ahead instead of applying for funding year by year.
- Open the Voluntary Nature Credits Market to accredited hunting groups so they can earn credits for verified biodiversity results.
- Require formal representation for the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association and Game Animal Council in predator-removal decisions affecting hunters.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“DOC has more than 950 huts and 15,000 kilometres of tracks to look after. It faces a 30 per cent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. The department will not clear that backlog on its own.

“Community groups already restore huts and maintain tracks at a fraction of the cost, but many survive from one discretionary grant to the next. ACT would give them the first opportunity for funding when they can offer a competitive option, including the security of multi-year contracts.”

ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Hunters are already in the hills running trap lines and removing predators, but the new nature-credit market does not recognise that work. Accredited hunting groups should be able to earn credits when they can show they have delivered real biodiversity gains.

“The New Zealand Deerstalkers Association and Game Animal Council should be formally represented when predator-removal operations affecting hunters are planned. Decisions are better when the people already doing the work are involved from the start, not consulted after everything has been settled.”

ACT candidate and former New Zealand Deerstalkers Association president Callum Sheridan says:

“The hunting community contributes hundreds of thousands of unpaid hours to conservation every year. Backing those groups to deliver measurable results would mean more work gets done in the backcountry and taxpayers get better value for their money.”

# Backing Small Business

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/backing-small-business> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Backing Small Business

Small businesses turn hard work and good ideas into opportunities for other New Zealanders, from a first job to the higher wages that come with growth.

Every cost and stupid rule imposed by Government makes that growth harder, leaving workers with fewer opportunities and customers paying more.

ACT has already cut red tape for small businesses in Government. This package goes further so the people who build businesses and those who work for them can get ahead through their own effort.

Read ACT’s full policy, Let small business get on with business, here.

#### ACT will:

- Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years, giving employers certainty and allowing productivity to catch up with past increases.
- Introduce a Training Wage set at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20 during their first 12 months with an employer.
- Allow employers and employees to begin protected negotiations about a consensual exit, while maintaining safeguards against coercion.
- Require personal grievance proceedings to be lodged with the Employment Relations Authority within three months of the grievance being raised, rather than leaving claims hanging over a business for up to three years.
- Make payroll deductions for union fees voluntary, so employers are not forced to collect fees on a union’s behalf. This policy was developed from a Member's Bill by ACT MP Parmjeet Parmar.
- Allow businesses to deduct productive software and digital investment under clear and consistent tax rules.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Small Business spokesperson Laura McClure says:

“New Zealand will not become more prosperous by making it harder to employ somebody, take a chance on a young worker, resolve a dispute, or invest in technology.

“ACT’s approach is different from the assumption that every problem needs another rule. New Zealanders have enormous potential when Government gets out of the way and allows them to get on with reaching it.

“Successful small businesses get more people in work, and create higher wages. Achieving that requires a dedicated presence in Government focused on unlocking the potential of every New Zealander willing to build, hire, innovate, and take risks.”

documents/burglary.md.title: Three Strikes for Burglary
documents/burglary.md.text:
# Three Strikes for Burglary

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/burglary> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Three Strikes for Burglary

ACT will introduce a Three Strikes for Burglary regime, requiring a minimum three-year prison sentence with no parole for anyone convicted of burglary three times.

In 2025, 184,000 New Zealanders were victims of burglary. Burglary is a recidivist crime, with the majority of people released from prison for burglary sent back to prison within two years. Nearly three-quarters are resentenced. Around one in four burglary victims have already been burgled before.

Judges keep using their leeway to give burglars more chances, and the burglars keep reoffending.

ACT says enough. If you keep breaking into people's homes, the warnings stop and real consequences kick in.

- ACT will create a new Three Strikes regime for burglary. Anyone convicted of burglary three times would receive a minimum sentence of three years in prison, with no parole, no home detention, and no early release.
- The policy would apply both to someone facing their third conviction, or to someone facing a single conviction of three or more counts of burglary.
- An aggravated burglary would trigger a strike under both this regime and the existing Three Strikes regime for violent crime.
- The judge would still retain full discretion to impose any sentence between the three-year minimum and the 10-year maximum.

Read the full policy

#### In our team’s words:

"Your home should be the one place where you feel safe," says ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee.

"It’s the place where you keep the things you've worked for, your family's memories, and the people you care about most. That sense of security should be absolute, but it’s undermined by every burglary in our neighbourhoods.

“This policy is not primarily about deterring crime. It is about preventing it. Imprisoning repeat burglars will protect New Zealanders from a small group of offenders who have shown, time after time, that they have no respect for other people's homes or property. They will not be able to victimise us from a jail cell.

"When someone does the right thing, gets up and goes to work to unlock their own potential, they shouldn’t have to worry about some deadbeat invading their home and taking their hard-earned property.

"ACT will unlock the potential of the justice system to protect victims, not make excuses for criminals.”

---

# Closing the Medicines Gap

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/closing-medicines-gap> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Health

## Closing the Medicines Gap

No New Zealander should have to empty their savings, uproot their family, or leave the country to access medicines Australians receive as a matter of course.

New Zealand spends just 4.9 per cent of its health budget on medicines. Australia spends 12.2 per cent, while the OECD average is 13.3 per cent. Australia funds 142 modern medicines that are not funded in New Zealand, and 38 per cent of those are cancer medicines.

Often, the medicine a patient needs is already on Pharmac's Options for Investment list. Pharmac has assessed it as worth funding, but it remains unavailable because the medicines budget has run out.

Pharmac negotiates hard and assesses which medicines will produce the greatest health gains. Then it runs out of money. Successive governments have given it a second-rate medicines budget and expected first-world results.

#### ACT will:

- Increase the share of the health budget spent on medicines by one percentage point each year, reaching parity with Australia in 2033.
- Set Pharmac's future funding increases in advance, allowing it to plan for more medicines on its Options for Investment list.
- Fund the change from expected growth in the health budget. It will not require additional taxes or reduce the size of the non-medicines health budget.
- Ask other parties to commit to the same seven-year path, so a change of government does not derail it.

Read the full policy

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Since taking responsibility for Pharmac and Medsafe, I have heard from hundreds of people whose treatment exists but is still out of reach. Often Pharmac has already assessed the medicine and put it on the Options for Investment list. The money simply is not there.

“New Zealand spends 4.9 per cent of its health budget on medicines. Australia spends 12.2 per cent. ACT would close that gap by lifting the medicines share one percentage point each year until we reach parity in 2033.

“Pharmac bargains hard and gets good value from every dollar. Governments have taken that efficiency for granted and left the budget too small. In Budget 2026, Health got an extra $1.5 billion and Pharmac got $13.5 million. Under our policy it would have received around $320 million more.”

ACT Health spokesperson Todd Stephenson says:

“Australia funds 142 modern medicines that New Zealand does not. Thirty-eight per cent are cancer medicines. Behind those figures are families draining savings, raising money, or moving overseas for treatment.

“We can close the gap without a new tax or cutting the rest of the health budget. Health spending is already growing. ACT would reserve one point of that growth for medicines each year, so more patients get treatment before they end up in hospital.”

---

# Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/crack-down-on-noisy-vehicles> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles

On some streets, loud exhausts and car stereos are a regular nuisance. Residents can report a noisy vehicle, but once it has gone, it’s hard to prove how loud it was.

Excessive vehicle noise is already against the law. ACT will make those rules easier to enforce in neighbourhoods where the problem keeps coming back.

Read ACT’s full policy, Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles, here.

#### ACT will:

- Introduce relocatable noise cameras that can be deployed in communities with persistent problems, collecting evidence when a noisy vehicle passes.
- Set enforceable roadside noise limits of 86 decibels on roads with speed limits of 50 km/h or less, and 90 decibels on roads with speed limits above 50 km/h and up to 70 km/h.
- Increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise, treating noise from equipment inside the vehicle consistently with noise from its engine or exhaust.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT's Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas says:

“Hard working Kiwis shouldn’t be punished by people who can’t take personal responsibility for their noise. Noise cameras enable evidence of offending to be collected the moment the offence occurs.

“Pairing technology with clear standards and real consequences will give residents the peace and quiet they deserve and ensure the comfort of many isn’t sacrificed for the noise of a few.”

---

# Deport Serious Offenders

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/deport> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

###### Immigration

## Deport Serious Offenders

Immigration must work for New Zealand. The system should welcome people, but only if they share values of tolerance, freedom and democracy, help build infrastructure, and play by the rules.

Today, Kiwis who are proud of our settler heritage are asking themselves why something doesn’t quite feel right with immigration. ACT believes their suspicions are correct.

Successive governments have let a skilled-migration system become a general-purpose labour tap. They have failed to enforce the rules they set. They have allowed infrastructure to fall further behind. And they have asked too little of people who want to benefit from the Kiwi character without supporting it.

ACT’s policy restores the basic bargain that New Zealand was built on. People are welcome here if they contribute, respect our democratic values, and help build the country.

ACT’s six-point immigration plan is:

1. Deport serious offenders

ACT will ensure Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more can be deported no matter how long they’ve been here. This goes further than the Government’s current proposal to extend liability to 20 years.

2. Skilled visas for skilled jobs

Accredited Employer Work Visas are meant to fill crucial skills gaps, but too often the gaps close and the categories remain wide open. ACT will have each skill category automatically expire every year. To remain open, they would need to show up-to-date evidence of demand.

3. Opportunity, not dependency

ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for all residence class visa holders. That means no jobseeker support, accommodation supplement, or income-tested benefits for a migrant’s first five years here.

4. A fair contribution for infrastructure

ACT will introduce a $6 per day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, on top of existing charges. This ensures migrants contribute to New Zealand’s infrastructure from day one, before they start paying tax. The fee is expected to raise around $80 million a year, while remaining more affordable than comparable visas in Australia and the United Kingdom.

5. Stronger English language requirements

ACT will extend basic English language requirements to all AEWV types. Lower standards will still be permitted for seasonal workers.

6. Enforce the rules

There are 20,980 known overstayers in New Zealand right now. ACT will establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash will be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying will lose their accreditation.

Read the full policy

#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand is a settler society. From those who arrived in open boats 700 years ago, to those who arrived at Auckland Airport this morning, our country has been built by people willing to make a journey to try and build something better,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Immigration has enriched New Zealand. In less than 200 years, New Zealand has gone from a series of isolated villages, to a network of modern cities connected by road, rail, air, and sea, with electricity, the internet, and the three waters.

“Each wave of settlement has also built the Kiwi character that is respected around the world. Kiwis are recognised in everything from business to sport to peacekeeping as resourceful and thoughtful, firm but fair people who keep their word and can fix anything.

“We need an immigration system that recognises New Zealand’s heritage as a nation of settlers. We need new migrants to grow and develop, but that migration must work for New Zealand.

“Success requires a common set of expectations; respect our freedoms, uphold our democratic values, contribute to infrastructure, speak English, obey the law, and fill genuine gaps in the economy.”

---

# Disrupt the Class, Leave the Class

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/disrupt-the-class-leave-the-class> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

## Disrupt the Class, Leave the Class

Most students behave well and want to learn. Serious or persistent disruption can take over a lesson, leaving the teacher to manage one student while everyone else waits.

The Education Review Office found in 2024 that around half of teachers deal with disruption in every lesson. Forty-seven per cent lose 40 to 50 minutes or more each day responding to challenging behaviour. In the 2022 PISA results, New Zealand had the worst behavioural climate in maths classes in the OECD. Half of teachers told ERO that behaviour had a large impact on whether they intended to remain in teaching.

ACT would create a quick response that sits below formal stand-down and suspension processes. A teacher could direct a seriously or persistently disruptive student to leave and go to a staffed, supervised space. A refusal would be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refused again after that escalation, staff could use reasonable force to remove them.

Removed students would stay under supervision in a pastoral office, dean's room or learning support room. Empty or lockable rooms could not be used. Corporal punishment would remain illegal. Any physical intervention would have to be reasonable, proportionate and authorised by law.

Read ACT's full policy, Strengthening teacher authority and stopping class disruption, here.

#### ACT will:

- Amend the Education and Training Act 2020 to give classroom teachers an explicit legal power to direct a student to leave for serious or persistent disruption and report to a staffed, supervised space.
- Require a refusal to be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refuses a second lawful direction after that escalation, staff may use reasonable force to remove them.
- Clarify section 99 of the Act so staff are protected when they use reasonable and proportionate intervention to prevent harm or the destruction of property.
- Require immediate removal followed by a mandatory stand-down or suspension for any assault on a teacher, student or other member of school staff. An assault that crosses the criminal threshold would be referred to Police Youth Aid on the first occurrence.
- Require a parent or guardian meeting when behaviour becomes serious or repeated, and when a student refuses a lawful direction to leave. Parents already working with the school in good faith over low-level disruption would not be called to a duplicate meeting.
- Escalate cases where a parent does not engage, either to the Ministry of Education or through the Oranga Tamariki and Police Youth Aid pathway. A parent who misses a mandatory meeting without a reasonable excuse could be fined up to $300 for a first offence and up to $3,000 for a later offence.
- Allow schools to recover the cost of deliberate property damage from a student's parents as a debt if it is not paid.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:

“Education is the key to a better tomorrow. Somehow, we've allowed disruptive students to steal valuable learning time from their classmates while teachers are denied the authority to stop them. How can we expect teachers to administer world-class education if we are not providing them with world-class support?”

“Most students behave well and want to learn. They should not have their education held hostage by a minority who refuse to respect their teacher or classmates. We should be supporting teachers and education.

“Corporal punishment would remain illegal, and removed students would stay supervised. Any physical intervention must be reasonable, proportionate and backed by law. A teacher's job is to teach. ACT will give them the authority to get on with it.”

# One Public Service for All

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/equal-service> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Democracy & Equal Rights

## One Public Service for All

ACT has already directed agencies to deliver services based on need, not identity. We have also strengthened the Public Service Act: public servants must stay politically neutral and appointments must be made on merit. But previous governments spent years building separate tracks for different groups, and too many of those rules remain.

ACT will remove them and build one public service with one standard for everyone that delivers help where it is needed and keeps public servants focused on the New Zealanders they serve. The same rules will apply, whoever you are.

Read ACT's full policy, One Public Service for All, here.

#### ACT will:

- End race-based hiring. Government jobs should go to the best candidate, whoever they are. But the law still tells public employers to shape employment policies around the aspirations and employment needs of particular ethnic groups. ACT will repeal those rules in section 73 of the Public Service Act and section 118 of the Crown Entities Act. Laws against discrimination and unsafe workplaces will remain. So will the rule that public service appointments must be based on merit.
- Deliver public services based on need, not race. ACT will put into law that public services should go to the people who need them, whoever they are. If two New Zealanders have the same need, government should treat them the same. The Government has already told agencies to follow that rule. ACT will put it in law so people can challenge decisions that break it in court.
- Keep spiritual practices voluntary. Taxpayer money isn't for running spiritual or religious activities at work. ACT will end the use of public time and public funds for this, whatever the tradition. Staff will remain free to practise their own religion, culture, or traditions in their own time, and workplaces can make reasonable arrangements for them.
- Remove cultural tests that have nothing to do with the job. Job ads should ask whether you can do the work, not whether you know the right cultural concepts or share the right worldview. ACT will tell agencies to remove these requirements from job ads and position descriptions unless the knowledge is actually needed for the job.
- Rewrite the Public Service Act. ACT will make these changes straight away, then rewrite the Act so the public service stays politically neutral, hires on merit, treats people equally, and is judged on whether services actually reach the people who need them.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

"To unlock New Zealand's potential we need one law for all, and one future together. That starts with a public service that treats people as individuals, hires the best people for the job, and delivers services according to need.

"Public service jobs should go to the best person for the job, regardless of race. Hiring and promotion should be based on merit, skills, experience, and what the role actually requires.

"If two New Zealanders have the same need, they should be entitled to the same treatment from government.

"Nobody should be expected to take part in a prayer, karakia, or other spiritual practice because they work for the Government.

“ACT will ensure a public service capable of unlocking the potential of all New Zealanders. It will be neutral, professional, focused on results, and treat every person as an individual."

# Equal Treatment at Universities

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/equal-treatment-at-universities> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

## Equal Treatment at Universities

Taxpayer-funded support at university should go to students who need it. It should not be allocated according to their race.

Universities can currently reserve scholarships, accommodation, study spaces and other opportunities on the basis of ethnicity. In 2024, the Government directed public agencies to allocate support according to need and value rather than ethnicity, but tertiary institutions were not covered.

ACT's Education and Training (Equal Treatment) Amendment Bill would apply that principle to tertiary education. Universities could still support students according to academic merit, economic hardship, disability, location or a need for academic help. Privately funded scholarships and grants could still be targeted according to the donor's wishes.

#### ACT will:

- Amend the Education and Training Act to prevent tertiary institutions conferring benefits on a person or group on the basis of race or ethnic origin.
- Apply the rule to scholarships, grants, financial assistance, accommodation, designated spaces and other benefits or opportunities.
- Preserve universities' ability to allocate support according to academic merit, academic need, geographic location, economic circumstances or disability.
- Exempt endowments, bequests and other assistance provided by private individuals, iwi, charities or trusts for a targeted purpose.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:

“Universities are independent, but most of their funding comes from taxpayers and legislation protects them from ordinary competition. With that privilege comes a basic obligation: taxpayer-funded opportunities should be open on equal terms.

“In 2024 the Government told public agencies to allocate services according to need and value rather than ethnicity, but universities were left outside that direction. My Bill would close that gap by applying the same principle to publicly funded tertiary institutions.

“The Bill would cover scholarships, grants, housing, designated facilities and other benefits. Universities could still recognise academic merit, provide extra academic support, respond to economic hardship or disability, and take account of where a student lives.

“Private generosity would remain private. If an iwi, charity or trust gives a university money for a scholarship aimed at Māori students, the university could continue to administer it. The change applies to the institution's own publicly funded resources: need, not race.”

# Expanding Charter Schools

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/expanding-charter-schools> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

## Expanding Charter Schools

The right school can change a child’s life. Charter schools give families more choice and educators the freedom to teach in ways that work for their students. Some cater for children with autism; others support high performance athletes. That freedom comes with clear standards for attendance and achievement, and schools can be shut down if they don’t deliver.

ACT brought charter schools back, and more than 2,000 students are already enrolled. We will protect them from Labour’s plans to shut them down and expand enrolments to 10,000 by the end of 2029, with the goal of a charter school option in every major town.

### ACT will:

- Protect charter schools from Labour’s plans to shut them down.
- Set a target of 10,000 charter school enrolments by the end of 2029, with annual reporting on progress.
- Help more suitable state and state-integrated schools convert to charter schools by removing unnecessary barriers relating to employment, property and funding.
- Encourage new charter schools where there is sufficient demand and a suitable sponsor, with the goal of a charter school option in every major town.
- Manage funding for growth transparently through existing education budgets.
- Retain strong performance standards for attendance, achievement, financial management and student wellbeing, with schools held accountable for results.

### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“When schools are given greater freedom to innovate and respond to the needs of their students, families benefit and students thrive.

“Families have deliberately chosen to move outside the traditional system because it was not meeting their needs. Hipkins is saying Labour would force them back in.

“Charter schools cost less to establish than equivalent state schools, and are accountable to deliver results – they can be shut down if they don’t.”

# A Fair Contribution for Infrastructure

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/fair-contribution> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Infrastructure

## A Fair Contribution for Infrastructure

New Zealand needs immigration. Employers cannot find every nurse, software engineer or farm worker they need within a working-age population of about three million. Migrants bring skills and help businesses grow.

Population growth also puts immediate pressure on housing and infrastructure. A temporary worker can use roads and public services from the day they arrive, before they have paid much New Zealand tax.

ACT will add a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas. It would sit on top of existing visa charges and is expected to raise about $80 million a year. At that rate, comparable visas would remain cheaper than those in Australia and the United Kingdom.

#### ACT will:

- Add a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas, on top of existing charges.
- Require temporary workers to contribute to New Zealand's infrastructure from their first day in the country.

Read ACT’s full immigration policy

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand still needs immigration. No modern export economy with a working-age population of about three million can produce every nurse, software engineer and farm worker it needs. Our economy and public services depend on people bringing skills here.

“That support cannot be taken for granted. Immigration has to work for the people already here, and population growth cannot be allowed to run down the infrastructure earlier generations built.

“At $6 a day, the visa would remain more affordable than comparable visas in Australia and the United Kingdom. Asking temporary workers to help with infrastructure is a fair part of an immigration system that keeps public confidence.”

# Fair Funding for Independent Schools

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/fair-funding-for-independent-schools> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

## Fair Funding for Independent Schools

The right school can change a child’s future. Parents who choose an independent school often make real sacrifices to pay the fees, while still paying taxes towards education. ACT will keep independent school funding in step with increases for state schools, helping ease pressure on fees so families can keep choosing the education that suits their child.

#### ACT will:

- Increase the independent school subsidy by the same percentage as state school operational funding in every future Budget.
- Retain the roll-growth funding changes secured in Budget 2025, so funding continues to adjust as more children attend independent schools.

A two per cent increase in state school operational funding would mean a two per cent increase in the independent school subsidy. Schools would have more certainty as they plan ahead, instead of seeing their support stay at the same dollar figure for years.

Debt measure.

ACT's path.

Each item's yearly effect on the operating balance and on cash comes from ACT's fiscal plan, for 2027/28 to 2030/31. Measures still to be announced are included in the totals. ACT's debt is Treasury's forecast less the running total of the cash improvement. Interest savings are charged on the average reduction in debt during each year, matching the financing-cost savings in ACT's model. All five tests are off by default.

Pay equity:

Budget 2025 booked about $2.7bn a year of savings from the Equal Pay Amendment Act. Labour will reinstate the regime but provides $558m a year (the $4 an hour rise), so the test adds the $2.14bn difference from 2027/28. Each test also carries interest at 4.7%.

Labour funds $146m, $295m and $149m to 2029/30 and nothing in 2030/31; the test adds $295m.

Labour says $10.5bn of its operating allowances is unallocated. Treasury's forecast already assumes allowances are spent, so costs paid from that room don't add to debt but leave nothing for other cost pressures. The debt figures assume Labour borrows instead.

Treasury's rule of thumb (PREFU 2026, Table 3.1): one percentage point faster nominal GDP growth raises tax revenue by $1.3bn, $2.8bn and $4.5bn in the first three years. The slider scales this from 2027/28 and lifts GDP in the ratios. It is not counted in ACT's costed plan.

Live figures.

The "since you arrived" counters use the same rate of new borrowing (about $727 a second) and the 2026/27 finance-cost forecast of $10.3bn (about $326 a second).

Crisis buffer.

Headroom is the gap between debt and 50% of GDP, the ceiling Treasury recommends in normal times (Investment Statement 2025). Treasury estimates shock responses have cost about 10% of GDP per decade since the late 1980s (Te Ara Mokopuna 2025), about $58bn at 2030/31 GDP.

Horizon.

The comparison runs to 2030/31, the last year of Treasury's forecast and of Labour's plan.

# ACT's Fiscal Plan

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/fiscalplan> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## ACT's Fiscal Plan

New Zealanders are working hard, but wages aren’t stretching far enough and too many young Kiwis see a better future overseas. Making life more affordable means growing wages as well as bringing costs down. That requires confidence to invest and build businesses here.

Government has to do its part by living within its means. Taxpayers are spending more than $1 million an hour on interest alone, money that could fund better healthcare or be left in your pocket. Cutting taxes by borrowing more would only pass the bill to the next generation, with interest.

ACT’s Fiscal Plan balances the books without new taxes and starts paying down debt. We’ll cut spending outside protected frontline services and make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers. We’ll also gradually raise the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, with compassionate early access for people who have spent much of their careers in physically demanding jobs.

The savings let us fund better services, including easier access to care through pharmacists, and remove tax on qualifying KiwiSaver investment earnings. More of your returns can stay invested and grow for retirement, without asking you to give up more of your pay today.

By 2031, debt will be $12.4 billion lower than current forecasts, leaving New Zealand better prepared for the next earthquake or major crisis. Balancing the books lays the groundwork for much lower, flatter taxes backed by lasting spending control. We’ll cut the waste to grow the country, Lock Labour Out and Unlock New Zealand’s Potential.

### ACT’s Fiscal Plan 2026

Our plan to unlock New Zealand's potential sets out how we’ll cut waste and fund better services, with the costings in full.

#### Explore ACT’s Fiscal Plan →

### Watch New Zealand’s debt grow

See how fast New Zealand’s debt is growing and the bill taxpayers are left to carry. Our debt ticker shows the scale of the challenge.

#### Watch the debt grow →

### ACT will:

- Balance the books with no new taxes, putting much lower taxes within reach.
- Cut $9.5 billion a year from spending outside welfare and protected frontline services once fully implemented.
- Make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers responsible for budgets and results.
- Remove tax on KiwiSaver investment earnings and discontinue the government contribution.
- Introduce a Carbon Tax Refund, returning net revenue from Emissions Trading Scheme auctions to New Zealanders.
- Gradually raise the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, with compassionate early access for people who have spent much of their careers in physically demanding jobs.
- Fund better healthcare, expanding pharmacist care and setting aside around $2 billion as a funding contingency for a National Cancer Centre.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“It is immoral to keep borrowing for political promises and sending the bill to the next generation. We are cutting waste, bringing the surplus forward, and using some of those savings to let New Zealanders build greater financial security.

“New Zealand needs a credible path to surplus without new taxes, and an economy where work, saving and investment pay off. A stronger ACT presence in government will provide the determination to deliver both. That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential.”

---

# Hunter-Led Game Management

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/game-management> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Hunters and Firearms

## Hunter-Led Game Management

Game animals on conservation land are managed by DOC, an agency whose legislation still starts from controlling or exterminating them. The Game Animal Council was meant to give hunters a meaningful role, but it can advise while DOC keeps the authority.

That model treats hunters as another group to consult instead of trusting the people who understand the herds and spend time in the country where they live.

ACT would put responsibility in the hands of the Game Animal Council. Game animals would be managed sustainably within conservation limits, with proper recognition for the value that healthy herds bring to hunters and regional communities.

#### ACT will:

- Transfer responsibility for managing game animals on conservation land from DOC to the Game Animal Council.
- Fully fund the Council to carry out its current and proposed responsibilities.
- Recognise game-animal and game-bird species in relevant legislation as valued natural resources to be sustainably managed.
- Designate New Zealand’s most valued game herds as Herds of Special Interest, beginning with Stewart Island whitetail deer.

Read the full policy

#### In our team's words:

ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Hunters have spent generations in the backcountry. They know the animals and the country because they are there every weekend, but Wellington still asks for their views after the real decisions have been made. Hunters should be helping to make those decisions from the start.

“The Game Animal Council was supposed to give hunters a genuine say. Instead, it was left advising DOC while DOC kept control. ACT would transfer game-animal management on conservation land to the Council and fund it properly to do the job.

“The law still begins from the idea that introduced game animals should be exterminated wherever possible. That makes no sense for valued herds that can be sustainably managed. ACT would recognise game animals and game birds as natural resources and use Herds of Special Interest to protect the best herds, starting with Stewart Island whitetail.”

ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“Healthy herds need proper targets and the surrounding environment needs protection. Hunters understand both sides of that equation. DOC would keep its wider conservation role, but the people who know the resource would make the game-management decisions.

“Hunters were promised a seat at the table and got another advisory role. They have earned real responsibility. The Game Animal Council should be judged on the results it delivers, not kept at arm’s length by the bureaucracy.”

documents/grazing.md.text:
# Grazing to Cut Pests and Fire Risk

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/grazing> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Rural

## Grazing to Cut Pests and Fire Risk

“Taxpayers are footing the bill for a helicopter spraying programme when a flock of sheep could be doing the job for free,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard as he releases new rural policy at Fieldays.

ACT will:

- Amend the Conservation Act 1987: ACT will give DOC explicit authority and direction to issue grazing licences for specified areas of conservation land where grazing supports vegetation management objectives.
- Target invasive plants and fire risk: ACT will establish a clear ecological framework to identify where grazing is appropriate to suppress conifer seedlings and other invasive vegetation, while reducing the fuel loads that contribute to devastating wildfires.
- Set practical licence conditions: ACT will ensure licences specify appropriate stocking types, rates, and duration, ensuring the land is managed effectively without burying farmers in bureaucratic red tape.
- Allow virtual fencing: ACT will recognise virtual fencing systems as a compliant method of stock exclusion to reduce the burden on farmers grazing their stock on DOC land.

#### In our team’s words:

“Taxpayers are footing the bill for a helicopter spraying programme when a flock of sheep could be doing the job for free,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard as he releases new rural policy at Fieldays.

"Wilding conifers are the largest invasive species challenge in New Zealand, choking 1.8 million hectares of land. The Government has invested sensibly into fighting them, but we can do a lot more by allowing farmers to graze livestock.

"DOC manages large areas of open country, former pastoral land, and other nonforest conservation land that could be safely grazed under controlled conditions. Too often, however, farmers seeking grazing concessions are met with resistance or unnecessary barriers. The result is less active land management, more wilding pines, and growing fuel loads that increase wildfire risk.

"By locking up the land and throwing away the key, the Government hasn’t just allowed invasive plants and pests to thrive; it has turned parts of the conservation estate into a severe wildfire risk. The heavy vegetation fuel loads left behind are a disaster waiting to happen.

"The current rules make it unnecessarily difficult to use targeted grazing on Crown conservation land. Instead, taxpayers are forced to pay for expensive aerial spraying and manual cutting. It is a regulatory failure that is actively harming the environment and wasting public money.

"Overseas, they know better. In the United States, Australia, and across Europe, targeted grazing is a standard, internationally recognised tool for managing invasive plants, controlling vegetation growth, and reducing wildfire fuel loads. Portugal even uses it specifically to build forest resilience against fires. It’s time New Zealand caught up. It’s time to stop treating farmers like the enemy and start treating them as part of the solution. We need to unleash practical, rural knowledge on this crisis.”

# Innovation Trials

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/innovation-trials> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Infrastructure

## Innovation Trials

Technology changes faster than the rulebook. Agricultural drones, driverless cars and new medical treatments are already being used overseas. In New Zealand, old rules can keep them out for years.

An Innovation Trial would let the Government set aside a particular rule for a limited test in one place. The approval would state the safety conditions and how the result will be measured. Bad results end the trial. Good results give the Government evidence to change the rule.

Government sometimes makes these exceptions after a company finds the right officials and persuades them to act. ACT would publish one application process that any company could use.

#### ACT will:

- Publish a permanent application process for Innovation Trials.
- Allow a specific regulation to be set aside for a limited test in one location.
- Set safety conditions and a way to measure the result before a trial begins.
- Use the Ministry for Regulation to help agencies identify existing exemption powers and run trials consistently.
- Invite companies working on autonomous vehicles, agricultural drones and medical technology to run trials in New Zealand.

Read David Seymour's speech

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Technology is what ultimately drives wages. People in the United States, Japan, Britain and Europe are using inventions that remain illegal here. Every year we wait leaves New Zealand workers further behind.

“Take agricultural spray drones. Once a drone weighs more than 25 kilograms, certification can cost up to $2,000 and take over a year. Australian farmers can use drones weighing up to 150 kilograms under a simple licence. Our officials have put the issue on a two-year work programme.

“An Innovation Trial lets the Government set aside the relevant rule for a limited test. The trial has conditions and an end date. We collect the evidence, see what actually happens and decide whether the old rule still makes sense.

“ACT will make that process available to any company through a permanent public application. New Zealand can then go to the people developing driverless cars, medical treatments and new farm technology and say: bring it here and prove it works.”

# Keep New Zealand Moving

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/keep-new-zealand-moving> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Infrastructure

## Keep New Zealand Moving

New Zealanders pay at the pump, through road-user charges, rates and tolls. They should see that money in reliable roads and shorter journeys. Instead, potholes go unfixed, new housing arrives before the roads needed to support it, and projects become slower and more expensive than they need to be.

ACT will put the basics first. We will build ahead of growth, maintain the network we already have, and stop transport money being diverted into vanity projects or procurement based on ethnicity. We will also stop unnecessary rules pricing families out of reliable vehicles.

New Zealand cannot unlock its potential while people and freight are stuck in traffic. ACT will build more, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver.

Read ACT’s full policy, Keep New Zealand Moving, here.

#### ACT will:

- Require major projects to publish the lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option, including the cost, delivery time and benefit-cost ratio of each.
- Build roads ahead of growth. On major two-lane growth corridors, 10,000 vehicles a day will trigger route protection, 15,000 will trigger consenting, design and a funded capacity plan, and 20,000 will trigger construction of additional lanes where growth continues.
- Require councils to repair potholes, drainage, and bridges before funding street redesigns, by protecting maintenance and renewal funding in the National Land Transport Fund so it cannot be raided for other projects.
- Make equal treatment a condition of Crown infrastructure funding. Ethnicity will not determine who can bid, how bids are scored, who receives preference or who must be subcontracted.
- Stop the National Land Transport Fund paying for non-functional art, monuments and decorative extras. Motorists’ money should build and maintain the transport network.
- Scrap unrealistic vehicle-emissions settings, oppose arbitrary age bans and require new rules to disclose their effect on vehicle supply and prices.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Infrastructure spokesperson Simon Court says:

"New Zealand does not need to accept deteriorating roads, unaffordable projects and congestion as the price of growth.

"The payoff for drivers and the public is more value from their every dollar with standard, proven designs and transparent published projects with their timelines.

"ACT will build more, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver, so New Zealand keeps moving."

# Keeping Children Safe

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/keeping-children-safe> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

###### Education

## Keeping Children Safe

Parents should be able to send their child to school, sport or a youth group knowing the adults in charge are safe to be there. The current system can leave three years between checks, even if worrying new Police information emerges in the meantime.

ACT will close that gap with one national card checked continuously. If someone is charged with a serious offence that could rule them out of working with children, their card can be suspended immediately. They must stop working with children while the case is assessed, and their employer will be told.

Read ACT’s full policy, Keeping Children Safe, here.

#### ACT will:

- Create one national card that paid workers and volunteers must have to be able to work with children. It will belong to them and last three years.
- Keep people convicted of specified serious offences against children out of covered roles.
- Keep checking cardholders against new Police information. If Police learn someone may be dangerous, their card can be suspended. That means they cannot keep working with children, and every linked organisation will be told.
- Give every cardholder practical child-protection training, refreshed when the card is renewed.
- Keep applications exempt or discounted for volunteers and students. Paid workers will pay about $108, which employers will often cover.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour says:

“Parents should be able to leave their children with a teacher, coach, afterschool carer, or volunteer knowing the adults around them are safe to work with children.

“The current system does not provide that reassurance. Safety checks are carried out by individual employers and generally only re-checked every three years. This provides only a snapshot of a person at one point in time, with no consistent system for identifying risks that emerge between checks.

“The Working with Children Card gives parents peace of mind about their child’s safety, and creates a smarter, less burdensome screening process for employers and workers.”

# Leave Spirituality out of Infrastructure

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/leave-spirituality-out-of-infrastructure> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Infrastructure

## Leave Spirituality out of Infrastructure

New Zealanders who put their own money into building homes and businesses deserve clear rules and respect for their property rights. Yet getting consent can mean paying for compulsory karakia or answering claims of spiritual harm. ACT will keep religion out of planning decisions, giving people greater freedom to build and invest in New Zealand’s future.

#### ACT will:

- Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from consenting. A belief or claim of spiritual harm could not, on its own, be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information or imposing conditions. The same rule would apply to every religion and belief system.
- Ban compulsory religious observances in consent conditions. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or pay for a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. People would remain free to do so voluntarily.
- Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes. Councils would work to clear, testable standards for water quality, ecosystem health and human health.

### In our team’s words:

ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson Simon Court says:

"None of this takes away protection for anything real. Heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation would all still be dealt with directly.

"The test is simple. Is there an identifiable physical effect, place, resource or legal right? If there is, deal with it. If the claimed effect exists only as a spiritual proposition, it isn't the planning system's job."

# Let Pharmacies Do More

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/let-pharmacies-do-more> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Health

## Let Pharmacies Do More

Someone with an ear infection should not have to wait a week to see a GP when a pharmacist can safely treat it.

One in four adults says the time taken to get an appointment was a barrier to seeing a GP. At the same time, New Zealand has more than a thousand community pharmacies staffed by qualified health professionals whose skills are not being fully used.

Pharmacists can already treat several common conditions. ACT would widen that list and set clear rules for when a patient needs to see a doctor.

#### ACT will:

- Let pharmacies treat more everyday conditions, including chest infections, ear infections, skin infections, acute pain, sore throats, tonsillitis, school sores, styes, gout, osteoarthritis, vaginal thrush and period pain, as well as provide STI self-swab testing.
- Allow accredited pharmacists to monitor stable hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol, and adjust medication within GP-set limits. Pharmacists could also order appropriate blood tests when requested or clinically necessary. GPs would retain overall clinical responsibility and visibility, with results recorded in the shared health record.
- Pilot pharmacy-based skin-lesion checks to help detect skin cancer sooner. Trained pharmacists would use dermatoscopes and an approved AI risk-assessment tool, with clear pathways for referral and monitoring.
- Remove barriers preventing new pharmacies from opening, including the five-pharmacy ownership cap and proximity restrictions, while cutting licensing red tape.
- Enable secure 24-hour prescription lockers so patients can collect eligible medicines when it suits them.

Read the full policy

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand is not short of medical expertise. The problem is access. GPs have long waiting lists, emergency departments are under pressure, and too many patients are stuck waiting for routine care.

“Pharmacists are trained health professionals, yet we still make them refer people back to a GP for conditions they could safely treat. If your pharmacist can sort it out, you should not have to join the GP queue.

“More than 120,000 people used the Minor Health Conditions Service pilot in 2023, and 88 per cent had their needs met at a pharmacy. We already know this model can work here.”

# Let the Kid on the Bus

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/let-the-kid-on-the-bus> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

###### Rural

## Let the Kid on the Bus

School transport rules are built around a child's nearest school. In rural communities, that can leave an empty seat passing a waiting child because their family chose a different school.

Parents then make the same trip in their own car or ute, spending time and fuel while a taxpayer-funded bus travels the route with room to spare.

ACT's Open Seat Rule would use that spare capacity. In most cases it would not require any extra spending. If demand fills a route, more buses could be funded from within the Ministry of Education's existing budget.

#### ACT will:

- Introduce an Open Seat Rule for school transport.
- Let any child living along an existing school bus route use the service when a seat is available, regardless of which school they attend.
- Provide an additional bus where demand on a route grows beyond its capacity.
- Fund any additional buses from within the Ministry of Education's existing budget by cutting waste.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT MP Andrew Hoggard says:

“In most cases this would not require any extra spending. If a route filled up, we would add buses and fund them from within the Ministry of Education’s existing budget by cutting waste. Money should get children to school, not be tied up in Wellington bureaucracy.

“The nearest-school rule does not reflect how rural communities live. Families choose schools based on where siblings go, the support available, and what works around jobs and farm life. They need flexibility, not hard-and-fast rules that leave children waiting and families paying for a second transport system.”

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“If a taxpayer-funded bus is already running with an empty seat, no child should be left on the roadside because of a Wellington rulebook. It is a small, common-sense change that saves families time and fuel while using the transport taxpayers have already paid for.”

# Local Tourism Dividend

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/local_tourism_dividend> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Infrastructure

## Local Tourism Dividend

Tourism supports businesses and jobs throughout New Zealand, but the communities that host visitors also carry the costs. Visitor numbers put pressure on local roads, wastewater systems, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, public spaces and other council infrastructure.

Visitors pay GST, and international visitors also pay the International Visitor Levy. Central government collects that revenue, while councils and their ratepayers meet many of the local costs. ACT’s Local Tourism Dividend will return $1 to a community for every commercial guest night it hosts.

The more visitors a community attracts, the more support it will receive. This applies the same principle ACT has secured for housing growth: when councils help enable economic activity that generates revenue for central government, they should share in the benefits.

ACT's full Local Tourism Dividend policy can be found here.

#### ACT will:

- Make an automatic annual payment to every territorial authority of $1 for each domestic and international commercial guest night recorded in its area through the Accommodation Data Programme.
- Base each payment on the most recently completed 12 months of guest-night data.
- Require no applications, matching funding or negotiations with central government.
- Provide approximately $40.6 million a year to councils based on 2026 guest nights, including $8.2 million for Auckland, $4.9 million for Queenstown and $2 million for Rotorua.
- Give councils flexibility to fund local roads, parking, water and wastewater infrastructure, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, public spaces, visitor amenities, events infrastructure and other services affected by visitor demand.
- Allow the Dividend to replace rates funding already being spent on eligible services, reducing the burden on local ratepayers.
- Fund the Dividend from the existing tourism appropriation instead of imposing a new bed tax that would raise prices and create more bureaucracy for accommodation businesses.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Councils will receive $1 for every guest night in their area, funded from the GST and visitor levies tourists already pay.

“If revenues allow and councils use funds wisely, the $1 rate may rise over time. This policy fixes a real problem without adding another charge to the hotel bill or expanding government,” says Mr Seymour.

“Households and businesses live within their means. Government should too. New taxes start small and tend to grow - this policy avoids that trap and keeps prices competitive for visitors.

“New Zealand is a top tourist destination but that success causes strains on local infrastructure. Ratepayers are too often left to pick up the bill. ACT’s Local Tourism Dividend gives councils the funding to keep pace, easing pressure on wastewater, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, and other services.
