# Make Farming Fun Again

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/make-farming-fun-again> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Rural

## Make Farming Fun Again

A strong payout is welcome. What matters is what’s left after the bills are paid. Farming should offer the chance to get ahead and build a future for your family.

ACT will drive down farming costs and give farmers more freedom to farm. We’ll keep agricultural emissions untaxed and remove costly resource consents for routine work that meets clear standards.

ACT has already eased winter grazing rules and kept agriculture outside the ETS. Party Vote ACT to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand’s potential, and give the next generation the freedom to farm.

Read ACT’s full plan to Make Farming Fun Again here.

### ACT will:

#### Drive down farming costs

- Keep agricultural emissions untaxed. Keep agriculture permanently out of the Emissions Trading Scheme and oppose any agricultural emissions tax or pricing scheme.
- Cut the carbon tax driving up the price of fuel and other farm inputs.
- Remove resource consent costs for routine farm work that meets clear national standards.
- Let farmers change what they farm without needing a resource consent where the change is consistent with National Standards.
- Make councils pay fair compensation when they restrict private land through overlays such as Significant Natural Areas or Outstanding Natural Landscapes. Protect farmers from a return to Labour-style Significant Natural Areas rules.
- Cut government waste and balance the books without new taxes. Return to surplus faster and pay down debt, helping ease pressure on inflation and interest rates. Keep the Reserve Bank focused on controlling inflation.

#### Give farmers the tools to grow

- Speed up access to proven agricultural chemicals and veterinary medicines by recognising trusted overseas approvals, reducing regulatory costs and improving access to competing products.
- Remove unnecessary restrictions on agricultural drones and other technology that can improve productivity and reduce operating costs.
- Introduce a Rural Workforce Visa and keep employment settings that make it easier for farms and rural businesses to recruit and employ staff.
- Cut red tape around homekill and make it easier for farmers to sell their products directly to consumers.
- Respect farmer-owned companies’ right to make commercial decisions without political interference.

#### Back rural families and communities

- Fund 100,000 additional rural Police patrol hours each year and establish a dedicated rural crime unit.
- Strengthen offences and penalties for livestock theft and poaching. Introduce Three Strikes for Burglary, with a minimum three-year prison sentence without parole on a third conviction.
- Increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, so farmers are less likely to be left with someone else’s clean-up bill.
- Allow rural children to use spare seats on existing school buses going to nearby schools wherever practical.
- Keep Agricultural and Horticultural Science as a standalone Year 11 subject.
- Strengthen vocational pathways into careers such as agriculture and horticulture.
- Expand everyday healthcare through pharmacies, including management of stable long-term conditions. Enable 24-hour prescription e-lockers, reducing travel and time away from the farm.
- Extend Text 111 eligibility to rural areas with unreliable voice coverage.

#### Back practical environmental work

- Commit to long-term funding to eradicate wilding pines, and direct DOC to coordinate pest control across public and private land, reducing the burden on individual farmers.
- Make permanent forest owners carry their forests’ long-term costs and risks, including sufficient pest control.
- Allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land to control weeds and fire risk.
- Redirect $4.5 million a year within MPI to keep catchment-group funding at $13.5 million, allowing further funding where groups demonstrate strong water-quality results.
- Expand voluntary conservation through biodiversity credits and the QEII National Trust.

#### Set clear rules farmers can work with

- Put property rights first in the national rules under the new RMA laws. Focus on measurable environmental harm and local conditions, developing standards with farmers, growers and councils.
- Introduce at least ten new permitted activity standards covering farm plans, vegetable growing, on-farm water storage, gravel extraction, drain maintenance, effluent management, fertiliser application, farm quarries, wetland restoration, and small- and medium-scale solar. Activities meeting those standards won’t need a resource consent.
- Keep freshwater farm plans practical and affordable, with clear rules focused on actual environmental harm and local conditions.
- Require councils to use a science-based national method for setting freshwater limits, reflecting differences between catchments. Remove Te Mana o te Wai and other vague spiritual concepts, and prevent their return under another name.
- Strengthen property rights through the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
- Review the Sharemilking Agreements Act so it reflects how farming businesses operate today.

#### End costly climate policy

- Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and end the Net Zero target.
- Abolish the Climate Change Commission.
- Remove the artificial ETS price floor encouraging blanket carbon farming.
- Recognise methane’s different warming effect from carbon dioxide.
- Prevent international climate commitments imposing costs overseas competitors avoid. Reconsider the Paris Agreement if New Zealand cannot secure a fair deal.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Agriculture Spokesperson Andrew Hoggard says:

“There’s nothing fun about paperwork, especially when it’s pointless, yet farmers have been hit with endless new rules and freshwater regulations, Significant Natural Areas [SNAs], winter grazing, emissions pricing, the ute tax, firearms changes, health and safety paperwork, and resource management red tape. Successive governments piled on the rules, adding costs and uncertainty to running a farm.

“Farmers do not need another politician telling them how to farm. They need a Government that respects property rights, sets clear rules around genuine environmental harm, and otherwise lets them get on with it.”

# ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life

*ACT New Zealand press release, 28 June 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-announces-policy-to-make-benefits-a-hand-up-not-a-way-of-life> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Sunday, 28 June 2026

## ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life

#### ACT Leader David Seymour today announced new welfare policy to restore fairness, personal responsibility, and the value of work to New Zealand’s benefit system

David Seymour

ACT today announced new welfare policy to restore fairness, personal responsibility, and the value of work to New Zealand’s benefit system.

“Welfare should unlock potential, not trap it. So why are we paying people to stay at home who could be doing jobs we are currently filling with migrants?" says ACT Leader Seymour.

“New Zealanders believe in helping people through tough times. But the deal has to be fair: if you can work, you should be taking real steps toward work, and taxpayer support should go to the essentials it was intended to fund.

“Under Labour, benefit dependency became normalised. The number of people on Jobseeker benefits has increased 73% in the past ten years. Jobseeker benefits alone now cost more than we spending on policing, and twice as much as the medicines budget.

“Behind those numbers are real people whose potential is being wasted. Every person who could work but is left on welfare is a life held back, a family with fewer opportunities, and a country that is poorer than it needs to be.”

ACT’s policy has two planks:

##### Tightening medical certification for health-related benefits

- All health and disability benefits will be independently issued by an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors.* A person’s usual GP or specialist will still be able to provide medical history, clinical notes, and supporting evidence.
- Assessments will be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion.
- Existing Jobseeker Support – Health Condition or Disability and Supported Living Payment recipients will be reassessed against the new criteria on a phased basis.
- Reassessment will begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic, where much of the recent growth has occurred.
- ACT will allow for long-term arrangements for those with a genuine, enduring disability or health condition so support stays in place for those who truly need it.

\*The Government has already established this as an option, but ACT will make it mandatory.

##### Managed assistance for long-term Jobseeker recipients

- ACT will introduce electronic money management for Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients who remain on a benefit for more than four months.*
- Their benefit will be delivered through an electronic payment card directed to essentials such as groceries, rent, power, transport, health and childcare.
- The card will block spending on alcohol, gambling, tobacco, and cash withdrawals.
- ACT will include carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.

\*New Zealand already has money management as an option in certain circumstances, but ACT will make it mandatory after the four-month threshold.

“Health-related welfare is one of the fastest-growing pressure points in the system. In ten years the number of New Zealanders on a health or disability Jobseeker benefit has nearly doubled, to 96,852. Another 96,000 are on the Supported Living Payment. Most of the growth is from new claims for psychological or psychiatric conditions

“Supported Living Payment recipients remain on benefit for an average of 13.3 years, while Jobseeker Health Condition or Disability recipients remain on benefit for an average of 6.1 years.

“Nobody should be denied support when they genuinely cannot work. But the public deserves confidence that the system is not being gamed, and that people are not being written off when work or greater independence is possible.

“Electronic money management means taxpayer support will not fund purchases that make it harder for people to get their lives back on track. If someone is receiving a benefit funded by working New Zealanders, that support should go to food, housing, power, transport, health, and childcare – not alcohol, gambling, or tobacco.

“Unlocking New Zealand’s potential means unlocking the potential of New Zealanders. That starts with a welfare system that backs people to move forward, rewards effort, protects taxpayers, and refuses to write people off."

###### Press Release

Tuesday, 8 September 2026

## ACT sets the No New Taxes agenda

#### “ACT is chalking up a taxpayer victory, after the National Party has adopted a version of our local tourism dividend," says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“ACT is chalking up a taxpayer victory, after the National Party has adopted a version of our local tourism dividend," says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“About two weeks after ACT pledged No New Taxes, the National Party followed suit. A few days later we announced a Local Tourism Dividend policy as an alternative to a Bed Tax, National has adopted a version of that policy as well.

"ACT is proud to have shaped the debate on this issue, when so many parties wanted to introduce a new tax, there is now a clear pathway to solve the same problem without a new tax.

“This is good news for the next Government, should we be re-elected. It is also another example of the value of ACT. We hold the line against new taxes, then come up with a better solution.

“As I said while announcing the policy, if revenues allow and councils use funds wisely, the $1 rate may rise over time. This policy fixes a real problem without adding another charge to the hotel bill or expanding government.

“It is a smarter alternative to a bed tax because it doesn’t impose a compliance burden on businesses, there is no new charge on the hotel bill, no new tax administration, and no legislation required to establish another tax. It uses the existing $185 billion revenue of the Government and Councils, rather than making the Government bigger.

"If there is a cut-and-dried case of the difference the ACT Party makes, it is the absence of a bed tax, a bank tax and the stamp duty on houses National would have put in place given the chance.

“Without ACT around the Cabinet table holding firm on No New Taxes, New Zealanders would already be paying more.

"ACT Ministers have driven $14 billion of savings across three Budgets, helping avoid more debt, taxes, and pressure on interest rates. That discipline has helped put the Government on a path back to surplus a year earlier, but it needs to be delivered year on year.

"A party vote for ACT is a steadfast anchor against the pressure for higher taxes and bigger government. This won’t be the last time the fiscal pressure comes on and our friends are tempted to eat the tax apple from the wrong tree. To balance the books with No New Taxes, Party Vote ACT in 2026."

# ACT supporting local tourism, not new taxes

*ACT New Zealand press release, 14 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-supporting-local-tourism-not-new-taxes> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Friday, 14 August 2026

## ACT supporting local tourism, not new taxes

#### ACT is announcing a Local Tourism Dividend to support visitor communities without introducing a new bed tax.

David Seymour

ACT is announcing a Local Tourism Dividend to support visitor communities without introducing a new bed tax.

“Councils will receive $1 for every guest night in their area, funded from the GST and visitor levies tourists already pay,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“If revenues allow and councils use funds wisely, the $1 rate may rise over time. This policy fixes a real problem without adding another charge to the hotel bill or expanding government,” says Mr Seymour.

“Households and businesses live within their means. Government should too. New taxes start small and tend to grow - this policy avoids that trap and keeps prices competitive for visitors.

“New Zealand is a top tourist destination but that success causes strains on local infrastructure. Ratepayers are too often left to pick up the bill. ACT’s Local Tourism Dividend gives councils the funding to keep pace, easing pressure on wastewater, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, and other services.

“This is a much smarter alternative to a bed tax for at least five reasons:

- No compliance burden: accommodation providers do not have to calculate, collect, file and pay a new tax.
- There is no tax administration, just an annual transfer to councils based on verified bed nights (already known) multiplied by one dollar, and IRD will not need to employ people to collect a new tax.
- Due to its simplicity, it can be implemented as soon as the next budget and start as early as July 1 next year. A new tax would take at least a year longer because it requires legislation.
- It will not raise the cost of staying in New Zealand, discouraging people from visiting the country, or reduce the revenue of accommodation providers.
- It makes use of the existing $185 billion revenue of the New Zealand Government and Councils, rather than increasing the overall size of Government in New Zealand with a new tax.

“This policy also builds on ACT’s GST-sharing model implemented this term that rewards growth and now applies to tourism.

“The Local Tourism Dividend gives visitors a fairer deal without a new tax. If a council attracts more visitors, it gets more funding - simple, fair, and fast."

# ACT: Time to end voting rights for unelected council appointees

*ACT New Zealand press release, 11 September 2025. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-time-to-end-voting-rights-for-unelected-council-appointees> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Thursday, 11 September 2025

## ACT: Time to end voting rights for unelected council appointees

#### ACT is campaigning to stop unelected appointees from holding voting rights on local council committees.

Cameron Luxton

ACT Local – the Party’s local government ticket – released its Democracy policy in Wellington today, which includes a commitment to oppose voting rights for unelected appointees.

Meanwhile, ACT’s spokesperson for Local Government, Cameron Luxton, has written to the Minister for Local Government and drafted an amendment to the Local Government Act that would give effect to this stance at a national level.

“With rates climbing and households squeezed, the people deciding how to spend ratepayers’ money ought to be held accountable. But right now, we’ve got councils appointing unelected people to committees with full voting rights," says Mr Luxton.

“These members are often appointed by mana whenua, but we’ve also seen Hastings District Council give voting rights to unelected youth councillors, and LGNZ's council rules template suggests all sorts of ‘experts’ and representatives could be appointed alongside councillors.

“These appointees never face the voters, but their decisions have a direct impact on household budgets. That undermines democracy and it undermines trust.

“ACT has no problem with councils bringing in outsiders to provide advice. But the power to vote should belong with elected representatives, not people handpicked behind closed doors. If you want a vote at the council table, you can stand in an election and make your case to voters like anyone else.

“ACT’s coalition agreement has restored communities’ right to vote on Māori wards. But some councils may be tempted to counter a public vote against Māori wards by turning around and appointing unelected representatives anyway, along the lines of Auckland Council’s Independent Māori Statutory Board. Meanwhile, we’ve seen cases, such as in Tauranga and Wellington, where both Māori ward councillors and unelected mana whenua appointees sit across the same table.

“Ratepayers are struggling under rising bills. The only real accountability mechanism they have is the ballot box. If you’re paying the bills, you should be able to choose who’s spending your money.

“My hope is that ACT’s proposal to end voting rights for unelected appointees will be adopted as an amendment to the Local Government Act. But local councils could just implement this change themselves. New Zealanders now have a chance to vote for ACT Local council candidates who will work to end voting rights for unelected appointees.

“ACT Local councillors will also oppose Māori wards, co-governance, progressive procurement, and race-based spending and consultation.”

#### ACT Local's Democracy Policy: Equal Rights. Equal Say.

Local issues of rates and roads can be addressed without dividing the community by race.

Equality before the law and local democracy are critically important. ACT Local candidates believe all New Zealanders are alike in dignity, and political rights should not depend on who your great-grandparents were.

Local government should reflect these democratic values and treat all citizens equally, including by ensuring only those elected by the public should have the power to make decisions on their behalf.

ACT councillors will:

- Oppose Māori wards that give voters different political rights depending on race.
- Oppose co-governance arrangements, such as joint-management agreements, that hand decision-making powers to unelected iwi.
- Oppose race-based services, funding, jobs, and consultation rights: council decisions based on need, merit, or value, not identity.
- End progressive procurement policies that award contracts based on who someone’s ancestors were, rather than who can deliver the best service at the best price for ratepayers.
- Oppose unelected decision-makers. Only publicly elected representatives should have the right to vote or be paid for decision-making roles on councils, committees, or subcommittees that spend ratepayer money or determine policy. That means: No unelected iwi representatives with decision-making power. No unelected youth councillors or under-16s sitting on council committees, as attempted by Hastings District Council. No other unelected appointees from business, environmental, or community groups with voting rights.

On unelected decision-makers:

These groups are welcome and encouraged to participate through submissions – just like everyone else. Unless they’re putting up the money, they shouldn’t decide how it’s spent.

The principle is simple: if someone spends ratepayer money or restricts how people use their property or live their lives, they should be someone voters can kick out.

Nothing in this policy would prevent the council from appointing suitably qualified individuals to the board of Council Controlled Organisations, where they bring professional expertise, clear accountability, and protection against politicisation that councillors themselves should avoid.

# ACT to abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes

*ACT New Zealand press release, 14 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-to-abolish-another-of-labour-s-renters-taxes> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Wednesday, 14 October 2026

## ACT to abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes

#### “ACT is campaigning to reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by abolishing loss ring-fencing for rental properties,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“ACT is campaigning to reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by abolishing loss ring-fencing for rental properties,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Median weekly rents rose by $180 during Labour’s time in government. Labour claimed it was helping renters, then made it more expensive to provide the homes they live in.

“There’s no such thing as a tax on landlords that renters can safely ignore. When Labour made rental housing more expensive to provide, tenants faced the consequences through pressure on rents, fewer homes, less choice, and poorer quality.

“ACT will allow residential rental losses incurred from the day the policy takes effect to be offset against other taxable income. This will apply to existing homes and new builds. Losses already ring-fenced will remain subject to the existing rules.

“If you’re a sole trader or make other investments, such as commercial property, your losses can be offset against your personal income. ACT’s proposal levels the playing field and ensures treatment is consistent.

“Labour’s policy meant legitimate losses could not be offset when cashflow is tightest, forcing landlords to wait until a property became profitable – when cashflow relief is needed least. If cashflow is tight, it’s much harder to carry out essential repairs if the tax deduction is delayed for years.

“The only way to secure more affordable housing for renters is to build more homes and reduce the costs that get passed through to renters.

“Removing ring-fencing will improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes. Alongside ACT’s resource management reforms and opening up access to new building materials, it will encourage supply and give renters more choice.

“Expect the usual cries of ‘tax cuts for landlords’. Labour played the same cynical game when the Government restored mortgage interest deductibility, yet with ACT in Government and rents flatlining, it's renters who have reaped the benefits. Nearly three years on, Labour has come to its senses and decided not to reverse ACT’s change.

“Our policy brings tax relief forward for losses that would eventually be deducted under the current rules. It doesn’t increase the total deduction. But some losses may never be used, and earlier deductions reduce government revenue in the meantime. So, we can’t say the policy has no fiscal cost.

“We estimated the cost by reversing the impact of the rules when the Government introduced them, consistent with Treasury’s approach.

“The policy is forecast to reduce government revenue by $264 million in year one, rising to $303 million in year four, and is accounted for in ACT’s fully-costed fiscal plan.”

# ACT to campaign on making Student Services Fees voluntary

*ACT New Zealand press release, 10 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-to-campaign-on-making-student-services-fees-voluntary> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Monday, 10 August 2026

## ACT to campaign on making Student Services Fees voluntary

#### ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.

Parmjeet Parmar

ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.

“Every domestic university student currently pays a compulsory Student Services Fee of up to $1,253 a year on top of tuition. Across a three-year degree this can add more than $4,000 to a student’s loan*. Because student loans are subsidised by the taxpayer, the compulsory fee also costs the taxpayer," says ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar.

“In 2011 ACT passed Voluntary Student Membership. As a result, students are no longer forced to join a student union. But universities have undermined the spirit of Voluntary Student Membership by absorbing the old association fee into a compulsory levy that students still cannot refuse. So, true freedom of association remains unfinished business.

“ACT will amend the regulations so universities must offer student services as a menu. Students would select the services they want and pay only for those, from fitness facilities to students unions and student media. Services not chosen would still be available on a transparent user-pays basis.

“Students should not be forced to fund unions, advocacy or student media they do not support. That is a matter of principle for ACT.

“Right now, student unions are running political campaigns to influence the election. They might even campaign to stop this policy. Students are forced to fund this activism, even if they disagree with it. ACT says unions are free to campaign, but no-one should be forced to fund them.

“Voluntary fees mean better-run services. If a union or any other university service struggles to attract willing subscribers, it can do what any other organisation or business does – improve its offering, or scale back its spending.

“ACT's policy will also restore the independence of unions to challenge university leadership. Unions are meant to hold the bosses to account, but there's a huge conflict of interest when they're dependent on the university for funding.

“Our policy would let students save up to around $4,000 on their student loan over the course of a degree. It would also save the taxpayer money, because student debt is subsidised. We will complete the unfinished business of Voluntary Student Membership and restore genuine choice.”

Editor's note:

\*After annual increases to the fee.

# ACT unveils plan for New Zealand’s first dedicated Cancer centre - Beyond Tomorrow

*ACT New Zealand press release, 21 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-unveils-plan-for-new-zealands-first-dedicated-cancer-centre---beyond-tomorrow> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Friday, 21 August 2026

## ACT unveils plan for New Zealand’s first dedicated Cancer centre - Beyond Tomorrow

#### “ACT will build New Zealand’s Starship for Cancer, the country’s first purpose-built comprehensive cancer centre, with two campuses in Auckland and Christchurch,” says ACT List Candidate Paul Henry.

Paul Henry

“ACT will build New Zealand’s Starship for Cancer, the country’s first purpose-built comprehensive cancer centre, with two campuses in Auckland and Christchurch,” says ACT List Candidate Paul Henry.

“Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year, by 2044 that number is expected to exceed 45,000.

“I’ve joined politics because I am ambitious for New Zealand and think it has endless potential. We should not accept being second-rate at treating a disease that touches almost every family.

“Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

“This is an aspirational policy, but it is realistic and practical. Comprehensive cancer centres are the gold standard internationally because they bring researchers, clinicians, universities, private providers and philanthropists together with world-class treatment, technology and clinical trials. They also help attract and retain the best oncologists, surgeons and scientists. If New Zealand cannot offer that environment, Australia and other countries will.

“The centres will be developed using a combination of public-private partnership financing, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment, and other private capital where appropriate. The indicative capital requirement is around $2 billion, with the final cost determined through the detailed business-case process.

“By partnering with New Zealand’s leading philanthropists, families, businesses, charitable trusts, community organisations and successful Kiwis, we can build something extraordinary.

“ACT will establish an independent philanthropic foundation from the beginning of the project to unlock extraordinary generosity, with major donors recognised through naming rights for appropriate parts of the Centres, including, for a transformational contribution, potentially a hospital itself.

“The recently introduced $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations will be removed for all charitable giving. If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity, not impose an arbitrary ceiling on it.

“This is an investment in New Zealand’s future. It is the type of project that makes New Zealand the envy of the world and attracts private healthcare investment, new technologies and therapies, teaching, medical research, and international clinical trials.

“New Zealand can build one of the world’s great cancer institutions. ACT will make it happen.”

# ACT unveils plan for radically simpler, smaller government

*ACT New Zealand press release, 28 June 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-unveils-plan-for-radically-simpler-smaller-government> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Sunday, 28 June 2026

## ACT unveils plan for radically simpler, smaller government

#### “New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential,” says ACT Leader Seymour.

David Seymour

“Making New Zealand affordable again must start at the top," says ACT Leader Seymour, announcing ACT's plan for a simpler, smaller government at the Party's 2026 Rally.

“New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential," says Mr Seymour.

“Today ACT is setting out the next level of detail in our policy with fewer departments, fewer ministers, and clear lines of accountability so taxpayers pay less and get better services.

“New Zealand has 78 ministerial portfolios, 28 ministers, and 43 departments. Norway has a similar population and runs with 20 ministers across 17 ministries. New Zealand’s oversized Government isn’t intentional, it’s like a hedge that stopped being trimmed years ago.

“The result is a Government that is too tangled to act. Housing, infrastructure, welfare dependency, crime, and health all cut across multiple agencies. When seven departments share a problem, it can stop being anyone’s job to solve it. Kiwis are left frustrated, bouncing between departments or denied straight answers.

“Sprawling, tangled bureaucracy is expensive. It costs money that can’t be returned to taxpayers, can’t pay down debt, can’t reach the nurse, teacher or police officer on the frontline, and can’t build the infrastructure we need.”

Under ACT’s plan:

• The 43 departments would be consolidated into 19 coherent departments.

• The 78 overlapping portfolios with 28 ministers would be collapsed into just 18 ministers.

• Each department would report to one minister for its budget and outcomes.*

• Ministers would be allowed to appoint chief executives for a fixed term, renewable once, with clear protections for officials.

• Chief executives could be removed by Ministers for specified reasons such as non-performance or policy misalignment, but they would retain public service protections and the right to return to a lower classified role.

• Operational independence would be protected by law for agencies that need it, such as Police, NZSIS, and NZDF.

ACT’s full proposal, ' ACT’s plan for a consolidated bureaucracy', can be found here.

“Overseas research shows more ministers with spending power means bigger deficits. When many ministers each control part of the budget, but the cost falls on the whole tax base, each has an incentive to grow their own spending while bearing only a fraction of the cost.

“ACT’s plan won’t affect frontline services like nurses, teachers, or police. If anything, it will make them more effective with clear lines of responsibility and a focus on their core role.

“The Coalition Government has accepted the argument for a smaller Government, but current changes are tinkering around the edges. Kiwis are tired of piecemeal change that takes forever, so ACT is proposing a thought-out plan for the whole government, that we can start rolling out immediately in the next term.

“ACT would also fix the broken accountability line between ministers and departmental chief executives. At the moment, ministers are held responsible for delivery, but they do not appoint the person leading the department responsible for that delivery. ACT would remove the Public Service Commission and allow ministers to appoint chief executives, and chief executives could be removed for specified reasons.

“That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential. A government with clear structure and limits, not the tangled result of accidental growth. Small enough to be accountable, simple enough to act, and focused on results for New Zealanders instead of managing itself.”

\*Except for the newly-created MCERT.

# ACT will introduce smarter screening to improve child safety

*ACT New Zealand press release, 18 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-introduce-smarter-screening-to-improve-child-safety> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Tuesday, 18 August 2026

## ACT will introduce smarter screening to improve child safety

#### ACT will campaign on introducing the Working with Children Card, a streamlined system for ensuring that any person who works with children has been properly vetted and is checked continuously for safety, says ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour.

Karen Chhour

ACT will campaign on introducing the Working with Children Card, a streamlined system for ensuring that any person who works with children has been properly vetted and is checked continuously for safety, says ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour.

“Parents should be able to leave their children with a teacher, coach, afterschool carer, or volunteer knowing the adults around them are safe to work with children.

“The current system does not provide that reassurance. Safety checks are carried out by individual employers and generally only re-checked every three years. This provides only a snapshot of a person at one point in time, with no consistent system for identifying risks that emerge between checks.

“The Working with Children Card would give parents confidence that their children are in safe hands. It follows the worker, is continuously monitored, considers additional relevant information, and replaces duplicated screening by individual organisations.

“Eligibility for the card will take into account relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings, and other records relating to children or child-related work.

“People who work with children have to undergo the same checks every time they start or change jobs. ACT’s plan would cut out the duplication and bureaucracy. Once issued, the card could be used across eligible jobs, schools, clubs, businesses, and community organisations. Employers would simply verify that the person holds a valid card.

“Placing the ownership with the individual rather than the employer will free up police and Ministry of Justice resources, and make it easier for small organisations to meet their child-safety responsibilities.

“The system ensures that cardholders are safe the whole time they work with children, not just up until a check was last completed.

“ACT will link the Working with Children Card to ongoing information from Police and relevant regulatory bodies, keeping it continuously up to date. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked and their employer notified. Employers would no longer have to wait for the next three-year check to discover that a worker’s circumstances have changed.

"It can take three years for a person's offending to be reported to their employer. In Queensland they update continuously with a similar system called the Blue Card. Last year they cancelled 2,438 people's Blue Cards due to up-to-the-minute information. In New Zealand those people would still be working with children.

“The Working with Children Card gives parents peace of mind about their child’s safety, and creates a smarter, less burdensome screening process for employers and workers.”

Note to editor: ACT's full policy, Keeping Children Safe, can be found here.

# ACT will invest $400 million to get Kiwis more GP appointments

*ACT New Zealand press release, 18 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-invest-400-million-to-get-kiwis-more-gp-appointments> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Sunday, 18 October 2026

## ACT will invest $400 million to get Kiwis more GP appointments

#### “ACT will invest an additional $400 million in general practice over four years to keep doctors in New Zealand, attract more from overseas, and deliver more GP appointments,” says ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas.

James Christmas

“ACT will invest an additional $400 million in general practice over four years to keep doctors in New Zealand, attract more from overseas, and deliver more GP appointments,” says ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas.

“Too many New Zealanders can’t get a GP appointment when they need one. In 2024/25, one in four adults and one in five children missed a GP visit because the wait was too long. That means parents worrying about sick children, people putting off treatment, and patients ending up in emergency departments unnecessarily.

“Labour’s policy to hand out three taxpayer-funded GP visits each year for the worried well will only make things worse. There’s no point promising more free appointments if there aren’t enough doctors to provide them.

“Rather than subsidising demand, ACT will increase the supply of appointments by keeping the doctors we’ve got, helping them see more patients, and attracting more from overseas.

1. Keep GPs working and in New Zealand

“The easiest doctor to recruit is the one you don’t lose. With 35 per cent of GPs intending to retire within five years and 18 per cent considering moving overseas, we need to make it more attractive for them to stay.

“ACT’s funding will help practices offer competitive remuneration, retain experienced staff, and encourage doctors to remain in practice rather than retire early or move overseas.

2. Help GPs see more patients

“We don’t have to wait for a new generation of doctors to graduate. We can make better use of the workforce we already have.

“GPs work an average of 33.9 hours a week, down from 36.4 a decade ago, while nearly one in ten works 19 hours or fewer. Restoring average hours to previous levels would be equivalent to hundreds of additional full-time doctors, without recruiting a single new GP.

“Not every GP can or wants to work more hours. But better funding could help practices offer extra hours, reward additional appointments, and encourage experienced doctors to keep working longer.

3. Attract qualified doctors from overseas

“We cannot afford to turn away qualified doctors because of unnecessary red tape. Work is already underway to streamline registration for overseas-trained medical professionals, including new fast-track pathways for qualified GPs.

“ACT will build on that progress by reforming and streamlining medical regulators to focus on getting safe, competent professionals into the health system, rather than putting unnecessary obstacles in their way.

“Unlocking New Zealand's potential means making sure poor health doesn't hold people back. Combined with ACT’s plans to close the medicines gap with Australia, introduce Pharmacy First, and establish a world-class cancer centre, ACT has the most credible and comprehensive plan to improve healthcare for New Zealanders.”

The funding will be an ongoing $100 million annual boost to general practice, on top of normal capitation increases, totalling $400 million over the first four years.

# ACT will make farming fun again

*ACT New Zealand press release, 20 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-make-farming-fun-again> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Sunday, 20 September 2026

## ACT will make farming fun again

#### “I’m launching ACT’s campaign to Make Farming Fun Again, because I’ve spent more than 20 years farming and have seen first-hand what happens when people in Wellington, who don’t understand farming, try to regulate every part of it,” says ACT Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

Andrew Hoggard

“I’m launching ACT’s campaign to Make Farming Fun Again, because I’ve spent more than 20 years farming and have seen first-hand what happens when people in Wellington, who don’t understand farming, try to regulate every part of it,” says ACT Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“There’s nothing fun about paperwork, especially when it’s pointless, yet farmers have been hit with endless new rules and freshwater regulations, Significant Natural Areas [SNAs], winter grazing, emissions pricing, the ute tax, firearms changes, health and safety paperwork, and resource management red tape. Successive governments piled on the rules, adding costs and uncertainty to running a farm.

“Farmers are exposed to risk that not many other industries are. In Wellington if there’s a heavy hail storm the bureaucrats work from home, on the farm it could mean you lose a crop and face huge losses.

“We can’t control the weather or foreign commodity prices, but we can stop the Government from causing headaches through pointless rules and red tape. That’s why I joined ACT and ran for Parliament.

“I want my daughters, if they choose farming, to have the freedom to farm well without the red tape I’ve faced for 20 years. As ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson, I cut unworkable winter grazing rules, kept farming out of the ETS by scrapping He Waka Eke Noa, halved Labour’s methane target, and killed the ute tax. We’ve simplified freshwater farm plans, put $79m into wilding pine control, restored 90-day trials, restored common sense to firearms laws, and brought common sense back to health and safety.

“Farmers do not need another politician telling them how to farm. They need a Government that respects property rights, sets clear rules around genuine environmental harm, and otherwise lets them get on with it.”

ACT has six pledges to make farming fun again:

1. Keep Wellington out of farming. Replacing the RMA is one of the biggest wins for rural New Zealand in decades. The next decisions are key for how well the new system works in practice. ACT will fight for National Policy Direction and National Standards that are clear, practical, locally responsive, and grounded in property rights.

2. Focus on practical environmentalism. Farmers have the incentives to look after their natural environment, because they depend on it for their livelihood. ACT will scrap Te Mana o te Wai and increase funding for rural catchment groups, allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land, and carry on the war against wilding pines.

3. Keep backing farmers on climate. ACT is the only party that has never supported introducing a price on agricultural emissions. We stood alone against the Zero Carbon Act, opposed He Waka Eke Noa and successfully fought to keep agriculture out of the ETS. We will keep it that way. No other party can say this. We’ll also scrap the climate policy that adds nothing but costs to our economy, like the Net Zero target, the Climate Change Commission and the Zero Carbon Act.

4. Give farmers the tools. New Zealand farmers have always been early adopters of technology, often in spite of, not because of, the government. ACT will continue to cut red tape to make agri-innovation easier.

5. Protect rural communities. We’ll crack down on rural crime with 100,000 extra police patrol hours, harsher penalties for burglary via three strikes, an Open Seat rule so rural children can always catch the bus, and improve access to healthcare by giving pharmacists more tools to treat common ailments.

6. Grow the economy. Farmers make long-term decisions about land, stock, machinery and staff. They need stable prices, lower interest rates and confidence that Government will live within its means and stay out of commercial decisions it has no business making. No other party is prepared to make the savings in Wellington that will balance the books faster than ACT, with no new taxes.

"I’m proud of ACT’s record standing up for rural New Zealand," says ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee.

“When no other party would, we were there giving farmers a voice. Whether it was standing up for licensed firearms owners or opposing the Zero Carbon Act. Now that we’re in Government we’ve been able to make progress in fixing these issues.

"Party vote ACT to unlock the potential of rural New Zealand.”

# ACT will protect the peace, crack down on noisy vehicles

*ACT New Zealand press release, 26 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-protect-the-peace-crack-down-on-noisy-vehicles> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Saturday, 26 September 2026

## ACT will protect the peace, crack down on noisy vehicles

#### “ACT will crack down on noisy vehicles and increase penalties for drivers being a nuisance to neighbourhoods,” says ACT Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas.

James Christmas

“ACT will crack down on noisy vehicles and increase penalties for drivers being a nuisance to neighbourhoods,” says ACT Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas.

“I’ve knocked on thousands of doors in recent months and have heard you loud and clear in Tāmaki: you want to turn down the volume. People should be able to sleep, relax and enjoy their homes without having their street turned into someone else’s racetrack.

“I can see the attraction for boy racers to come to Tāmaki, but it’s not fair on the families and working people who have their life disrupted just because they live in a great location in a beautiful part of Auckland.

“These kinds of disturbances are already illegal, but effective enforcement can depend on a Police officer happening to be in the right place at the right time. By the time a person makes a complaint and an officer shows up on the scene, the vehicle is normally long gone.

“Technology can solve that problem, and ACT will make it happen by:

1. Introducing noise cameras. ACT will establish a fleet of relocatable noise cameras that can be deployed in communities suffering persistent problems with excessively noisy vehicles.

2. Establishing an objective and enforceable noise standard. The current law relies on a largely subjective test, which is difficult to enforce automatically. ACT will introduce a clear roadside noise limit that approved noise cameras can measure.

3. For those who want to pump up the volume, we are going to pump up the penalty. ACT will increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise by ensuring it is treated consistently, regardless of whether the noise comes from equipment inside the vehicle or from the vehicle’s engine or exhaust, and is punished appropriately.

“Hard working Kiwis shouldn't be harassed and inconvenienced by people who can’t take personal responsibility for their noise. Noise cameras enable evidence of offending to be collected the moment the offence occurs.

“Pairing technology with clear standards and real consequences will give residents the peace and quiet they deserve and ensure the comfort of many isn’t sacrificed for the noise of a few.”

ACT's full policy document can be found here.

# ACT will remove the cap on generosity

*ACT New Zealand press release, 7 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-remove-the-cap-on-generosity> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

###### Press Release

Wednesday, 7 October 2026

## ACT will remove the cap on generosity

#### “If New Zealanders want to give to a good cause they should be encouraged to do so. ACT’s Fiscal Plan, released on Sunday, will do away with the $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“If New Zealanders want to give to a good cause they should be encouraged to do so. ACT’s Fiscal Plan, released on Sunday, will do away with the $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“A small number of generous donors have changed lives for an enormous number of Kiwis. Their generosity should be welcomed, not punished.

“Just look at the good these donations bring about. In Wellington a brand-new children’s hospital has opened, this wouldn’t have been possible without the generosity of Sir Mark Dunajtschik and Dame Dorothy Spotswood.

“If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity, not impose an arbitrary ceiling on it.

“On Sunday ACT will release its fiscal plan. It will remove locks on New Zealand’s potential like the charities cap, and it will get rid of the waste that prevents us from growing the economy.”

# ACT will stop any proposed VPN ban

*ACT New Zealand press release, 7 July 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act-will-stop-any-proposed-vpn-ban> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Tuesday, 7 July 2026

## ACT will stop any proposed VPN ban

#### "ACT will prevent any ban on VPNs," says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

"ACT will prevent any ban on VPNs," says ACT Leader David Seymour.

"The Government is united in condemning China’s missile launch, and to be consistent it’s critical we don’t adopt Chinese-style intrusions into internet privacy.

" Speculation over a VPN ban exposes the problem with well-intentioned efforts to protect children from harm.

“Any ban strong enough to stop a motivated teenager is strong enough to violate all of our privacy. On the other hand, motivated teenagers will skirt anything weaker in an instant. The Australians have found this, with 80 per cent of teens ignoring the ban.

"If a teenager can bypass a social media ban with a VPN, then the ban isn't effective. If the Government responds by restricting VPNs, it is no longer regulating children's access to social media, it is regulating how every New Zealander uses the internet.

"VPNs are legitimate privacy and security tools. Businesses use them to protect commercial information. Journalists use them to protect sources. Ordinary New Zealanders use them to secure their personal information on public Wi-Fi. They are an essential part of modern cybersecurity.

"ACT was very clear on this point when we filed our differing view on the social media inquiry: 'The countries that have placed restrictions on VPNs include North Korea, China, Russia, Turkmenistan, and Iran. These countries use these restrictions to suppress their citizens' free speech, often in the name of protecting from online harm.'

"New Zealand should not be borrowing ideas from the authoritarian internet playbook. We should be defending the values that separate free countries from controlled ones.

"Social media harms for children are real, but any response must work for adults too. If making a ban work requires controlling the privacy tools used by ordinary people, then it's time admit the policy doesn't work and pursue better solutions."

# ACT’s plan to increase supermarket competition

*ACT New Zealand press release, 28 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/act%E2%80%99s-plan-to-increase-supermarket-competition> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Monday, 28 September 2026

## ACT’s plan to increase supermarket competition

#### “While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives. ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter the New Zealand market,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives. ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter the New Zealand market,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“The disease of New Zealand politics today is cynical, focus-group driven, knee-jerk reactions to large problems. Politicians hear a complaint and try to play the hero by attacking a group of New Zealanders as the scapegoat of the hour.

“This politics erodes the trust and certainty needed for investment and innovation. It’s careless about the long-term effect on our country so long as those behind it think they’ll get a short-term political gain.

“We’ve seen it over and again these last six years as prices have risen as fast as, or faster than, wages. When petrol felt expensive, Jacinda said we were being ‘fleeced’ by the petrol stations. When rents went up, new taxes and regulations were put on landlords. When butter was in the news, it was Fonterra, then electricity companies, then banks, now supermarkets.

“None of this pile on mentality has made life more affordable. It’s usually ended with another layer of regulation and bureaucracy, such as the Grocery Commissioner and supplier code. New Zealand has simply been left divided and blame-happy by this pattern of political behaviour.

“The current pathway is too complex and too costly for entrants to take the risk. You have to deal with dozens of regulators - The Commerce Commission. MPI. WorkSafe. IRD. Customs. NZTA. The Privacy Commissioner. Police. MBIE. And then your local council. If you want to operate in more than one town, that's not one council, that's every council, each with their own rules, timelines and processes.

“And then there's resource consent. To open one new supermarket in New Zealand, on average, you are looking at two years and a million dollars before you’ve laid a brick.

“ACT would create a one-stop consenting shop for new market entrants - a single point where a business looking to open, or open multiple sites, can get their consents, their liquor licences, their approvals, in months, not years.

“A one-stop shop means the next entrepreneur who wants to build the next Kai Co doesn't need a team of consultants and two years of patience just to get out of the starting blocks.

“We’ll also change product labelling laws. Right now, anyone selling imported food not labelled for New Zealand has two options. They can do an expensive run of product packaged specifically to our regulations, or they need to unload pallets, open each box, and stick nutrition labels over each product individually. That’s why the Dr Pepper you get at the dairy has a little white sticker over the nutrition panel.

“ACT will allow food labels for trusted regulatory systems like UK, EU and US by default. This will lower the barrier to entry for international supermarkets, who will no longer need to do expensive runs of products specifically for the tiny Australasian market to open stores. ACT will roll out the welcome mat.

“We’ve seen the impact of heavy-handed intervention with the oil and gas exploration ban. When the Government signals that successful businesses can simply be broken apart, potential new entrants are less likely to invest here.

“Ironically, draconian regulations can make supermarket competition worse. We won’t get Aldi, or Coles, or Walmart to come to New Zealand if they believe it’s politically fashionable to attack their investments after a few bad polls. Already, the previous Government had to exempt Costco from supplier obligations or they wouldn’t come.

“Rather than joining the race to the bottom where we attack successful businesses, ACT’s policy is to make it easier for new businesses to come here, compete, and expand.”

# Campaign launched to acquire land for new school in Epsom

*ACT New Zealand press release, 30 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/campaign-launched-to-acquire-land-for-new-school-in-epsom> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Wednesday, 30 September 2026

## Campaign launched to acquire land for new school in Epsom

#### “I will be campaigning for the Government to acquire the University of Auckland Epsom Campus for educational purposes, creating a new school to serve the community,” says MP for Epsom David Seymour.

David Seymour

“I will be campaigning for the Government to acquire the University of Auckland Epsom Campus for educational purposes, creating a new school to serve the community,” says MP for Epsom David Seymour.

“This project will protect the existing Grammar zones by creating a new education option without changing the zoning. If the land is not used for a new school, the substantial land that the University is selling will be developed into high density housing, exacerbating the immense pressure already on the existing Grammar zones.

“I have been engaged on the future of this land since at least 2019, when I first met with the University about their plan to exit the Epsom Campus. I have primarily been concerned with ensuring the two existing schools at the southern end, Auckland Normal Intermediate and Kohia Terrace School, do not lose their fields or walkable access. The Ministry of Education has been in negotiations to secure at least that much land.

“However, new developments have shifted my focus to acquiring the land in its entirety, something I previously did not think possible or affordable.

“In July I was approached by the Principals of Auckland Grammar School and Epsom Girls’ Grammar school. They and their boards would like to co-sponsor a co-educational high school on the land, initially using the existing buildings.

“Since their approach, I have sought assurance from the Minister of Education the land will not be sold in the immediate future.

“The support of Mrs McNaughton and Mr O’Connor means the school would be backed by two of the country’s greatest educators. It would be the only co-educational school in the area, something I know some parents would prefer for their children.

“It would be a school of excellence, taking pressure off the existing schools without removing the entitlement for those in zone to attend the traditional Grammars if they wish to.

“The cost of the land is substantial, I have also asked the Minister to investigate other land holdings the Ministry of Education has that might be sold to cover the cost. For example, the Ministry bought a substantial piece beside Alexandra Park in the 1990s that has not been used.

“The school should be unzoned and accept students from across the city. Taking pressure off Mt Albert Grammar that is successful to bursting point. It also fulfils the original Auckland Grammar ethos, ‘for persons of all classes and races who may inhabit this colony.’

“The continued use of the land for education would ensure that the property remains open, green space. Everyone accepts that central Auckland will intensify over time, but more terraced housing and apartments makes it even more important that green spaces and local facilities like schools are provided.

“This land and its future use are not only important to the Epsom community, but families across the Auckland region who want a quality education. Whoever forms the next Government, I will be taking it to them as a critical project for our community and those surrounding it.”

# Carbon auction farce why ACT will cut the Carbon Tax

*ACT New Zealand press release, 7 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/carbon-auction-farce-why-act-will-cut-the-carbon-tax> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Monday, 7 September 2026

## Carbon auction farce why ACT will cut the Carbon Tax

#### “Barring a miracle, tomorrow’s carbon auction will further expose the absurdity of a climate policy that has lost touch with economic reality,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“Barring a miracle, tomorrow’s carbon auction will further expose the absurdity of a climate policy that has lost touch with economic reality,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“The Government will miss out on around $195 million dollars of revenue, under ACT’s policy that could be given to households as a Carbon Dividend. Instead, the price will stay artificially high and instead of getting a dividend, families will pay extra on their power and petrol.

“Sensible climate policy should preserve jobs and an affordable life while ensuring New Zealand does no more than the countries we trade and compete with.

“Every party except ACT supported the Zero Carbon Act. That led to crazy climate targets and settings that now mean the Government refuses to sell carbon credits for less than $71, when exactly the same units are trading on the market for around $50.

“No rational buyer is going to pay $71 for something they can buy for $50.

“In three years only two of 24 auctions have sold a unit. The last six Government auctions have failed to sell a single unit. Tomorrow, as a result, there will be up to 3.9 million units available. Unless something dramatically changes, taxpayers are staring at another auction where the Government prices itself out of its own market.

“It is a lose-lose. The Government gets no auction revenue and households and businesses still face the Carbon Tax through higher petrol, power, freight and grocery prices.

“ACT would cut the waste in climate policy so we can grow the country.

“We would scrap the arbitrary Net Zero 2050 target and repeal the Zero Carbon Act. Instead of imposing costs our competitors are unwilling to bear, we would match them so we maintain market access without putting unnecessary costs on Kiwis.

“We would also scrap wasteful bureaucracy like the Climate Change Commission and remove the artificial auction price floor so the Government can sell units at the price the market is actually willing to pay.

“And we'd return 100 per cent of the net revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund rather than giving politicians another pot of money to spend.

“At a carbon price of around $55, the ETS costs an average household an estimated $478 a year. ACT says that if New Zealanders are going to pay a carbon price, the revenue should come back to them.

“ACT will cut unnecessary costs, protect Kiwi jobs, return carbon revenue to households and let innovation deliver cleaner solutions.

“Cut the waste, grow the country, and unlock New Zealand’s potential.”

# Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

*ACT New Zealand press release, 10 September 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/finish-the-settlements-wind-up-the-waitangi-tribunal> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Thursday, 10 September 2026

## Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

#### “ACT will complete the remaining historical Treaty claims, end the Waitangi Tribunal’s contemporary jurisdiction, and wind it up once its historical work is finished, ACT Leader David Seymour says.

David Seymour

“ACT will complete the remaining historical Treaty claims, end the Waitangi Tribunal’s contemporary jurisdiction, and wind it up once its historical work is finished, ACT Leader David Seymour says.

“The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand’s constitutional landscape for more than fifty years. It has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances. But no institution should exist just because it always has.

“ACT supports completing full and final historical Treaty settlements as a pragmatic way to resolve past injustices. This includes where the Crown confiscated land or otherwise breached property rights. That work should be finished properly.

“But the Tribunal that exists today is very different from the institution established in 1975.

“Through urgent and Kaupapa inquiries, the Tribunal now passes judgement on day-to-day government policy. It proposes alternative policy settings and seeks to steer decisions that properly belong to elected Governments and Parliament. This is not the Tribunal’s role and never was.

“As we approach 2040, two centuries since the signing of the Treaty, it is time to complete the historical settlements and move New Zealand forward.

“Every New Zealander deserves strong legal protections and access to the courts, regardless of ancestry. ACT believes those protections should be strengthened for everyone, not maintained through a permanent separate system for one group.

ACT will move New Zealand beyond the Waitangi Tribunal with four reforms:

01 Complete the historical settlement process

Every eligible historical claim before the Tribunal should be heard and resolved. ACT will limit the Tribunal to historical claims lodged by 1 September 2008. End its role in reviewing current government policy and actions. Ensure that all existing historical claims will still be heard and completed.

02 Stop the activism

New Zealanders choose policy at elections, and a parallel tribunal shouldn’t override that. After 50 years of evolution, its modern role no longer continues to serve New Zealand well. ACT will end the Waitangi Tribunal’s jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, leaving it to focus solely on completing the remaining historical claims.

03 Protect everyone’s rights through the law

No group should need a separate tribunal for rights that should be protected for everyone under ordinary law. Equally, no Government should unlawfully take property, interfere with rights, or act outside the law. Every New Zealander should be able to challenge this in our courts. ACT has already announced that we’ll add property rights to the Bill of Rights protecting everyone’s rights through law.

04 Wind up the Tribunal when the job is done

The Tribunal’s historic work is finite and nearly completed. ACT will not set an arbitrary deadline that rushes the remaining claims. ACT will amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed.

“As 2040 approaches, we should complete the remaining historical settlements, protecting every New Zealander’s right under the same law and courts, and move forward under one law for all with one future together.”

Note to editors: ACT’s full policy here.

# Harsher penalties for trashing communities

*ACT New Zealand press release, 16 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/harsher-penalties-for-trashing-communities> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

###### Press Release

Friday, 16 October 2026

## Harsher penalties for trashing communities

#### “ACT will increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, and punish anyone using the land as their personal tip," says ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

Andrew Hoggard

“ACT will increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, and punish anyone using the land as their personal tip," says ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

"Illegal dumping is vandalism by another name. It's unfair on ratepayers, damaging to the environment, and shows a complete disregard for people who take pride in their communities.

“Communities are being forced to foot the bill for this behaviour. Thousands of tonnes of illegally dumped waste are collected every year, with clean-up costs running into the millions. That cost ends up being borne out of ratepayers' backpocket.

"Every mattress dumped on a roadside, every trailer-load of rubbish abandoned, and every pile of waste thrown into a ditch ends up becoming someone else's problem, both from the costs to clean it up and the effect on the land. Dumped rubbish can contaminate streams, harm livestock, attract pests, and create fire hazards.

"Anyone who thinks that is acceptable needs to face the kinds of consequences that will make them reconsider.

“ACT will increase the infringement fee for illegal dumping from $400 to $1,000, with repeat offenders facing fines of $2,000. For the most serious offences, courts will have the power to impose higher penalties.

“In my own community, I've come home to find someone had walked down to the local river to burn a pile of nappies, glass bottles, and tin cans. They did this right beside our favourite swimming hole and a spot where the local primary school comes to learn about river ecology.

“The current $400 penalty isn't cutting it. If you're prepared to dump rubbish beside a river, and leave someone else to deal with the mess, a slap on the wrist isn't much of a deterrent.

"It's not good enough that hard-working families are left paying the price for people who think the roadside or a rural area is their personal tip.

"Most New Zealanders do the right thing. They pay for rubbish collection, use transfer stations, and follow the rules. For those who don't, stronger penalties send a simple message: if you dump your rubbish illegally, you'll face consequences."

# Keep agriculture in the curriculum

*ACT New Zealand press release, 9 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/keep-agriculture-in-the-curriculum> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

###### Press Release

Friday, 9 October 2026

## Keep agriculture in the curriculum

#### “ACT will campaign for agriculture to remain a subject in the Year 11 school curriculum,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

Andrew Hoggard

“ACT will campaign for agriculture to remain a subject in the Year 11 school curriculum,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“In September, I wrote to Education Minister Erica Stanford asking her to confirm that Agricultural and Horticultural Science will remain as a standalone subject in the Year 11 Science curriculum. I’m gutted to learn this isn’t the case.

“We’re a food and fibre producing nation so learning about our biggest exporter shouldn’t be an unconventional subject.

“Food and fibre exports are forecast to reach $64.3 billion in the year to June 2026, we should encourage more young Kiwis to learn the ropes, but interest will shrink if we don’t make it easily available.

“Over the last nine years 111,693 have studied Agricultural and Horticultural Science across 359 schools. 63 percent of students taking the subject are at urban schools. It is not only rural students who benefit, for many young people in towns and cities this may be their only structured chance to learn how the industry works.

“Removing agriculture as a Year 11 standalone subject sends the wrong message. For schools with strong agricultural programmes – such as Feilding High School, which recently featured on Country Calendar – this change creates a real challenge for them, by leaving a gap in their Year 11 programme.

“It’s also an industry loaded with well-paying jobs if only talented young Kiwis would take them. Given that dance is a standalone subject at Year 11, I don't understand why schools that already have a programme, and have a student demand for it, can't have the opportunity to teach it."

# Landmark social media settlement shows better way forward

*ACT New Zealand press release, 27 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/landmark-social-media-settlement-shows-better-way-forward> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Thursday, 27 August 2026

## Landmark social media settlement shows better way forward

#### “ACT welcomes the changes Meta has agreed to make to its social media platforms in the United States. We are calling on Meta and all similar companies to treat New Zealand children the same as they will be required to treat American children,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

David Seymour

“ACT welcomes the changes Meta has agreed to make to its social media platforms in the United States. We are calling on Meta and all similar companies to treat New Zealand children the same as they will be required to treat American children,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Protecting children online is a serious problem, that’s why ACT pushed for Parliament to investigate the issue. We are now seeing a genuine, realistic solution take shape.

“As part of a settlement with US states, Meta has agreed to make significant changes to its platforms. These include a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers, locking most teen accounts between midnight and 6am, switching off push notifications overnight and during school hours, and giving parents greater power to supervise and restrict their children’s accounts. Teenagers would also need parental approval to loosen the main restrictions.

“The best thing the New Zealand Government could do for young New Zealanders is tell Meta we want to have the same settings here, and challenge other major social media companies to match them. That would be a more effective and realistic solution than implementing a ban which won’t work and is fraught with unintended consequences.

“The problem with these bans is that teenagers are smarter and more determined at using the internet than adults. Anything strict enough to stop motivated teenagers will affect adult freedom, but teenagers will drive a bus through anything loose enough to not affect adults.

“Instead of pretending teenagers can simply be kept off social media because politicians say so, it changes the features that encourage excessive use, gives parents greater control, and puts responsibility on the companies designing the platforms.

“Before Parliament creates another bureaucracy with unintended consequences, imposes widespread online identification, starts restricting legitimate privacy tools, or threatens companies with fines they’ll never pay, we should look to implement the solution right in front of us.”
