# Leave spirituality out of infrastructure

*ACT New Zealand press release, 3 October 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/leave-spirituality-out-of-infrastructure> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Saturday, 3 October 2026

## Leave spirituality out of infrastructure

#### "New Zealanders should be able to build a house, a solar farm or a factory without being made to take part in, or pay for, a religious ceremony as a condition of consent," says ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson, Simon Court.

Simon Court

New Zealanders should be able to build a house, a solar farm or a factory without being made to take part in, or pay for, a religious ceremony as a condition of consent," says ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson, Simon Court.

Planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.

"Unfortunately, emerging litigation has seen spiritual effects increasingly become part of our resource management system.

“For example, some housing developments must invite iwi to perform a karakia before construction begins, with the developer paying for it. IKEA’s Sylvia Park consent requires invitations to seven mana whenua groups to attend karakia and ceremonies at specified construction milestones. Solar farms at Ongaonga and Ōpunake have similar conditions. The Ōtākiri water-bottling dispute reached the Supreme Court, where evidence about te mauri o te wai was considered.

“The new Planning Act and Natural Environment Act, which received Royal assent this week, are a significant improvement. They do not carry over the RMA’s spiritual-value requirement. But leaving a requirement out is not the same as ruling it out. Without a clear boundary, people can still bring spiritual matters back in under broader cultural-effects provisions, leaving councils and courts to draw the line case by case.

“ACT will finish the job.”

ACT will:

- Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. A religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act.
- Ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fund a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. Anyone who wants to do these things voluntarily still could.
- Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes. Councils would work to clear, testable standards for water quality, ecosystem health and human health.

"None of this takes away protection for anything real. Heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation would all still be dealt with directly.

"The test is simple. Is there an identifiable physical effect, place, resource or legal right? If there is, deal with it. If the claimed effect exists only as a spiritual proposition, it isn't the planning system's job."

###### Press Release

Saturday, 10 October 2026

## New Zealand can't keep exporting taxpayers' money

#### “New Zealand is in the sh*t, can we seriously afford to be sending millions of dollars overseas for tripe like ‘climate-smart’ passionfruit?” asks ACT list candidate Paul Henry.

Paul Henry

“New Zealand is in the sh*t, can we seriously afford to be sending millions of dollars overseas for tripe like ‘climate-smart’ passionfruit?” asks ACT list candidate Paul Henry.

“ACT will cut wasteful and low-priority MFAT spending, focus New Zealand’s aid on our national interests, and make every programme prove its value to taxpayers.

“New Zealand has good reason to spend overseas – a stable, prosperous Pacific, strong trade ties and the ability to help when disaster strikes. But foreign aid is taxpayers’ money, and should face the same scrutiny as spending here at home.

“Here’s an uncomfortable truth, our economy is too small. Our bureaucracy is too big. We cannot spend our way to prosperity. We need to be disciplined if we’re to get the books back in order.

“ACT will reduce foreign aid to 2017 levels, excluding support for Ukraine. This will save around $283 million a year.

“Since 2024, MFAT spent $15 million on developing countries to prepare for the Paris Agreement – an agreement that is broken and cannot accommodate targets that reflect the real warming impact of New Zealand’s emissions.

“Nearly $21 million was spent on sustainable agriculture investment in Africa; $6.3 million to develop different crops in Timor-Lester; $6.2 million on supporting gender diversity for Climate-Smart Passionfruit chain in Viet Nam; $5.1 million to Timor-Leste to publish three educational magazines – I could go on, but just like we don’t have the money for this nonsense, I don’t have the heartbeats for it either.

“That’s already around $50 million for other countries and their pet projects. This is absolutely barking mad.

“ACT will be campaigning to give MFAT a reality check on behalf of taxpayers. We cannot afford this kind of spending when our own country is paying an eye-watering debt – a debt that already costs us almost $25 million a day just in interest payments.

“If nothing changes, the best-case scenario is our grandchildren will still be paying the interest on our debt. Worst-case the Greens get in and then it will be our great, great, great grandchildren’s problem as well.

“I didn’t stand for ACT for something to do. I stood because I believe in New Zealand’s extraordinary potential – and I won’t stand by while taxpayers’ money goes to solving other countries’ problems before our own.

“ACT wants to invigorate New Zealand with the aspiration and ambition the country was once world famous for. Party Vote ACT to cut the waste and grow the country.”

# One Law for All, One Future Together

*ACT New Zealand press release, 17 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/one-law-for-all-one-future-together> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Monday, 17 August 2026

## One Law for All, One Future Together

#### ACT has refined its plans to tackle the high church of Treatyism in its next term of Government.

Free Press

#### The Haps

Parliament was in recess last week, but politics continued. ACT celebrated David Seymour’s reforms to school attendance with record numbers (11,579) of Not Enrolled students returned to school in the first half of this year. Charter school enrolments, meanwhile, increased 18 per cent in six months. Many charter schools are now looking for bigger buildings because space is their constraint. Giving communities a chance to compete for education funding is ACT philosophy in action, and it’s transforming lives let down by the state system.

The Party also released new policy that was welcomed as ‘a breath of fresh air and common sense.’ The Local Tourism Dividend would give a Council one dollar for each bed night tourists stay in the Council’s area.

It would help Councils support tourism without a new tax to administer. Councils and tourism operators have been braying for a new tax for years, ACT strongly opposes any new tax, because once they’re in, they always grow. The policy, and five reasons why it’s better than a new tax, are here.

#### One Law for All, One Future Together

The current Government was elected to fix the rampant and deliberate racism that grew up under its predecessor.

Since November 2023 it has: removed the separatist Māori Health Authority, given communities a referendum on Māori words, cancelled Three Waters with its co-governed boards, replaced the ‘Aotearoa Histories Curriculum’ with a balanced view of human history in New Zealand, issued a Cabinet Circular that services must be delivered on need, not race, so things like diabetes medicines and bowel cancer screening are no longer funded along racial lines… We could go on, but the point is a lot has been done.

For all the progress that has been made, though, there is a niggling feeling that the public service has carried on its merry way, giving a big fat finger to the Government of the day. It shows up when karakia are required at the start of meetings, job ads advertise for knowledge of te ao Māori (but no other culture), and people lose out because they didn’t ‘demonstrate their commitment to te tiriti in the home.’

Last week’s Free Press argued that Treatyism has become New Zealand’s new religion. Colonisation was the original sin, but if you wear the adornments around your neck, practice the rituals before your meetings, and smite non-believers as ‘racist’ then, maybe, you will be saved.

The Public Service has become the church of New Zealand’s new religion, and if you doubt that you only need to look at the Ministry of Education’s Tātai Pou Competency Matrix. A workers’ competency is ranked from ‘unsatisfactory’ to ‘high.’ You don’t just need to promote Treatyism to move up the matrix, you need to promote it to others to be highly competent.

If you are not a believer, even not practicing in your home, you may not get a job in the public service.

Missionaries would be proud, but our country was built on secularism and tolerance. The Treaty says every New Zealander should have the ‘same rights and duties’. In 1847, between the Treaty and the first Parliament, Governor Grey issued an education ordinance requiring school instruction to be secular for parents who demanded it, while acknowledging many parents would want religious instruction. Parliament’s 1877 Education Act also demanded education be secular.

Not long after that, Kate Sheppard, perhaps the greatest New Zealander and a devout Christian, said “All that separates, whether it be of race, class, creed or sex, is inhuman and must be overcome.” A century later New Zealanders protested en masse against apartheid, even at the expense of seeing the ABs.

New Zealand is a society founded, at least in part, on secularism and racial equality. What is happening in the Public Service, in spite of the elected Government, is counter to the foundations of secular tolerance this country is built on, and must be overcome.

That’s why the ACT Party has launched policy to remove Section 73 of the Public Service Act 2020, the section that requires the Public Service carry out discriminatory hiring. The Party pledges to upgrade its successful Need-not-Race Cabinet Circular to law enforceable in Court. It will ban taxpayer financing for cultural practices. It pledges to separate spiritual rituals from government work.

The full policy is here, but one question remains. Wasn’t this done already? Yes, ACT negotiated to reform the Public Service Act, and improvements were made. The roughest edges of that law made under the Labour-Green-New Zealand First Government in 2020 have been knocked off. The new Section 11A says Chief Executives should focus on performance first.

But, even Free Press underestimated the religious fervour that drives Treatyism. Learning from this term of Government, ACT has refined its plans to tackle the high church of Treatyism in its next term of Government.

#### A way to help

If you like what ACT has been saying and doing, and want to see us return after the election with an even stronger team, here’s a good way to help.

Friends of ACT, Grace and Jonathan Ayling, have generously donated a special run of ACT Pinot Noir, with all profits going directly towards ACT’s 2026 election campaign.

Click here to buy yours now and support the campaign to Unlock New Zealand’s potential.

# Your pharmacist should be your first stop

*ACT New Zealand press release, 6 August 2026. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/news/your-pharmacist-should-be-your-first-stop> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Press Release

Thursday, 6 August 2026

## Your pharmacist should be your first stop

#### ACT Party Leader David Seymour today released Pharmacy First – ACT's plan to get New Zealanders care without the wait by expanding what pharmacists can do and removing barriers to new pharmacies.

David Seymour

ACT Party Leader David Seymour today released Pharmacy First – ACT's plan to get New Zealanders care without the wait by expanding what pharmacists can do and removing barriers to new pharmacies.

ACT will let pharmacists treat more conditions, manage stable long-term conditions, catch cardiovascular and skin cancer risk early, cut red tape stopping new pharmacies from opening, and introduce 24-hour prescription collection through secure electronic lockers.

"In many cases, your pharmacist is the healthcare professional closest to you," Mr Seymour said. "They're trained, they're trusted, they're often available the same day.

“The rules confine pharmacists to a small number of permitted services. Meanwhile, time that pharmacists used to spend ‘counting and pouring’ is being freed up by automation, at the same time that community pharmacies are under serious revenue pressure.

“Pharmacists have the capacity, the need, and the proximity. All that's missing is permission.

"One in four adults and one in five children cannot see a GP when they need to – a figure that has more than doubled in four years. A highly qualified healthcare professional is standing right there at your local shops, ready to help. The rules just need to get out of the way.

"This policy builds on changes ACT has already delivered in Government. Pharmacists are now treating UTIs, conjunctivitis, chest infections, and ear infections. We've introduced 12-month prescriptions for stable patients, and given pharmacists prescribing rights for the first time. New Zealanders have welcomed our moves to empower pharmacists and patients, so today's announcement is the next step."

More conditions covered at your pharmacy

ACT will expand the Minor Ailments Scheme to include conditions pharmacists are trained to assess and treat:

- Throat and ENT: acute sore throat
- Skin and eyes: school sores (impetigo), stye
- Ear, nose and throat: tonsillitis and acute sore throat
- Musculoskeletal and pain: gout, osteoarthritis
- Sexual and reproductive health: vaginal thrush; chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing (self-swab kits), period pain
- Blood tests: pharmacists will be able to order appropriate blood tests directly, at a patient's request or where they identify a clinical need

A full list of ailments ACT is proposing pharmacists to treat can be found here.

"Every condition will include a clear protocol for when patients need to be referred to a GP or specialist," says Mr Seymour. "Doctors still have an important role here, but ACT will make sure that for cases a pharmacist can handle, you don't have to wait two weeks to get help."

"Consultation fees will stay capped at $20 for most patients and $5 for Community Services Card holders. The Government funds the balance."

Routine monitoring of long-term conditions

“For the roughly one million New Zealanders managing stable hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol, an annual GP appointment to renew the same medication is often a formality – but getting that appointment is not.

“Pharmacists already see these patients regularly, know their medicines, and are well placed to carry out routine monitoring. ACT will let accredited pharmacists provide funded annual medication reviews for stable patients, order the standard blood tests needed to monitor treatment, and adjust doses within clear, GP-set clinical limits. Anything outside those limits, or any new diagnosis, goes straight back to the patient's GP.”

Catching skin cancer sooner

“New Zealand has one of the world's highest melanoma rates, but most people must either wait for a GP or pay out of pocket to have a suspicious lesion checked. Pharmacies are often the first place people raise these concerns – there just isn't a consistent pathway for what happens next.

“ACT will allow pharmacy-based skin concern service. Trained pharmacists would record relevant risk factors and take high-quality dermatoscope images, using technology to help identify concerning changes over time. Patients who meet clear risk thresholds would be referred to a GP or specialist.

"This is not a full diagnosis service, but it would give people – especially in rural communities – a place to have a concern taken seriously and acted on quickly."

More pharmacies where you need them

"Rules that prevent new pharmacies from opening will go," says Mr Seymour.

"The five-pharmacy ownership cap – a restriction the Government's own October 2025 Regulatory Impact Statement admits is 'not being meaningfully followed' – will be explicitly removed. Proximity requirements that block new pharmacies from opening near existing ones will also go. Any pharmacy that meets safety and quality standards should be able to open.

"Pharmacy licence renewals will move from annual to five-yearly after the first year, saving pharmacists $1,000 in compliance costs each year and freeing them to focus on patients, not paperwork. Pharmacy Accuracy Checking Technicians will be allowed to transfer between pharmacies without having to sit a new course, making it easier for pharmacies, especially in smaller communities, to attract and retain staff.

"The current rules don't protect people, but they do make it harder to open pharmacies and harder to staff them. ACT's plan to empower pharmacists will create demand for more pharmacies in more communities. So, we're removing the barriers to get them there."

24-hour e-lockers

"For New Zealanders managing stable long-term conditions, ACT will enable secure prescription e-lockers – allowing patients to collect pre-dispensed medicines at any time using a digital code, similar to click-and-collect at a supermarket," says Mr Seymour.

"Lockers will not be used to dispense controlled drugs, refrigerated medicines, or medications requiring monitoring.

"This is a practical fix for rural communities where pharmacy hours are limited and collecting a prescription means a long drive at inconvenient times.

"The pharmacy network in New Zealand has enormous, untapped capacity," Mr Seymour said. "ACT is going to unlock it, so that when you're unwell, your pharmacist is the first stop. We will make life easier for Kiwis seeking basic care, and free up GPs to see patients in greater need, more quickly."

# No Tax on KiwiSaver Earnings

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/no-tax-on-kiwisaver-earnings> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## No Tax on KiwiSaver Earnings

A lifetime of work and saving should give you the freedom to enjoy retirement. Yet the Government takes a cut of your KiwiSaver earnings every year, leaving less of your money to grow for the years ahead.

ACT will reward saving by letting you keep those earnings. You’ll be able to build a bigger nest egg for the retirement you want, without giving up more of the pay you need today.

Try our calculator to see how much you'd save.

Read our full policy, No tax on KiwiSaver earnings, here.

#### ACT will:

- Remove tax on qualifying investment earnings inside KiwiSaver funds, allowing your returns to stay invested and grow tax-free.
- End the annual Government Contribution for members receiving employer contributions, replacing it with tax relief on their KiwiSaver earnings.
- Put safeguards in place to keep KiwiSaver focused on retirement saving and prevent it being used to shelter large existing investment portfolios from tax.

#### In our team’s word’s:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Other parties want to force your money into KiwiSaver, then tax you. ACT says it should be your choice, but if you save for the future we will let you get the full benefit of compounding returns instead of taxing you every step of the way.

“Every time you get taxed on your earnings you don’t just lose that money, but all the future savings that would be compounded from it.

“A country builds wealth when more people own assets, have savings, invest in productive enterprise and have the confidence to think decades ahead."

# No Votes for Unelected Reps

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/no-votes-for-unelected-reps> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Democracy & Equal Rights

## No Votes for Unelected Reps

Your council spends your rates and decides what you can do with your property. You should be able to vote out every person who has a vote at the council table. ACT will remove voting rights from unelected appointees, including members of Auckland’s Independent Māori Statutory Board.

Councils across New Zealand have put appointees on committees alongside elected councillors. These appointees can swing a decision, but ratepayers have no way to remove them at an election. ACT will stop councils doing this.

In Auckland, two Houkura members of the Independent Māori Statutory Board vote on council committees dealing with natural and physical resource management. They hold those votes by appointment. ACT will remove those voting rights. Anyone who wants a vote at the council table can stand for election and ask Aucklanders for their support.

ACT stands for one law for all with one future together. If you want political power, you should stand for election like anyone else.

Read our announcement here.

#### ACT will:

- Change the Local Government Act so unelected members of council committees and subcommittees cannot vote or count toward quorum.
- Change the law governing Auckland Council so unelected members of the Independent Māori Statutory Board cannot vote on council committees.
- Apply the same rule to every appointee, whether they represent iwi, youth councils, business groups, or community organisations.
- Leave council decisions to the elected representatives ratepayers can vote out.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Local Government spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“With rates climbing and households squeezed, the people deciding how to spend ratepayers’ money ought to be held accountable. But right now, we’ve got councils appointing unelected people to committees with full voting rights.

“ACT’s coalition agreement has restored communities’ right to vote on Māori wards. But some councils may be tempted to counter a public vote against Māori wards by turning around and appointing unelected representatives anyway, along the lines of Auckland Council’s Independent Māori Statutory Board. Meanwhile, we’ve seen cases, such as in Tauranga and Wellington, where both Māori ward councillors and unelected mana whenua appointees sit across the same table.

“Ratepayers are struggling under rising bills. The only real accountability mechanism they have is the ballot box. If you’re paying the bills, you should be able to choose who’s spending your money".

---

# One Law for All. One Future Together.

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/one-law-for-all> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

## One Law for All. One Future Together.

#### One law for all means the same rights, the same duties, and the same protection under the law.

## One Law for All.

#### New Zealand should be a country where everyone is equal before the law, Parliament makes the law, Government is bound by the law, and the property people work hard for is secure.

#### These are basic foundations of a free and democratic country. But over time, vague Treaty clauses and expanding judicial interpretations have blurred who gets to make the rules.

#### ACT will:

#### Ensure Parliament Makes the Rules

Enshrine in the Constitution Act that Parliament makes the law, Government is bound by it, and every New Zealander is equal before it.

#### Protect Property Rights

Protect your home, farm, business, and other property by adding property rights to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.

#### Rein in the Activist Courts

Stop courts using broad Treaty interpretations to impose obligations Parliament never actually legislated.

#### Require Clarity When Referring to the Treaty

Make Parliament say clearly what it means when it refers to the Treaty, instead of leaving courts and officials to fill in the gaps.

#### Join the Campaign for Equal Rights

###### Submit

###### Submit

## One Public Service.

#### Previous governments spent years building separate tracks for different groups, and too many of those rules remain. ACT will remove them and build one public service with one standard for everyone.

#### ACT will:

#### End race-based hiring.

Government jobs should go to the best candidate, whoever they are. But the law still tells public employers to shape employment policies around the aspirations and employment needs of particular ethnic groups. ACT will repeal those rules in section 73 of the Public Service Act and section 118 of the Crown Entities Act. Laws against discrimination and unsafe workplaces will remain. So will the rule that public service appointments must be based on merit.

#### Keep spiritual practices voluntary.

Taxpayer money isn’t for running spiritual or religious activities at work. ACT will end the use of public time and public funds for this, whatever the tradition. Staff will remain free to practise their own religion, culture, or traditions in their own time, and workplaces can make reasonable arrangements for them.

#### Rewrite the Public Service Act.

ACT will make these changes straight away, then rewrite the Act so the public service stays politically neutral, hires on merit, treats people equally, and is judged on whether services actually reach the people who need them.

#### Deliver public services based on need, not race.

ACT will put into law that public services should go to the people who need them, whoever they are. If two New Zealanders have the same need, government should treat them the same. The Government has already told agencies to follow that rule. ACT will put it in law so people can challenge decisions that break it in court.

#### Remove cultural tests that have nothing to do with the job.

Job ads should ask whether you can do the work, not whether you know the right cultural concepts or share the right worldview. ACT will tell agencies to remove these requirements from job ads and position descriptions unless the knowledge is actually needed for the job.

## Free Speech for All.

#### Professional regulators exist to protect the public by setting standards for competence, safety and conduct at work. They should not decide which lawful political or personal views a New Zealander is allowed to hold.

#### ACT will:

#### Protect Lawful Expression

Ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice.

#### Ensure Neutrality

Require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues.

#### Axe Irrelevant Training

Restrict mandatory training to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety.

#### Strengthen Judicial Oversight

Strengthen judicial oversight so courts can rein in regulators that go beyond their legal powers.

#### Preserve Regulators Core Purpose

Preserve regulators' ability to act against genuine professional misconduct, harm to clients or patients, and breaches of professional duties.

## Our Record.

#### In Government, ACT has driven major changes toward equal rights, democratic accountability and a politically neutral public service.

#### Making need, not race, the rule for public services

ACT secured a Cabinet circular directing agencies to target services according to individual need instead of using ethnicity as a proxy.

#### Removing race-based institutions and legal duties

The Government abolished the Māori Health Authority, removed race-based requirements from health law and repealed section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act so decisions focus on children's safety and wellbeing.

#### Restoring local democracy

ACT secured the return of binding local referendums on Māori wards. The Government has also adopted the substance of Cameron Luxton's Member's Bill so unelected council appointees will no longer be able to vote or count toward quorum under the Local Government Act.

#### Putting merit and neutrality back into the public service

The Public Service Amendment Act reinforces political neutrality, merit-based appointments and professional competence, and removes statutory requirements to pursue demographic representation in public-service employment.

#### Ending race-based procurement targets

ACT secured the removal of the target requiring eight per cent of government contracts to be awarded to Māori-owned businesses. Public contracts should be awarded on value and performance.

#### Protecting liberties and property rights in lawmaking

The Regulatory Standards Act requires new laws to be assessed openly against principles including personal liberty, property rights, equality before the law and good legislative process. An independent Regulatory Standards Board can examine complaints and report publicly.

#### Stopping state-backed speech policing

The Government halted Labour's proposed hate-speech expansion and agreed to disestablish the Broadcasting Standards Authority after ACT challenged its attempt to extend broadcasting rules to podcasts and online media.

#### The coalition Government has not gone as far as ACT would like, but it has gone further than it would have without ACT.

## Fighting for a free, fair and equal New Zealand.

#### We are proud to represent ACT’s values of freedom, personal responsibility, and opportunity for all New Zealanders.

# Open the Backcountry

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/open-the-backcountry> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Hunters and Firearms

## Open the Backcountry

Much of New Zealand’s public land is difficult to reach. In rugged country such as Fiordland, a helicopter can be the only practical way in, yet large areas remain closed by no-fly and no-landing lines with no clear conservation or safety reason.

Commercial venison recovery is also caught between DOC rules and aviation regulation. DOC can dictate the type of helicopter an operator uses even though aircraft safety is already regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority.

ACT would make access decisions clear and defensible, leave aviation safety to the aviation regulator and give hunters a proper role in balancing recreational hunting with commercial recovery.

Read the full policy

#### ACT will:

- Allow the Game Animal Council to designate sensible and accessible helicopter landing sites.
- Require DOC to use clear, public and consistent tests when deciding where aircraft may land.
- Direct the Outdoor Access Commission to make hunting access a priority in its work programme.
- Stop DOC dictating which helicopters commercial venison recovery operators can use, leaving aircraft safety to the Civil Aviation Authority.
- Allow the Game Animal Council to restrict commercial take by animal gender when necessary, so recreational hunters and recovery operators can fairly share a well-managed resource.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Public conservation land belongs to New Zealanders, but large parts of it are effectively closed off. In country such as Fiordland, a helicopter can be the only realistic way in. Access restrictions should have a clear conservation or safety reason, not survive because of an old line on a map.

“Better access is not a licence to ignore conservation limits. It means opening the country New Zealanders already own under rules that are clear, justified and fair to the people who use it.”

ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“ACT would let the Game Animal Council identify sensible landing sites and require DOC to use a clear and public test. We would also tell the Outdoor Access Commission to prioritise hunting access when it works to secure routes onto public land.

“DOC currently makes commercial venison recovery operators use expensive turbine helicopters. Aircraft safety is the Civil Aviation Authority’s job. DOC should manage conservation effects and leave aircraft standards to the regulator established for that purpose.

“Current permits can also let commercial operators strip out the trophy stags recreational hunters value most. Where necessary, the Game Animal Council would be able to restrict take by animal gender so commercial recovery and recreational hunting can share the resource fairly.”

# Open the Door to Supermarket Competition

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/open-the-door-to-supermarket-competition> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Open the Door to Supermarket Competition

The weekly shop is expensive enough without Government making it harder for another supermarket to open. Kiwis need more businesses competing for their custom and giving them a reason to shop elsewhere.

Before a new competitor sells its first bottle of milk, it has to navigate approvals from councils and government agencies. Open in several towns and the local requirements change each time. Alcohol licensing can hold up an opening. Imported food may need special packaging or a sticker on every item before it can be sold here.

Those costs favour the businesses already here. ACT will make it easier for new supermarkets to open and grow, s shoppers have more places to take their business.

#### ACT will:

- Create a one-stop consenting shop. Bring the consents, licences and other approvals needed to open stores into one coordinated process, including when a business wants to open across multiple council areas. The aim is to get decisions in months, rather than years.
- Make alcohol licensing faster and simpler. Deal with applications earlier, instead of leaving licensing hearings until a new supermarket is almost ready to open.
- Recognise food labels from trusted overseas systems by default. Accept labels that meet UK, EU or US requirements, removing the need for New Zealand-specific packaging runs or item-by-item relabelling simply because the information is presented differently.
- Cut regulatory barriers to opening new stores. Remove unnecessary and inconsistent local requirements that add cost and delay when a supermarket wants to open in a new town.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“ACT would create a one-stop consenting shop for new market entrants - a single point where a business looking to open, or open multiple sites, can get their consents, their liquor licences, their approvals, in months, not years.

“ACT will allow food labels for trusted regulatory systems like UK, EU and US by default. This will lower the barrier to entry for international supermarkets, who will no longer need to do expensive runs of products specifically for the tiny Australasian market to open stores. ACT will roll out the welcome mat.

“Rather than joining the race to the bottom where we attack successful businesses, ACT’s policy is to make it easier for new businesses to come here, compete, and expand.”

# Paris Needs to Change

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/paris> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Rural

## Paris Needs to Change

ACT is announcing a science-based climate policy that puts New Zealand's interests first. If the Paris Agreement cannot accommodate targets that reflect the real warming impact of New Zealand's emissions, then New Zealand should leave it.

ACT’s proposed NDC would:

- Recognise a split gas approach that treats long-life gases like carbon dioxide and short-lived gases like methane differently. That is critical for recognising the efficiency of our agricultural sector.
- Revisit the Emissions Reduction Plans. ACT will reset these around realistic targets, the split-gas approach, and genuine environmental outcomes rather than compliance with a framework designed for industrialised economies with fundamentally different emissions profiles to ours.
- Keep agriculture out of the Emissions Trading Scheme. New Zealand dairy has a carbon footprint 46% lower than the global average. ACT opposes methane pricing because taxing the world's most emissions-efficient farmers won't change the climate. Putting a price on that isn't climate policy – it's a tax on the world's most efficient food producers, which makes your groceries more expensive while shifting production to countries that do it worse.

#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand's farmers are the most emissions-efficient in the world, yet they are treated like climate villains and punished by climate targets that ignore the difference between methane from livestock and carbon from fossil fuels,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“The Paris Agreement provides a pathway for New Zealand to issue its own Nationally Determined Contribution. ACT is campaigning to do that in the next term of Parliament so we can have a plan that is ambitious for New Zealand and reflects the science of climate change.

“Under the current approach, prime farmland gets converted to pine trees, farmers face new costs for emissions they're already managing efficiently, and global emissions don't drop – because other countries with higher-footprint production simply fill the gap. That's not an environmental outcome. That's an economic and environmental own-goal.

"Current climate targets treat methane from a cow the same as carbon from a coal burner. That just isn’t scientific. “The result is that New Zealand farmers are being told to cut production while other countries increase output. That's not reducing global emissions, it's sending our jobs, our land, and our food production offshore – to countries that produce it less efficiently and with a higher carbon cost. It's exporting jobs, investment, and food production overseas.”

ACT Climate spokesperson Simon Court says: “ACT will submit a new Split-Gas emissions target that focuses on actual warming. Long-lived gases will continue on a path to lowering emissions, while biogenic methane will be managed under a No Additional Warming approach.

“We will also permanently keep agriculture out of the Emissions Trading Scheme. Taxing the world's most emissions-efficient farmers won't change the climate. It will just make food more expensive and push production into less efficient countries.

“ Last year, ACT made it clear that the Paris Agreement is broken and that New Zealand deserves a better climate deal. Today, we are putting forward exactly what that better deal looks like.

“New Zealand produces dairy with a carbon footprint 46% lower than the global average. We should be expanding our production, not retreating. ACT is the only party with the courage to stand up to the UN, rewrite the rules, and secure a future where farming grows.”

# A real pathway to a trade

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/39242/attachments/original/1792377066/A_real_pathway_to_a_trade.pdf?1792377066> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

20.10. 2026

A real pathway to a trade ACT will end the obsession with university as the default pathway and give young New Zealanders a proper pathway into the trades.

New Zealand’s education system has been obsessed with pushing young people towards university. Success has too often been measured by whether a student goes on to get a degree, while trades have wrongly been treated as a second-best option. It’s an outdated attitude that has done a disservice to generations of young New Zealanders. For a bright, ambitious young person, becoming an electrician, builder, mechanic or engineer can be the most intelligent decision they ever make. They can earn while they learn, build valuable skills, avoid taking on a large student loan, and potentially go on to run their own business and employ others. A university degree can be a great investment. But so can a trade. Neither should be treated as inherently superior to the other. Yet our education system doesn’t reflect that reality. Schools have well-established pathways for students heading to university. Students interested in building, engineering, agriculture, mechanics or other vocational careers face a far less straightforward route. Opportunities depend heavily on which school they attend and whether that school can navigate a maze of funding programmes, eligibility rules and capped places.

The result is that talented students can reach the end of school without ever having a serious opportunity to discover whether a trade might be right for them. ACT wants to put an end to this university-first mindset and put trades on an equal footing. The Government has already made a good start. The replacement of NCEA will include industryled subjects with national curricula developed alongside the Industry Skills Boards established at the start of 2026. These subjects will cover areas ranging from building and construction to primary industries. The Government has also moved money away from Fees Free towards funding for Trades Academies. They provide valuable opportunities, but places remain capped and the programme has traditionally focused on students at risk of disengaging from school. There are good local examples of what can be done. Ashburton College and Palmerston North Boys’ High School have developed strong vocational programmes with local employers and communities. The problem is that schools have largely had to build these systems themselves. ACT would build a proper national pathway so that choosing a trade is just as straightforward and respected as choosing university.

A real pathway to a trade 20.10.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

01

Funding that follows the student

Schools should not lose money because a student spends part of the week learning somewhere else. Under the current system, a student may spend time with an employer or another training provider. That can reduce the funding available to their school even though the school remains responsible for that student. This gives schools a financial reason to keep students in the classroom. ACT would protect a school’s base and equity funding when a student undertakes approved vocational learning away from school. Schools would also receive funding for each student enrolled in an approved industry-led subject, for up to two subjects per student each year. The amount would depend on the cost of providing the subject. A course involving workshops, specialist equipment or higher safety requirements would receive more than one that can largely be taught in a classroom. The average topup is expected to be around $2,000 per student per subject. Existing funding from STAR, Gateway, Trades Academies and Vocational Pathways would be brought together as part of the new system. This is expected to be funded without needing any new spending outside of Education baselines. These programmes already support vocational education, but they operate through separate funding streams, rules and application processes. Several are also capped, meaning schools can only offer as many places as the programme allows. ACT’s system would be uncapped. Once a student enrols in an approved industry-led subject, the funding would follow them.

ACT will fund approved industry-led subjects through an uncapped per-student entitlement that follows enrolment.

02

An Industry Award with the same standing as University Entrance

University Entrance gives students, families and universities an easily understood indication that someone is prepared for tertiary education. There is no equivalent for a student preparing to enter industry training. ACT would create a family of Industry Awards for senior secondary students. An Industry Award would require a student to complete set requirements relevant to that industry alongside completed aligned academic subjects. For example, a student working towards a Primary Industries Award, might combine vocational subjects with agricultural science, biology or business studies. The award would give employers and training providers a simple indication that a student has already completed relevant learning and is ready to take the next step. It would not become a compulsory entry requirement for an apprenticeship. Employers would remain free to hire whoever they choose. ACT would work with Industry Skills Boards and NZQA to ensure that credits earned through approved industry-led subjects can be recognised after students leave school and count towards relevant apprenticeship and vocational qualifications, where appropriate. Students would be able to earn both an Industry Award and University Entrance in the same year. A student who begins preparing for a trade at 16 or 17 should still be able to choose university later.

ACT will establish Industry Awards that recognise preparation for industry training alongside University Entrance.

A real pathway to a trade 20.10.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

03

Keep adding new industry subjects

The Government has already identified a range of subjects for Industry Skills Boards to develop as part of the new curriculum. That list should keep changing as industry changes. Technology is creating new combinations of skills. Electronics and mechatronics are already being incorporated into the curriculum, and other areas will emerge as employers adopt new technology and new industries develop. Industry Skills Boards are better placed than the Ministry of Education to identify those changes. They should have an ongoing role in proposing and developing new subjects where there is genuine employer demand. A vocational curriculum designed today will become dated quickly if it is treated as finished.

ACT will have Industry Skills Boards continue developing industry-led subjects as technology and workforce needs change.

A trade should be an equal choice New Zealand needs skilled builders, electricians, mechanics, engineers and other tradespeople just as much as it needs university graduates. It’s absurd that we’ve spent decades encouraging bright young people to see university as the ultimate measure of success, while making it unnecessarily difficult for them to pursue practical careers. An apprenticeship shouldn’t be seen as a consolation prize for someone who didn’t go to university. For many young people, it will be the better choice. ACT will remove barriers to meaningful vocational education give students qualifications that recognise their preparation for industry, and give their future employers a greater say in what is taught. The purpose of education should be to help young people realise their potential, not steer them all down the same path.

A real pathway to a trade 20.10.2026

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 3

<!-- page 4 -->

Introduction New Zealanders are working hard, but wages do not stretch far enough. A comfortable retirement feels distant, even impossible, and young people are looking overseas for higher wages. The cost-of-living crisis is not only about high costs, the other half is about low wage growth. A more affordable life needs higher wages, and that requires confidence to invest and innovate. Any Government serious about making life affordable needs policies that promote investment and innovation. That won’t happen if the Government can’t even balance its own books. Yet the return to surplus keeps slipping further away and debt continues to grow. Taxpayers are being forced to spend more than $1 million an hour just paying interest on existing debt. That is money taken from health, education, infrastructure or lower taxes. ACT’s plan lowers debt by $12.4 billion. Less debt gives New Zealand room to respond to the next earthquake, a financial crisis, pandemic or other disruption. We need the financial capacity to support recovery without placing an unmanageable burden on taxpayers. It is immoral to cut taxes by borrowing. That simply pushes the bill onto future generations, with interest. Our priority is to balance the books with no new taxes, then deliver large-scale, broad-based tax relief. Lasting tax reductions must be backed by lasting spending control. ACT’s Fiscal Plan prioritises balancing the books and paying down debt, laying the groundwork for much lower, flatter taxes in the future. A forecast surplus is only credible if the Government is prepared to make the decisions needed to achieve it. That requires stronger spending control than we have seen to date, a sustained commitment to ending waste, and the discipline to resist new spending that cannot justify its cost. ACT’s Fiscal Plan sets out those choices. It makes government smaller and more accountable, reduces spending that fails to deliver value, and puts superannuation on a more sustainable path through gradual changes and provision for compassionate early access.

executives and remove them for failing to deliver results. Clear accountability will help deliver the savings in this plan. Spending discipline also makes room to improve the services people rely on. This plan funds better healthcare, stronger protection against crime, investment in local infrastructure and practical education initiatives. These include ACT’s Pharmacy First Policy, and young investor policy. While broad-based tax cuts are not in ACT’s Fiscal Plan, several strategic tax cuts are. These targeted changes are funded by the Plan’s savings, rather than additional borrowing, while bringing the return to surplus forward. ACT will remove tax on KiwiSaver investment earnings. It supports greater personal retirement saving and lets more of people’s returns compound over their working lives. People who put money aside for their future should receive more of the benefit. Broader tax reductions can follow once the books are back in surplus. The cap on the donation tax credit is removed and additional targeted tax relief is funded in this Plan but yet to be announced. By 2031, debt will be $12.4 billion lower under ACT’s Plan than current Treasury forecasts. New Zealand needs a credible path to surplus without new taxes, and an economy where work, saving and investment pay off. A stronger ACT presence in government will provide the determination to deliver both. That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential.

David Seymour ACT Leader

That work must start at the top. It is not credible for ministers to demand public sector savings while New Zealand has more ministers than most other countries, nearly twice as many as Japan. Excessive governance doesn’t just send the wrong signal, it is inefficient. Government has become tangled in overlapping departments and ministerial portfolios, leaving responsibility for budgets and results unclear. ACT will simplify government to 19 departments and 18 ministers, with clear responsibility for each department’s budget and performance. Ministers will be able to appoint chief

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 4

<!-- page 5 -->

Headline Figures ACT’s Fiscal Plan improves the operating balance in every year of the forecast period compared to the current Government’s plans. By 2030/31, OBEGAL reaches a surplus of $13.6 billion, compared with $8.9 billion under current Government plans. OBEGALx reaches $16.4 billion, compared with $11.7 billion. OBEGALx moves into a small surplus in 2027/28, a year before the Government’s current plans. The conventional OBEGAL returns to a $5.1 billion surplus in 2028/29.

Net core Crown debt, excluding the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, is lower than currently forecast each year and is $217 billion by June 2031. That is $12 billion lower than forecast in the Pre-election Fiscal Update. ACT’s new spending initiatives will be funded separately from the operating allowances, ensuring the remaining $2 billion annual allowance is available to meet cost pressures and fund improvements in essential public services, including health and education.

Tax Changes No Tax on KiwiSaver Earnings

Uncapped Donation Tax Credit

ACT will remove tax on qualifying investment earnings inside KiwiSaver funds. Tax taken from a return today also removes the returns that money could earn in future. Letting earnings stay invested gives savers the full benefit of compounding and helps them build retirement savings without requiring them to give up more take-home pay.

ACT will reintroduce an uncapped donation tax credit to encourage substantial philanthropic contributions, including towards the proposed National Cancer Centre. People willing to support public-benefit projects should not face an arbitrary ceiling on the tax recognition of their generosity.

Carbon Tax Refund ACT will return net carbon auction revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund. Carbon pricing raises the cost of fuel, electricity and other goods. Returning the revenue helps households meet those costs with an estimated $100 per household at current prices and prevents the ETS becoming another source of discretionary government spending. If the carbon price drops, Kiwis will instead benefit directly from lower prices for things like fuel and electricity.

Reform Crypto Tax Treatment ACT will establish clearer tax rules for digital assets, including a 12-month bright-line rule for qualifying personal investments and an exemption for low-value purchases. Professional traders and businesses will continue to be taxed under existing rules. Clearer treatment gives investors certainty and prevents small everyday transactions generating disproportionate tax paperwork.

Tax relief to be announced There is additional targeted tax relief to be announced costing $264 million in the first year.

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 5

<!-- page 6 -->

New Operating Expenditure ACT’s Fiscal Plan provides additional funding for the following areas including Health, Education, Infrastructure, and Law and Order.

Expand Pharmacy Care for Minor Ailments ACT will fund an expanded minor ailments scheme so accredited pharmacists can treat more common conditions, with clear referral pathways when a doctor is needed. Using the skills of community pharmacists makes care easier to access and frees GPs to focus on more complex patients.

Local Tourism Dividend ACT will pay councils $1 for each commercial guest night recorded in their district to support tourism-related infrastructure costs. Visitors generate revenue for central government but place demands on local roads, toilets, wastewater systems and public spaces. Sharing the benefits of tourism gives councils a reason to welcome visitors and reduces the burden on ratepayers without imposing a new bed tax.

Young Investors Fund The Plan provides approximately $35 million a year for a Young Investors Fund to encourage savings and financial literacy. This would give Year 11 students $500 in a controlled investment account, supported by financial education. Students would progress from term deposits towards managed funds and equities as they demonstrate the necessary knowledge. A small real investment gives students a reason to engage with saving, risk and business ownership, including those who would not encounter investing at home.

Overstayers Investigation Unit ACT will establish a dedicated unit within Immigration New Zealand to investigate and enforce overstaying rules. Clear responsibility makes enforcement more accountable and supports confidence in a migration system that welcomes people who contribute and follow the rules.

Rural Crime Funding ACT will fund additional rural policing, targeting 100,000 extra patrol hours a year and a dedicated rural crime unit. Distance and isolation make rural communities vulnerable to theft, poaching and livestock crime. A more visible police presence and better coordination improve protection where help can otherwise be far away.

Electronic Money Management ACT will introduce electronic money management for work-ready Jobseeker recipients who remain on a benefit for more than four months. Payments will be directed towards essentials such as rent, groceries, power and transport, while blocking alcohol, tobacco, gambling and cash withdrawals. This keeps taxpayer support focused on basic needs while maintaining an incentive to return to work.

Three Strikes for Burglary ACT will require a minimum three-year prison sentence without parole for offenders who meet the proposed Three Strikes for Burglary threshold. Repeated burglary causes lasting harm and takes away people’s sense of safety in their own homes. Keeping persistent offenders out of the community protects potential victims and makes the consequences clear.

Working with Children Check ACT will introduce a portable national clearance for paid workers and volunteers who work with children, with ongoing checks against new Police information. A check performed years ago can miss a risk that emerges later. Continuous monitoring, linked to employers and organisations, closes that gap while a portable clearance reduces repeated applications.

Independent Schools ACT will index the independent school subsidy to public school operational funding uplifts. Independent schools provide diversity and choice in New Zealand’s schooling system.

Initiative to be announced There is one remaining initiative to be announced which will cost $100 million per year.

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 6

<!-- page 7 -->

Operating Savings Reduce Future Operating Allowances ACT will reduce future operating allowances from $2.4 billion to $2 billion per year. Reducing these allowances by $400 million a year will encourage greater spending discipline while retaining $2 billion in new funding each year to meet emerging needs and improve frontline services. Because the savings accumulate over successive Budgets, this will improve the operating balance by $400 million in 2027/28, rising to $1.6 billion annually by 2030/31. Combined with ACT’s wider programme of reducing waste, this will help bring the books back into surplus sooner without increasing taxes.

Reduce Non-Frontline Spending From 2017 to 2023 under Labour, public service staffing ballooned by 39 per cent and government spending surged by 67.1 per cent, yet public services got worse. Taxpayers were paying more and getting less. ACT will return non-welfare spending outside protected frontline services to its 2017 level per person, adjusted for inflation and wage growth. We will protect the spending growth since 2017 in core frontline services such as health, education, defence, police, and children’s services. The adjustment will be phased in over three years, with 33 per cent of the savings target achieved in 2027/28, 66 per cent in 2028/29 and 100 per cent in 2029/30. This gives agencies time to plan and implement changes while maintaining essential services. ACT’s proposal to consolidate government departments will support this work. Giving each minister clear responsibility for a department’s budget and results makes it easier to identify waste, implement changes and hold decision-makers accountable.

The following examples sit within the overall savings programme. They are not additional savings on top of the headline total.

Abolish Demographic Ministries ACT will remove separate demographic ministries and place responsibility for effective services with the agencies that deliver them. Policy should respond to people’s needs, while avoiding duplicated advice and administration organised around identity. This will save around $187 million a year.

Reduce Foreign Aid to 2017 Levels ACT will reduce foreign aid to 2017 levels, excluding support for Ukraine. With the Government borrowing to meet its commitments, overseas spending must be weighed against domestic priorities and debt reduction. This will save around $283 million a year.

Bring other spending back to 2017 levels ACT will take an across-government approach, excluding protected areas, to reducing spending to 2017 levels adjusted for wages, inflation, and population growth. In some areas the savings will be more than the excess growth since 2017, in others the increased spending will be justified. For example, in 2027/28, spending on the Ministry of Social Development’s non-benefit budget (excluding Oranga Tamariki) will be $400 million higher than in 2017, even after adjusting for wage growth, inflation and increases in caseloads. If non-ETS environmental spending had kept pace with population, wages, and prices since 2017, it would be $890 million in 2027/28. In reality, it is $1.38 billion.

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 7

<!-- page 8 -->

Savings from transfer payments Gradually Increase the Superannuation Age

Bring Disability Benefits Under Control

ACT will gradually increase the age of eligibility for NZ Superannuation by three months a year, reaching 67 by

2035. As people live longer, keeping the age unchanged places a growing burden on working taxpayers. A staged increase gives people time to plan and makes the pension more sustainable. Early compassionate access will be provided for those who have spent a substantial portion of their career in physically demanding jobs.

ACT will require independent medical certification against clear criteria for health and disability benefits, with phased reassessment of existing recipients. People with genuine, enduring conditions will retain appropriate long-term support. Consistent assessment helps distinguish those unable to work from those who can work with support, protecting the safety net and reducing avoidable dependency. Our costing is based on bringing the number of mental health claimants back to its pre-pandemic level, relative to the working-age population, over four years.

Restrict Immigrant Access to Benefits ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for residence class visa holders. Immigration should bring opportunity and contribution, with newcomers expected to support themselves during their initial years here.

Remove KiwiSaver Subsidies ACT will replace the annual Government Contribution for members receiving employer contributions with relief from tax on qualifying investment earnings. This redirects support towards leaving savers’ own returns invested, where they can compound over time.

Consequential reduction in financing costs Lower Financing Costs Reducing borrowing also reduces the cost of servicing government debt. These consequential savings grow as the Plan takes effect, reaching $452 million in 2030/31. Lower interest bills make future budgets easier to balance without raising taxes.

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 8

<!-- page 9 -->

Non-Operating Changes Anti-social noise cameras

Epsom Secondary School Contingency

The Plan provides $2 million in 2027/28 for relocatable anti-social noise cameras. Excessive noise from operating a vehicle in an anti-social manner is already unlawful, but evidence is hard to collect after the perpertrator has gone. Cameras deployed in persistent problem areas make enforcement more practical and give communities a way to restore peace and quiet.

The Plan includes a $150 million capital contingency in 2027/28 for a new Epsom secondary school. The proposal would acquire the former University of Auckland Epsom campus for educational use. Providing another school can expand choice for families and relieve pressure on existing schools. The allocation is a contingency.

National Cancer Centre Contingency

Maintain the Suspension of NZ Super Fund Contributions

ACT’s Fiscal Plan includes a capital contingency of $2 billion for the proposed National Cancer Centre. The policy brings complex treatment, research, clinical trials and specialist expertise together at campuses in Auckland and Christchurch. Concentrating those capabilities can improve care and attract philanthropic and private investment. The contingency provides fiscal room while the funding mix and delivery arrangements are developed; it is not a statement that all project costs must be met by taxpayers.

ACT will maintain the suspension of contributions to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. Borrowing to place more money in investment markets adds risk to the Crown’s balance sheet while taxpayers are already paying interest on debt. Prioritising lower borrowing is a prudent use of limited resources.

ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 | 9

<!-- page 10 -->

# ACT’s Plan to Make Farming Fun Again

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/37460/attachments/original/1789711573/ACT's_plan_to_Make_Farming_Fun_Again.pdf?1789711573> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

ACT’S PLAN to

MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 2 -->

FOREWORD f r om ANDREW HOGGARD MP ACT Agriculture Spokesperson and dairy farmer

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 3 -->

I got into politics because confidence in rural New Zealand was at an all-time low. For years, farmers had been hit with one new rule after another. Freshwater regulations, Significant Natural Areas, winter grazing rules, emissions pricing proposals, the ute tax, firearms laws, health and safety paperwork, and layers of resource management red tape all added cost and uncertainty to running a farm. I had spent more than 20 years farming and had seen first-hand what happens when people in Wellington who don’t understand farming try to regulate every part of it. Things are much better now, thanks to ACT pushing the Government to go much further and faster in delivering real change for Rural New Zealand than it would have without ACT. The ute tax is gone. He Waka Eke Noa is gone. Agriculture has been kept out of the ETS. Freshwater farm plans are being simplified. The methane target has been halved. We have stopped the expansion of Significant Natural Areas, cut back unworkable winter grazing rules, restored 90day trials, and are replacing the Resource Management Act with new laws based on property rights. But there is much more to do. I want my daughters, if they choose farming, to have the freedom to farm well without the red tape I’ve faced for 20 years. That means getting the next big decisions right. Replacing the RMA is a major step forward. Further decisions about the national instruments and detailed standards under the new system will also have a significant impact on what farmers can do with their land. Freshwater rules still need to be rewritten. Te Mana o te Wai needs to be scrapped. Climate policy needs to reflect the science of methane and the fact that New Zealand is a world-leader in agricultural efficiency. ACT is the only party that has never supported introducing a price on agricultural emissions and we opposed the Zero Carbon Act when every other party supported it. I’m also acutely aware of the challenges facing rural communities in relation to rural school buses, access to healthcare, rural crime, and illegal rubbish dumping. ACT has a plan to address each of these important issues. Farmers do not need another politician telling them how to farm. They need a Government that respects property rights, sets clear rules around genuine environmental harm, and otherwise lets them get on with it. That is what this plan is about. Let farmers farm.

Andrew Hoggard MP ACT Agriculture Spokesperson Dairy farmer

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 4 -->

ACT’S RECORD f or RURAL NEW ZEALAND ACT went into Government promising to get Wellington off farmers’ backs. Since then, ACT has:

- Replaced the Resource Management Act with a system based on property rights

- Kept agriculture out of the ETS

- Scrapped He Waka Eke Noa

- Slashed Labour’s methane target

- Axed Labour’s ute tax

- Simplified freshwater farm plans

- Wound back unworkable winter grazing regulations

- Halted the expansion of Significant Natural Areas

- Restored 90-day trials for every employer

- Refocused health and safety laws on actual risk

- Reformed agricultural chemical and veterinary medicine regulation

- Delivered an additional $79 million in funding for wilding pine control

- Replaced the Arms Act with a new law focused on targeting criminals rather than punishing licensed firearm owners The next job is to lock those gains in and go further.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 5 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 6 -->

1 KEEP WELLINGTON OUT of FARMING Replacing the Resource Management Act is one of the biggest wins for rural New Zealand in decades. The legislation puts property rights at the forefront, but further decisions will still matter greatly for how the new system works in practice. Key decisions will be made through the new system’s national instruments, including National Policy Direction and National Standards. ACT needs to be in a strong position in the next Government to ensure key decisions put rural New Zealand front of mind. ACT will:

- ensure National Policy Direction puts property rights first and focuses on actual environmental harm;

- make sure rules recognise local conditions instead of imposing one-size-fits-all solutions from Wellington;

- keep standards clear, measurable and practical;

- remove Te Mana o te Wai and other vague spiritual concepts from freshwater regulation while backing practical steps to improve water quality;

- ensure those concepts do not simply reappear under another name in the new system;

- protect farmers from a return of Labour-style Significant Natural Areas;

- strengthen property rights through the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act; and

- expand voluntary and incentive-based conservation, including biodiversity credits and mechanisms such as the QEII National Trust. The replacement RMA creates a huge opportunity. ACT will make sure the detailed rules and national instruments deliver on its promise of a simpler, property-rights-based system.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 7 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 8 -->

2 PRACTICAL ENVIRONMENTALISM Farmers have every incentive to look after the land and water their businesses depend on. ACT believes environmental policy should focus on outcomes, work with farmers and recognise that New Zealand is not one giant catchment. ACT will:

- increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping;

- provide an additional $4.5 million a year for rural catchment groups to improve water quality, maintaining total funding at the current level of $13.5 million a year, with scope for further increases where groups can demonstrate strong results;1

- keep freshwater farm plans workable, practical and affordable;

- continue the war on wilding pines, building on the additional $79 million over three years already secured;

- allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land to control weeds, wilding pines and fire fuel; and

- ensure permanent forest owners carry the long-term costs and risks created by their forests, including sufficient pest control

1 This will be funded by reprioritising existing MPI spending, including from programmes such as the Primary Sector Growth Fund, which recently used taxpayer money to fund research for a private company into whether people sleep better on wool or synthetic bedding.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 9 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 10 -->

3 BACK FARMERS on CLIMATE New Zealand farmers produce food with some of the lowest emissions intensity in the world. Taxing production here does not stop people eating, it simply shifts production to countries that will produce the same food less efficiently. ACT is the only party that has never supported introducing a price on agricultural emissions. We stood alone against the Zero Carbon Act, opposed He Waka Eke Noa and successfully fought to keep agriculture out of the ETS. We will keep it that way. ACT will:

- keep agriculture permanently out of the Emissions Trading Scheme;

- oppose any agricultural emissions tax or pricing scheme;

- scrap the Net Zero target;

- repeal the Zero Carbon Act;

- abolish the Climate Change Commission;

- recognise the different warming effects of methane and carbon dioxide;

- ensure New Zealand’s international climate commitments do not force our farmers to bear costs their overseas competitors avoid; and

- scrap the artificial ETS price floor that props up the carbon price and makes blanket carbon farming artificially attractive. If New Zealand cannot secure a fair international climate deal, ACT is prepared to reconsider our participation in the Paris Agreement.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 11 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 12 -->

4 GIVE FARMERS THE TOOLS to GROW New Zealand farmers have always been early adopters of technology, often in spite of, not because of, the government. ACT will continue to cut red tape to make agri-innovation easier. ACT will:

- speed up access to proven agricultural chemicals and veterinary medicines;

- recognise trusted overseas approvals instead of forcing New Zealand to reinvent the wheel;

- cut unnecessary restrictions on agricultural drones;

- remove barriers to new farming technology;

- maintain employment settings that make it easier for farmers to hire and give people opportunities; and

- introduce a Rural Workforce Visa providing a reliable pathway for workers needed by farms and rural businesses.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 13 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 14 -->

5 BACK RURAL COMMUNITIES Rural New Zealand produces much of the wealth New Zealand depends on. It deserves public services that work. ACT will:

- fund 100,000 additional rural Police patrol hours every year;

- establish a dedicated rural crime unit;

- strengthen offences and penalties for livestock theft and poaching;

- extend Text 111 eligibility to rural areas where unreliable mobile coverage makes voice calls difficult;

- introduce Three Strikes for Burglary, so repeat burglars face a minimum three-year prison sentence without parole on their third conviction;

- introduce an Open Seat Rule so rural children can use spare seats on existing school buses going to nearby schools wherever practical;

- allow pharmacists to provide more everyday healthcare and manage more stable long-term conditions removing pressure on hospitals and GPs;

- enable 24-hour prescription e-lockers, making it easier for rural patients to collect medicines without a long trip during limited pharmacy opening hours; and

- remove red tape relating to homekill and make it easier for farmers to sell their products direct to consumer.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 15 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 16 -->

6 RESPONSIBLE GOVERNANCE f or A STRONGER ECONOMY Farmers make long-term decisions about land, stock, machinery and staff. They need stable prices, lower interest rates and confidence that Government will live within its means and stay out of commercial decisions it has no business making. ACT will:

- retain the Reserve Bank’s focus on keeping inflation under control so interest rates stay low;

- balance the Government’s books without introducing new taxes;

- return the books to surplus faster;

- keep finding savings so debt can be paid down rather than passed on to the next generation;

- maintain ACT’s commitment to No New Taxes; and

- keep cutting unnecessary regulation that raises the cost of doing business.

- respect the right of farmer-owned companies to make commercial decisions without politicians treating them as instruments of government policy.

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26

<!-- page 17 -->

Authorised by C. Purves, w ww.act.org.nz

<!-- page 18 -->

ACT’S PLAN TO MAKE FARMING FUN AGAIN

20 . 09 . 26
