documents/pdf-finish-the-settlements-win.title: Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal
documents/pdf-finish-the-settlements-win.text:
# Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/37097/attachments/original/1788930341/Finish_the_settlements__wind_up_the_Waitangi_Tribunal_FINAL.pdf?1788930341> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

10.0 9. 2026

Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal ACT will complete the remaining historical Treaty claims, end the Waitangi Tribunal’s contemporary jurisdiction, and wind it up once its historical work is finished.

The Waitangi Tribunal has made an important contribution to New Zealand. It was established in 1975 to investigate contemporary claims that the Crown had breached the Treaty. In 1985, Parliament extended its jurisdiction back to 1840, allowing it to investigate historical grievances and helping create the pathway for the Treaty settlement process. ACT supports completing full and final historical Treaty settlements as a pragmatic way to resolve past injustices, including where the Crown confiscated land or otherwise breached property rights. That work should be finished properly. But the Tribunal that exists today is very different from the institution established in 1975. Its contemporary inquiries have become increasingly ideological and expansive. Through urgent and kaupapa inquiries, it now routinely passes judgment on ordinary questions of government policy, proposes alternative policy settings, and seeks to influence decisions properly belonging to elected Governments and Parliament. The people who created the Tribunal would scarcely recognise the institution it has become. As New Zealand approaches 2040, two hundred years after the signing of the Treaty, it is time to complete the historical settlement process and move forward.

If the Government breaches someone’s rights today, New Zealanders should have strong legal protections and access to the courts regardless of their ancestry. ACT believes those protections should be strengthened for everyone, not maintained through a permanent separate system for one group.

01

Complete the historical settlement process

The Waitangi Tribunal’s historical jurisdiction has played an important role in identifying past Crown wrongdoing and establishing the basis for settlements. The Crown confiscated land, failed to recognise legitimate property rights, and committed other historical injustices for which those affected often had no realistic avenue of redress. Those claims should be heard and resolved. But a settlement process must eventually settle something. Parliament has already recognised the need for an end point. In 2008, it closed the door to new historical claims by setting 1 September 2008 as the statutory deadline for lodging them. The Tribunal itself now has a goal of completing its Inquiry into Remaining Historical Claims by 2030. Every eligible historical claim already before the Tribunal should be able to run its course.

Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal 10.09.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

ACT will limit the Tribunal’s jurisdiction to historical claims lodged by the existing 1 September 2008 statutory deadline and end its power to inquire into contemporary Government policy and conduct. Existing historical claims will still be heard and completed. 02 Stop the activism The Waitangi Tribunal was originally created to hear contemporary claims. But its ability to perform that role credibly depends on public confidence that it approaches those questions with restraint, objectivity, and respect for the proper role of democratic institutions. ACT does not believe the modern Tribunal meets that test. Its urgent and kaupapa inquiries increasingly resemble alternative policy processes. They range across questions such as citizenship, public-sector pay, electoral law, government communications, health, child welfare, resource management, and the design of legislation itself. Kaupapa inquiries in particular attempt to review whole areas of public policy and recommend how governments should govern them. That is the job of Ministers and Parliament. The Tribunal should not operate as a parallel policy institution, producing its own prescriptions for how elected Governments should exercise their mandate. After fifty years of institutional evolution, its contemporary jurisdiction no longer continues to serve New Zealand well.

ACT will end the Waitangi Tribunal’s jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, leaving it to focus solely on completing the remaining historical claims.

03 Protect everyone’s rights through the law Ending contemporary Tribunal claims does not mean giving governments a free hand to violate people’s rights. If the Crown unlawfully takes someone’s property, interferes with their rights, or otherwise acts outside the law today, that person should be able to challenge the Government through the courts. That protection should apply equally to every New Zealander. ACT has already announced that we will strengthen property rights for everyone by adding them to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. That would protect the peaceful enjoyment of property and provide that people should not be deprived of it except in the public interest, on just terms, and in accordance with law. Governments would face greater scrutiny when they interfere with people’s homes, farms, businesses, land, or other property. Those are protections every New Zealander should have. ACT does not believe one group should require a separate tribunal to protect interests that should instead be protected for everyone through the ordinary law. The answer to weak property rights is stronger property rights, not permanent parallel institutions. In fact, the Tribunal has opposed measures intended to strengthen protections against arbitrary government action, including the Regulatory Standards Act.

ACT will strengthen protection of property rights for all New Zealanders and ensure actual breaches of property rights by the Crown are dealt with through the ordinary legal system.

Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal 10.09.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

04 Wind up the Tribunal when the job is done The Waitangi Tribunal is currently established as a permanent commission of inquiry. ACT does not believe it should be permanent. Its historical work is finite and nearing completion. ACT will not impose an arbitrary calendar deadline that risks rushing legitimate historical claims simply to meet a date. Instead, the Tribunal will remain in existence only for as long as it takes to complete the historical work already before it. Its funding will reduce with its remaining workload so its resources remain focused on completing that task. Once the final historical claims have been completed, the reason for retaining the Tribunal will have come to an end.

Settle the past, strengthen the future The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand’s constitutional landscape for more than fifty years and has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances. But institutions should not exist simply because they have existed for a long time. As we approach 2040, the focus should be on completing the remaining historical settlements, protecting the rights of every New Zealander through the same law and courts, and moving forward under one law for all and one future together.

ACT will amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed.

ACT will finish the historical settlement process, strengthen property rights for all New Zealanders, and wind up the Waitangi Tribunal when its historical work is complete.

Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal 10.09.2026

documents/pdf-immigration-policy-stateme.title: Making immigration work for New Zealand
documents/pdf-immigration-policy-stateme.text:
# Making immigration work for New Zealand

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/mailings/49491/attachments/original/immigration_policy_statement_04.pdf?1777609770> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

03.05. 26

Making immigration work for New Zealand ACT is announcing new policy to make immigration work for New Zealand. One that welcomes people, but only if they share values of tolerance, freedom and democracy, help build infrastructure, and play by the rules.

01

Deport serious offenders

Residency is a privilege. When you commit a crime serious enough to receive a 10-year sentence, your victims don’t have a time limit on their suffering, so there shouldn’t be a time limit on accountability. ACT will ensure Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more can be deported no matter how long they’ve been here. This goes further than the Government’s current proposal to extend liability to 20 years. 02 Skilled visas for skilled jobs Accredited Employer Work Visas are meant to fill crucial skills gaps, but too often the gaps close and the categories remain wide open. Since July 2022, 2480 fast food workers were approved, compared to just 1,052 software engineers. 2,119 beauty therapists were approved, compared to

just 30 biomedical engineers. New Zealand even approved visas for 35 newspaper deliverers. ACT would have each skill category automatically expire every year. To remain open, they would need to show up-to-date evidence of demand. 03 Opportunity, not dependency Coming to New Zealand should be a path to opportunity – not a path to welfare. ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for all residence class visa holders. That means no jobseeker support, accommodation supplement, or income-tested benefits for a migrant’s first five years here. 04 A fair contribution for infrastructure New Zealand has an infrastructure deficit. More people means more pressure on our roads, schools, and hospitals – new capacity has to be paid for.

<!-- page 2 -->

ACT will introduce a $6 per day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, on top of existing charges. This ensures migrants contribute to New Zealand’s infrastructure from day one, before they start paying tax. The fee is expected to raise around $80 million a year, while remaining more affordable than comparable visas in Australia and the United Kingdom. 05 Stronger English language requirements If you want to live for any serious amount of time in New Zealand, you should be able to credibly speak the local language. Yet, for three of the five AEWV levels, there are no English language requirements.

ACT will extend basic English language requirements to all AEWV types, with higher standards for student and resident visa holders. Lower standards will be permitted for seasonal workers. 06 Enforce the rules There are 20,980 known overstayers in New Zealand right now. We need a clear, dedicated Government response. ACT will establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash will be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying will lose their accreditation.

ACT’s policy restores the basic bargain that New Zealand was built on. People are welcome here if they contribute, respect our democratic values, and help build the country.

documents/pdf-keep-new-zealand-moving.md.title: Keep New Zealand Moving
documents/pdf-keep-new-zealand-moving.md.text:
# Keep New Zealand Moving

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/36934/attachments/original/1788396907/Keep_New_Zealand_Moving.pdf?1788396907> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

0 4.0 9. 2026

Keep New Zealand Moving ACT will get more transport infrastructure built from every dollar, stop road-user revenue being wasted, build roads ahead of growth, and stop unnecessary rules pushing up the cost of getting around. New Zealanders pay a lot for transport through fuel tax, road-user charges, rates and tolls. They rightly expect that money to be spent building and maintaining the transport network. The current National Land Transport Programme forecasts $32.9 billion of investment over three years. More broadly, New Zealand has spent an average of 5.8 per cent of GDP on infrastructure each year over the past two decades – towards the upper end of the OECD – yet ranks towards the bottom for the value it gets from that investment. The problem is not simply how much we spend, but what we get for it. Too much is swallowed by optional extras, overengineered designs, deferred maintenance and rules that put politics ahead of value. Families are priced out of newer vehicles, while public contracts can still be shaped by ethnicity rather than merit. Every dollar wasted is a dollar that cannot fix a road, relieve congestion or stay in the pockets of New Zealanders. ACT will focus transport spending on movement, safety and resilience, demand value from every project, and then get out of the way of the people who build, drive and invest. ACT will keep New Zealand moving with six reforms to build more, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver.

01

Build what works

ACT will require major projects to publish the lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option, including the cost, delivery time and benefit-cost ratio of each. Where excessive design assumptions materially increase cost, the additional cost and benefit must also be disclosed. New Zealand has made simple infrastructure too complicated to build. Good engineering must manage genuine safety and resilience risks, but it must also identify safe, workable and affordable solutions. The Infrastructure Commission found this problem is widespread. Of 64 proposals submitted at stages requiring robust options and economic analysis, only 14 provided enough information to assess. Just two had properly considered cost when narrowing their options. The Commission warned that failing to consider lower-cost or non-built solutions may be contributing to infrastructure cost growth. The Burnside Bridge shows how this happens. The 99-metre single-lane bridge was badly damaged and closed after Cyclone Gabrielle. The council estimated that replacement could cost up to $16 million, but says this was a high-level estimate prepared without site, flood or geotechnical investigations or a settled bridge design. NZTA declined to fund a repair or replacement and allocated up to $560,000 to demolish the bridge and make the site safe.

Keep New Zealand Moving 04.09.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

A bridge builder initially proposed a simplified $2.75 million replacement, but later advised that a bridge meeting full public-road requirements would likely cost $6–9 million, subject to further investigation. The council has now authorised up to $100,000 to test a targeted repair. Overly conservative assumptions present the same risk. RCP8.5, the highest-emissions climate scenario, was used in flood assessments for the Woodend Bypass and Hastings’ Mangarau Stream works. At Woodend, NZTA’s expert found that RCP6.0 would produce rainfall estimates 5–10 per cent lower but would not materially change the assessed flooding outcomes. Neither project published a comparison showing the additional cost and benefit of designing around RCP8.5. The lesson is not that safety or resilience should be compromised. It is that the lowest-cost safe option must be properly investigated, priced and tested before high-level estimates, excessively conservative assumptions or optional design features become embedded in a project. Infrastructure should meet sound engineering standards and address real risks. Not every project needs to be bespoke or gold-plated at the expense of the people paying for it.

02 Build for growth ACT will require major growth areas to have funded transport-capacity plans, protect future routes early, and use clear traffic triggers to move projects from planning into construction so infrastructure arrives with growth. New Zealand keeps adding homes, jobs and freight demand, then acting surprised when the roads cannot cope. Councils approve development, the Crown controls the state highway, and each waits for the other to pay. Too often, the houses and traffic arrive years before the roads needed to carry them. Mill Road in South Auckland shows the problem. Rapid housing and business growth has pushed parts of the two-lane corridor towards or beyond 20,000 vehicles a day, yet additional road capacity has repeatedly lagged behind development. SH16

through north-west Auckland tells a similar story at a productivity-crushing 35,000 vehicles per day on a two-lane road. The same pattern is emerging around Tauranga, Hamilton, Queenstown and other fast-growing centres. Road charges, tolls, developer contributions, council funding and private capital can all bring investment forward. Development should help pay for the infrastructure it requires instead of loading every cost onto existing ratepayers or waiting for a single Crown cheque. ACT will make growth trigger action. On major two-lane growth corridors, 10,000 vehicles a day will trigger route protection, 15,000 will trigger consenting, design and a funded capacity plan, and 20,000 will trigger construction of additional lane capacity where growth is continuing. That means land is protected and projects are ready to build before congestion becomes entrenched.

03 Fix the network first ACT will protect maintenance and renewal funding in the National Land Transport Fund so it cannot be raided to pay for new capital projects. Road users see the basics failing: potholes left unrepaired for too long, blocked drains, weak bridges, recurring slips and roadworks that drag on while traffic-management bills grow. A dependable network starts with looking after the roads, bridges and drainage New Zealanders already rely on. GPS 2024 started turning that around by ringfencing pothole-prevention funding. In 2024/25 NZTA resurfaced 1,928 lane kilometres of state highway and rehabilitated another 349 lane kilometres, exceeding both targets. ACT will make that discipline permanent rather than let maintenance become the balancing item when new projects cost more than expected. Every Government Policy Statement should set a protected three-year allocation sufficient to meet published road-condition, resurfacing and rehabilitation targets. Once that allocation is set, NZTA should not be able to transfer it to new capital projects during the programme period.

Keep New Zealand Moving 04.09.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

04 Put delivery before ethnicity

05 Make road money deliver roads

ACT will make equal treatment a condition of Crown infrastructure funding. No Crown-funded project will use ethnicity to decide who can bid, how bids are scored, who receives preference or who must be subcontracted. Ethnicity-based spending targets and reporting requirements will also go.

ACT will ensure that non-functional art, monuments and decorative amenity features are ineligible for National Land Transport Fund funding.

Public contracts should be awarded on price, capability, safety and delivery - not ethnicity. In Government, ACT helped scrap Labour’s target for eight per cent of relevant Crown contracts to go to Māori businesses. Public money should buy the best result, with suppliers competing on equal terms. But these policies remain in local government. Auckland Transport directed $64.48 million to Māori-owned businesses in 2024/25, around 3.2% of expenditure. Its target rises to 5 per cent in 2025/26, with a longer-term goal of 10 per cent of supply-chain spending with Pakihi Māori. The $1.39 million Te Kia Ora Marae carpark was tendered only to Amotai-registered Māori-owned businesses. Auckland Transport’s Kake Mai programme also requires head contractors on new capital projects to partner with selected Māori and Pasifika-owned businesses. Closed tenders can be efficient where there is a genuine commercial reason to limit bidders. Ethnicity is not one. Small and emerging firms - including Māori and Pasifika businesses - should get a fair shot through simpler tenders, smaller contract packages and fewer barriers, and win work because they can deliver. ACT will put equal treatment into Crown funding agreements. Use ethnicity to decide who competes, who gets the work or where the money is spent, and the project will not receive Crown funding. Taxpayers will fund delivery – not ethnicity targets.

Motorists pay fuel taxes and road-user charges and rightly expect that money to be spent maintaining and building roads. Yet core transport budgets are still used for public art, decorative landscaping and cultural monuments that do not make a journey faster, safer or more reliable. For example:

- $630,599 for the 12-metre Te Manu Rangimaarie sculpture at the Piarere roundabout.

- $810,000 for the Te Waka sculpture on the Waikato Expressway.

- $2.238 million on the Oaro-to-Clarence corridor, including four pouwhenua, nine tekoteko, tunnel and surface murals, three artwork panels, artwork at stopping sites and palisade fencing.

- $1.876 million for five sculptures on Te Ahu a Turanga.

- $200,000 for the Hemo sculpture in Rotorua.

- $3.7 million for 35 pou and two taonga artworks on Te Ara Tupua. This illustrates a prioritisation problem. The true total is unknown because NZTA does not calculate or publish how much it spends nationally on art and other amenity features. The costs are bundled into individual project budgets, where each extra can be defended as a small proportion of a much larger project. Philanthropists, environmental groups, businesses, iwi and communities should be free to add the features they value, but those extras should be funded through voluntary contributions, sponsorship or local fundraising – not the roading budget.

Keep New Zealand Moving 04.09.2026

<!-- page 4 -->

06 Keep vehicle prices down for families ACT will scrap unrealistic vehicle-emissions settings, oppose arbitrary age bans and other rules that price affordable used vehicles out of the market, and require new proposals to disclose their effect on vehicle supply, prices and fleet turnover. Most New Zealanders do not replace an old car with a brand-new one. They trade up to the safest, most reliable vehicle they can afford. Used imports still account for around two in every five light vehicles entering the fleet and provide reliable cars around the $15,000 price point. But used-import passenger registrations have fallen from around 165,000 in 2017 to 85,000 in 2025, while the average age of New Zealand’s light passenger fleet has risen from 14.3 to 15.3 years. More than four in ten light vehicles are now at least 15 years old. Restricting affordable imports can make that worse. A family priced out of a ten-year-old Japanese hybrid does not suddenly find another $20,000 for a new car. They keep the old one longer. Standards should reflect the vehicles

actually available from Japan, our main source of used imports, not assume every household can afford new. ACT will make affordability the test. If an emissions, testing, or age rule reduces the supply of affordable vehicles, pushes up prices or keeps older cars on the road longer, ACT will scrap it.

Keep New Zealand moving New Zealand does not have to accept deteriorating roads, rising project costs and worsening congestion as the price of growth. We can build and maintain more with the money New Zealanders already pay by focusing on the basics and demanding value from every dollar. That means road funding for roads, practical engineering, maintenance before vanity projects, new capacity before congestion becomes entrenched, affordable vehicles for families, and public contracts awarded on merit. Transport is part of a bigger challenge. New Zealand needs to become a country that can once again build useful infrastructure at a reasonable cost and in a reasonable time.

ACT will build more, maintain what we have, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver – so New Zealand keeps moving.

Keep New Zealand Moving 04.09.2026

documents/pdf-let-small-business-get-on-.title: Let small business get on with business
documents/pdf-let-small-business-get-on-.text:
# Let small business get on with business

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/37328/attachments/original/1789360133/Let_small_business_get_on_with_business.pdf?1789360133> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

15.0 9. 2026

Let small business get on with business ACT will lower the cost and risk of employing people, make employment law simpler and fairer, and modernise tax rules so small businesses can hire, invest, and grow.

When Government makes hiring someone more expensive, managing an employment relationship more difficult, or resolving a problem more legally risky, businesses respond by hiring fewer people, offering fewer hours, or simply deciding not to take a chance on someone. That means the cost is not only borne by the employer. It is borne by the young person who cannot get their first job, the worker who misses out on extra hours, the person trying to get back into work, and the employee whose wage cannot rise because more of the business’s budget is being absorbed by regulation and compliance. Successful businesses employ people, invest in their communities, develop new products, pay wages and taxes, and compete to give customers better choices. Their success creates opportunities for other New Zealanders. That is why ACT believes Government should make it easier to do business, not pit employers and employees against each other when their success goes hand in hand. ACT has already delivered major changes in Government. We have repealed Fair Pay Agreements, restored 90-day trials, simplified employment law, replaced the broken Holidays Act, reduced unnecessary health and safety paperwork, and established a Ministry for Regulation dedicated to challenging rules that impose more cost than benefit. But there is more to do. Small businesses need certainty over their costs, confidence to take a chance on new workers, simpler ways to resolve employment problems, and tax rules that reflect the way modern businesses actually operate.

01

Freeze the minimum wage for three years

ACT will freeze the adult minimum wage for three years. When Government increases the cost of employing someone faster than productivity is growing, that cost has to show up somewhere. For a small business operating on tight margins, it can mean higher prices, fewer hours, reduced hiring, lower investment, or deciding not to create a job in the first place. The people most exposed are often those with the fewest alternatives. An experienced and highly productive worker will generally earn more than the minimum wage anyway. It is younger workers, people with less experience, and those trying to get back into work who are most likely to miss out when the minimum cost of hiring them rises beyond what an employer can justify. Wages can sustainably rise when workers become more productive and businesses can afford to pay more. But New Zealand’s productivity performance has been weak while Governments have continued increasing the cost of employing people regardless. A three-year freeze would give productivity and market wages time to catch up, while giving businesses certainty over one of their largest costs. Employers would remain free to pay more, as many already do.

Unlock New Zealand’s Potential 15.09.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

02

Introduce a Training Wage

ACT will establish a Training Wage at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20, available for their first 12 months with an employer. Getting your first job is harder when Government requires an employer to pay an inexperienced teenager almost the same minimum rate as an experienced adult from day one. Employing a young person often means taking a chance. They may need more supervision, more training, and time to learn the habits and skills expected in a workplace. The law should recognise that reality rather than pricing young people out of opportunities to gain experience. The Training Wage will be set at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage. It would apply to workers aged under 20 for the first 12 months they work for a particular employer. For workers covered by the new regime, it would replace the existing restrictive Starting-Out wage criteria. Ordinary employment protections would continue to apply. A meaningful Training Wage would reflect the additional cost of training inexperienced workers and give employers a stronger reason to create entry-level jobs. Early employment matters. A first job teaches practical skills, reliability, confidence and experience that make it easier to get the second job and the third. Government should be helping young New Zealanders onto the employment ladder, not pulling the first rung out of reach.

03

Allow protected employment exit negotiations

ACT will allow protected, without-prejudice negotiations so employers and employees can mutually agree an employment exit without unnecessary legal risk. Not every employment relationship works out. Sometimes the employer and employee can both see that the relationship has run its course, but the law makes having an honest conversation unnecessarily risky. Employers can be reluctant even to raise the possibility of an agreed departure because they

fear the conversation itself may later be used against them in a personal grievance or unjustified dismissal claim. Instead of encouraging an early, sensible resolution, the system can push both sides towards formal processes, lawyers, escalating costs, and greater conflict. Under this policy, an employer could invite an employee to discuss ending the employment relationship by agreement, including an offer of compensation. The employee would be under no obligation to participate or accept an offer. Those discussions would generally not be admissible in later employment proceedings. This will give adults room to have a practical conversation and reach an agreement without turning every difficult employment relationship into a legal battle.

04

Shorten the time limit for personal grievances

ACT will limit the time to take a personal grievance to the Employment Relations Authority to 90 days after it is raised, while retaining the existing rules for sexual-harassment grievances. Employment disputes should be resolved promptly, not left hanging over an employer for years. Under current law, an employee generally has 90 days to raise a personal grievance, but can then have up to three years to take it to the Employment Relations Authority. That can leave businesses facing prolonged uncertainty and the risk of litigation long after an employee has left or a dispute appeared to have ended. ACT would retain the existing 90-day period for raising a grievance. Once raised, the employee would generally have a further 90 days to take the matter to the Authority if it cannot be resolved. That period could be extended by written agreement between the employer and employee. Existing exceptional-circumstances provisions would remain, and the separate three-year timeframe for sexual-harassment grievances would not change. People should have a fair opportunity to pursue a genuine grievance, but businesses should also be able to move on once a reasonable period has passed.

Unlock New Zealand’s Potential 15.09.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

05

Make unions collect their own fees

ACT will end compulsory employer collection of union membership fees and make payroll deductions voluntary. Union membership is an agreement between a worker and a union. Collecting union membership fees should therefore be a matter for unions and their members. At present, employers can be required to deduct union fees from employees’ wages and transfer the money to the union. That makes a private membership arrangement someone else’s payroll administration. Modern banking makes it simple for unions to arrange direct payment with their own members. Employers and unions would remain free to agree voluntarily that the employer will deduct and transfer membership fees, but neither side would be compelled to do so.

06

Modernise the tax treatment of software and digital investment

ACT will modernise tax rules for software and digital investment so businesses can deduct productive technology investment on a clear and consistent basis. The way businesses invest has changed faster than the tax system. A modern small business may invest in software development, cloud systems, digital platforms, customised databases, automation, or other technology that is just as important to productivity as a machine sitting on the factory floor. New Zealand’s tax rules already recognise some software as depreciable property, but the treatment of modern digital investment can depend on technical distinctions about how software was acquired, developed, configured, or delivered.

That complexity can produce different tax treatment for investments that perform essentially the same economic function. Tax rules should not push a business towards one technology simply because Inland Revenue treats it more favourably than another. A good system should be as neutral as possible between physical and digital investment and recognise that software often becomes obsolete far more quickly than traditional plant and equipment. The Government should not penalise a business for investing in the technology that will make it more productive.

Back the people who create opportunity New Zealand will not become more prosperous by making it harder to employ somebody, take a chance on a young worker, resolve a dispute, or invest in technology. Small-business owners put their own time, savings and reputations on the line. When they succeed, they create jobs, train workers, serve customers, generate new ideas, and provide the tax base that funds everything Government does. ACT’s approach is different from the assumption that every problem needs another rule. New Zealanders have enormous potential when Government gets out of the way and allows them to get on with reaching it. Freezing mandated cost increases, opening the door to young workers, reducing employment-law uncertainty, cutting pointless payroll administration, and encouraging productive investment will give small businesses greater confidence to grow. That means more businesses competing, more people being hired, more investment taking place, and ultimately higher productivity and higher wages.

ACT will cut the cost, risk and red tape of doing business to unlock New Zealand’s potential.

Unlock New Zealand’s Potential 15.09.2026

documents/pdf-local-gov-letter-on-bill.m.title: Letter to the Minister of Local Government on unelected committee members (8 September 2025)
documents/pdf-local-gov-letter-on-bill.m.text:
# Letter to the Minister of Local Government on unelected committee members (8 September 2025)

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/mailings/34443/attachments/original/Local_Gov_Letter_on_Bill.pdf?1757481657> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

Hon. Simon Watts Minister of Local Government By Email: S.Watts@ministers.govt.nz 08/09/2025 Dear Minister, I am writing to raise my concern about local authorities appointing unelected representatives to council committees and subcommittees, with full voting rights. With voting local elections underway this week, New Zealanders have the opportunity to appraise their local candidates and hold to account their elected representatives. However, not all decisionmakers around council tables will be subject to this democratic test. Local authorities across the country have increasingly added unelected members to committees with voting rights. These members are often appointed by mana whenua, but may also include representatives of youth, business, or environmental lobby groups. Regardless, voters expect that decisionmakers can be held accountable and unelected appointees simply do not meet this standard. This undermines the democratic process and the integrity of the system. This issue is especially relevant as rising rates place pressure on household budgets. The ballot box is the only real accountability mechanism available to ratepayers – but that accountability disappears when councils appoint unelected individuals. Appointees who are not answerable to voters have no democratic incentive to reject wasteful spending or keep rates affordable. With ACT’s support, the Government has moved to defend local democracy by restoring the public’s right to vote on the existence of Māori wards. However, I am concerned that this move fails to address the greater problem of unelected members. Councils may move to counter a public vote against Māori wards by appointing unelected mana whenua representatives to council committees, along the lines of Auckland Council’s Independent Māori Statutory Board.

<!-- page 2 -->

In fact, in some territories we see councils with both Māori ward councillors and unelected mana whenua representatives, as is currently the case at Wellington City Council. To address this, I have drafted the Local Government (Restoring Democratic Integrity) Amendment Bill. This Bill would ensure that unelected members of committees or subcommittees do not have voting rights and do not count towards quorum. This protects a council’s ability to access outside expertise when appropriate, while making clear that voting power must rest with those who have the public mandate and who are accountable to voters. I urge you to consider adopting this as a Government Bill. This would reinforce the Government’s commitment to local democracy and help rebuild public confidence in local decision-making. Please find attached to this letter a copy of my Bill. I look forward to your response. Yours sincerely,

Cameron Luxton MP ACT New Zealand Parliament Buildings Cameron.Luxton@parliament.govt.nz

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/mailings/34443/attachments/original/Local_Government_%28Restoring_Democratic_Integrity%29-v1.9.pdf?1757481693> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

DRAFT FOR CONSULTATION

Local Government (Restoring Democratic Integrity) Amendment Bill Member’s Bill

Explanatory note General policy statement This Bill amends the Local Government Act 2002 to prohibit unelected members from being given voting rights on a local authority’s committees or subcommittees. Local authorities nationwide have been adding unelected people to committees with voting rights without voter consultation. This undermines the democratic process and democratic integrity. The Bill is a significant measure in protecting public trust in governance decisions, ensuring that decisions are made by those who are accountable to voters. Clause by clause analysis Clause 1 is the Title clause. Clause 2 is the commencement clause and provides for the Bill to come into force on the day after Royal assent. Clause 3 identifies the Local Government Act 2002 as the Act that the Bill amends.

Part 1 Amendments to principal Act Clause 4 and the Schedule provide for transitional matters. Clause 5 amends clause 23 of Schedule 7 of the Act to discount non-voting members from quorum calculations. This clause also amends clause 31 to clarify that only elected members of a local authority can be members of a committee or subcommit‐ tee unless the local authority expressly resolves otherwise, and to provide that mem‐ bers of a local authority’s committees or subcommittees who are not elected members of the local authority are not entitled to vote at meetings of those committees.

The effect of this amendment is that members appointed by Houkura (the independent Māori statutory board provided for in the Act) would not be able to vote on those committees.

# No tax on KiwiSaver earnings

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/38054/attachments/original/1790978996/No_tax_on_Kiwisaver_earnings_FINAL.pdf?1790978996> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

0 4.10. 2026

No tax on KiwiSaver earnings ACT will give New Zealanders a better deal for retirement by removing the tax on KiwiSaver earnings.

Other parties at this election want to make New Zealanders put more money into their KiwiSaver, leaving less in their back pocket to fund today’s cost of living. ACT is the only party proposing to stop taking money out of their KiwiSaver through taxes. People should be encouraged to build savings of their own so they can live a comfortable life in retirement. But the tax system currently works against them. The Government taxes your KiwiSaver investment earnings year after year, for as long as you save. The result is less money reaching people’s accounts, less money compounding over a working life, and smaller retirement savings than New Zealanders would otherwise have. ACT will remove the tax on New Zealanders’ KiwiSaver earnings. We will give New Zealanders a better deal for retirement that rewards saving and leaves more of their own money invested for the future.

01

Stop taxing your KiwiSaver earnings

The biggest advantage of saving for retirement is time. Money invested early can earn a return, those returns can earn further returns, and over decades compounding can turn relatively modest contributions into a substantial nest egg.

1

But KiwiSaver investment earnings are taxed every year. That does not just remove the tax paid today. It also removes every future return that money could have earned.

ACT will remove tax on qualifying investment earnings inside KiwiSaver funds, allowing returns to remain invested and compounding tax-free.1 Sensible rules will be put in place to protect the integrity of the tax system and ensure that KiwiSaver remains a genuine retirement savings vehicle and not a way to shelter large existing investment portfolios from tax.

02

End the money-go-round

The Government currently taxes money growing inside KiwiSaver, then gives some savers a small annual Government Contribution back. The only real winner from this money-go-round is the bureaucracy that clips the ticket along the way. ACT would rather stop taking the money in the first place.

ACT will end the KiwiSaver Government Contribution for members receiving employer contributions and replace it with substantially greater tax relief inside their KiwiSaver accounts.

This tax relief would also apply non-KiwiSaver superannuation schemes.

No Tax on KiwiSaver earnings 04.10.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

03

Case studies

More for retirement without less for today

The examples below provide an indication of the impact on different Kiwis’ KiwiSaver balances, and highlight the significant impact of investing long-term. 2

- A 20-year-old builder earning $60,000 would see an additional $209,486 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

- A 25-year-old graduate earning $80,000 would see an additional $173,522 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

- A 25-year-old nurse earning $100,000 would see an additional $217,366 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

- A 35-year-old supermarket worker earning $60,000 would see an additional $64,182 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

- A 40-year-old small business owner earning $120,000 would see an additional $69,100 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

- A 50-year-old office manager earning $80,000 would see an additional $20,878 in their KiwiSaver by the time they reach age 65.

The Government should not be taxing people for doing the right thing. New Zealand should be a country where people are encouraged to work, save, invest and build assets of their own. ACT’s changes mean more of your investment returns stay invested, and more of your money is left to compound over your working life. That means a bigger retirement nest egg without forcing New Zealanders to give up more of their pay today.

ACT will stop taxing the investment earnings inside KiwiSaver, and end the bureaucratic money-go-round of taxing savings only to hand a small portion back.

documents/pdf-one-law-for-all-policy-06..text:
# One Law for All Policy

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/36437/attachments/original/1787277161/One_Law_for_All_policy_06.pdf?1787277161> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

23.08.2026

One Law for All. One Future Together. ACT will put equal rights and the rule of law at the heart of our constitution, protect your property, put Parliament back in charge of the law, and stop vague Treaty clauses that leave courts and officials to decide what the law means.

Every New Zealander should be equal before the law. Parliament, democratically elected by the people, should make the law. Everyone, including the Government, should be bound by the law. And the property people work hard to build and own should be protected. These principles speak to who we are as a country, our national identity, and what we hold as important. They should guide every Government, policymaker, court, and person exercising public power. But they are not as clearly reflected in our law as they should be. Courts have increasingly developed Treaty principles and tikanga beyond what Parliament has clearly written into law, while Parliament has too often used vague Treaty clauses that leave judges and officials to decide what those laws mean. ACT will change that. Many New Zealanders will have strong views on how these proposals should be implemented. ACT is open to that debate, but firm about the principles and results we expect.

01

Enshrine core democratic principles in law

ACT will put three fundamental principles into the Constitution Act: Parliament makes the law, the rule of law is fundamental, and every New Zealander is equal before the law. The Constitution Act 1986 is one of the most important parts of our constitutional framework. It sets out the basic structure of government, but says surprisingly little about the principles our democracy stands for. ACT will add three principles to the Constitution Act:

- Parliament is sovereign;

- the rule of law is fundamental; and

- all New Zealanders are equal before the law. These principles are the foundation of a free society and deserve a clear place in New Zealand law in their own right.

One Law for All. One Future Together. 23.08.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

02 Protect your property in the Bill of Rights

03 Put Parliament back in charge of the law

ACT will add property rights to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, giving stronger protection to your home, farm, business, and other property.

ACT will reassert that Parliament has the final say, not the courts.

New Zealand protects many basic rights in the Bill of Rights Act but property is missing. ACT will insert into the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act a property right modelled on similar clauses from other jurisdictions including the peaceful enjoyment of property and no deprivation except in the public interest, on just terms, and in accordance with law. The things you have worked, saved, and taken risks to own should not be vulnerable to unfair government action. Property rights matter well beyond cases where the Government takes someone’s land. Regulations and government decisions can also wipe value from property, or restrict how it can be used. Putting property rights in the Bill of Rights would mean governments face greater scrutiny when they interfere with what people own. It would not give courts the power to strike down laws passed by Parliament. But it would make governments explain and justify interference with property more clearly. As with other rights in the Bill of Rights, Courts would be required to interpret legislation so that a meaning consistent with the right must be preferred where possible.

Recent Supreme Court decisions have pushed the line further than Parliament ever legislated. Parliament has pushed back in some instances such as the Smith v Fonterra case and the Marine and Coastal area case. But others such as Ellis, where the Supreme Court widely expanded the use of tikanga in the law have not been responded to. New Zealanders elect Parliament to make the law and courts have an essential role interpreting and applying that law. But the balance is lost when judges create new legal duties that Parliament has never written into law, or which it has clearly chosen to address in other ways. ACT will push back where courts have clearly gone beyond what Parliament has enacted. We will make clear when tikanga can be used by the courts. Our starting point is that it should apply only where it is directly relevant to the case (for example, a dispute between iwi), or where Parliament has expressly provided for it. It should not gradually become a separate source of law applying to broad areas of unrelated law without Parliament ever deciding that it should. We will amend the Legislation Act 2019 to ensure statutes mean what Parliament enacted, read in the context of the time they were passed, and so that judge-made presumptions can resolve ambiguity but cannot override clear statutory language. We will define the ‘rule of law’ in the Senior Courts Act 2016 to make clear that the law should be certain and Parliament has the final say.

One Law for All. One Future Together. 23.08.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

04 Stop vague Treaty clauses creating uncertainty and dividing New Zealanders ACT will stop governments writing vague Treaty clauses into law and leaving courts and officials to decide what they mean. Parliament also has a job to do. Often the courts are responding to a lack of clarity or Parliament’s silence on a particular area of law when they make decisions that substantially change the interpretation of the law. When Parliament refers to the Treaty, it should say exactly what it means. Too often, laws use broad phrases such as “give effect to the principles of the Treaty” or “have regard to the principles of the Treaty” without saying what those words actually require. That leaves major decisions to officials and courts after the law has been passed. It creates

uncertainty for everyone. Over time, those vague clauses can be used to create new duties and different treatment based on race that Parliament never clearly agreed to. ACT will put a stop to that. Before any Bill containing a reference to the Treaty is drafted, Cabinet must explicitly agree what Treaty interests, if any, are engaged, on whom they fall, and what specific obligations they create. In addition, when an existing law is being changed or replaced, the Treaty interests must be identified and listed specifically, and any vague or high-level clauses removed. Regulatory Impact Assessments should explain what each Treaty clause will actually do in practice, including what decisions it changes, what it costs, and how it will be enforced. These changes will be made through Cabinet rules, the Cabinet Manual, and changes to legislation where needed.

One law for all means the same rights, the same duties, and the same protection under the law. That is how we build One Law for All and One Future Together.

One Law for All. One Future Together. 23.08.2026

# Backing Hunters

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/36342/attachments/original/1787117027/policy_backing_hunters_02-2.pdf?1787117027> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

2 5 . 0 7. 2 6

Backing Hunters ACT is announcing a plan for hunting and conservation, one that funds the volunteers already maintaining our huts and trap lines, puts hunters in charge of managing game animals within firm conservation limits, and reopens the backcountry New Zealanders already own.

New Zealand’s laws still treat game animals as pests to be controlled, and in national parks, exterminated as far as possible. They fail to properly recognise hunters for their added value to conservation, game animal management and back country maintenance contribution, sidelining a large, skilled, and motivated workforce already in the hills. It is clear DOC cannot manage that country on its own. ACT’s plan will treat hunters and the animals they value as part of the solution, not the problem, placing delivery and decisionmaking in their hands.

Island whitetail deer and Himalayan tahr have no plan recognising their value. The current Government is already recognising valued species like Wapiti and Sika, we should continue this work.

PART ONE — HUNTERS IN CHARGE OF GAME ANIMALS

PART TWO — FUNDING & DELIVERY

01 Empowering hunter led management

03 Fund the volunteers who maintain the backcountry

Game animals on conservation land are managed by the one agency whose default is to control or exterminate them. The Game Animal Council was created to give hunters a real say but was handed a seat at the table rather than a hand on the levers.

ACT will transfer responsibility for managing game animals on conservation land from DOC to the Game Animal Council, meaning hunters will set the targets rather than just being consulted. This will include full funding for all their current and proposed duties. 02 Protect our most valued herds The law still treats introduced game animals as pests to be exterminated “as far as possible,” and treasured herds like Stewart

ACT will recognise game animal and gamebird species as valued natural resources to be sustainably managed in relevant legislation, and designate New Zealand’s most valued game herds as Herds of Special Interests, starting with Stewart Island whitetail deer.

DOC manages over 950 huts and 15,000 km of tracks but is failing to deliver on their upkeep. DOC faces a 30% maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. Hunting, tramping, and conservation groups already restore huts and maintain tracks at a fraction of the cost using volunteers and common sense but survive hand- to-mouth on annual discretionary grants.

ACT will require DOC to give the first right of funding to community groups, if they can provide a competitive option. This would allow for multi-year contracts, giving Kiwis a hand in maintaining and protecting the back country amenities they enjoy.

Backing Hunters 25.07.26

<!-- page 2 -->

04 Reward hunters for pest control Recreational hunters are already in the hills running trap lines and removing predators, but the new nature-credit market does not recognise their efforts, and they are routinely shut out of pest-control decisions affecting them.

ACT will open the Voluntary Nature Credits Market to accredited hunting groups so they can earn biodiversity credits for verified results and ensure the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association (NZDA) and Game Animal Council

(GAC) are formally represented in predator removal decision-making.

PART THREE — ACCESS TO THE BACK COUNTRY 05 Fairer venison recovery DOC’s arbitrary rules force commercial venison recovery operators to use expensive turbine helicopters. Aircraft safety should be the Civil Aviation Authority’s job, not DOC’s. Current permits also let operators strip out the trophy stags that recreational hunters value most.

ACT will leave safety to the CAA and stop DOC from dictating which helicopters recovery operators can use. ACT will allow the GAC to restrict commercial take by animal gender when necessary, so operators and recreational hunters share a well-managed resource fairly. 06 Open the backcountry from the air For rugged backcountry like Fiordland a helicopter is the only time efficient way in, yet huge areas are closed by no-fly and no-landing zones, defined by legacy lines on a map with no clear conservation or safety reasoning.

ACT will allow the Game Animal Council to designate sensible, accessible landing sites and require DOC to adopt clear, public and uniform testing processes for simplistic assessment. 07 Making hunting access a priority Much of New Zealand’s public land is hard to access. Securing access for hunters isn’t a priority for the body responsible.

ACT will direct the Outdoor Access Commission to prioritise access for hunting in its work programme.

PART FOUR — PROTECTING LAWFUL HUNTING 08 Stopping dangerous interference with hunting Hunters acting safely and within the law can be deliberately obstructed by people who step into the line of fire to stop a shot being taken. This is dangerous and a deliberate disruption of a lawful activity, yet no specific offence addresses it.

ACT will create an infringement offence for deliberately standing in the line of fire of a lawful hunter, deterring dangerous sabotage and keeping the backcountry safe for everyone. 09 Protecting game bird shooters from harassment Drones or helicopters can be used by activists todeliberately scatter or flush out game birds. This disturbs the birds and often is used simply to try and sabotage a lawful hunt. There is currently little legal remedy to deal with this.

ACT will create an infringement offence for harassing game bird shooters with drones or helicopters, protecting both the birds and the hunters who value them.

ACT’s plan backs the people already in the hills, the hunters, volunteers and clubs who look after the land we all own, to manage it for conservation, recreation and the regions, instead of locking them out.

Backing Hunters 25.07.26

# Closing the medicines gap

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/36341/attachments/original/1787116696/policy_document_medicine_04-3.pdf?1787116696> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

2 6 . 0 7. 2 6

Closing the medicines gap No New Zealander should have to empty their savings, uproot their family, or leave the country to access medicines Australians receive as a matter of course. ACT will put New Zealand on an achievable pathway to close the medicines funding gap with Australia by 2033.

The medicines gap New Zealand currently spends just 4.9 per cent of its health budget on medicines. Australia spends 12.2 per cent, while the OECD average is 13.3 per cent. Australia funds 142 modern medicines that are not funded in New Zealand. Thirty-eight per cent of those are cancer medicines. Often, the medicine a patient needs is already on Pharmac’s Options for Investment list. Pharmac has assessed it as a treatment worth funding, but it remains unavailable because the medicines budget has run out. Pharmac is not the problem. It negotiates hard, secures low prices, and identifies medicines that deliver real health gains. The problem is that successive governments have expected Pharmac to deliver first-world healthcare with a second-rate medicines budget. Pharmac’s cost-effectiveness has effectively been punished. In Budget 2026, the health system received a $1.5 billion funding uplift, but Pharmac received only $13.5 million. While Pharmac is required to extract the greatest possible value from every dollar, the wider health system does not always face the same discipline.

The Government has made more medicines available than any recent government. However, that is cold comfort to a family whose loved one is still waiting for treatment. Medicines promises cannot be made lightly. Desperate patients have too often been let down by political commitments that were not credible or achievable. New Zealand needs a clear, sustainable funding pathway that can command support across Parliament and endure beyond a single term of government.

ACT’s commitment: A pathway to parity ACT will put New Zealand on a pathway to close the seven-percentage-point medicines funding gap with Australia. The proportion of the health budget spent on medicines will increase by one percentage point each year until New Zealand reaches parity with Australia in 2033. This will mean more New Zealanders receive medicines that Pharmac has already identified as worth funding, rather than remaining on waiting lists because the budget has been exhausted.

Closing the medicines gap 26.07.26

<!-- page 2 -->

The policy will steadily change the composition of a growing health budget. It will not increase total health spending beyond what is already expected, require additional taxes, or reduce the size of the non-medicines health budget. Health spending has grown by an average of eight per cent a year over the past five years. ACT would direct one percentage point of annual growth toward medicines. Had the policy applied in Budget 2026, the medicines budget would have increased by approximately $320 million. The remainder of the health system would still have received an increase of around $1.2 billion. This is a gradual and achievable approach. It recognises that governments must make choices within the health budget and gives Pharmac a reliable pathway to fund more modern treatments over time.

Why fund Pharmac? Pharmac plays a vital role in New Zealand’s health system. It negotiates prices, assesses clinical benefits, and decides which medicines will produce the greatest health gains from the funding available. Its Options for Investment list contains medicines Pharmac considers suitable for funding when sufficient budget becomes available. Increasing the medicines share of the health budget will allow more of those treatments to reach patients. Modern medicines can also reduce pressure elsewhere in the health system. Effective treatment can prevent hospital admissions, allow people to remain healthier for longer, and help patients continue working and paying taxes. The policy is therefore not simply about spending more. It is about spending smarter and recognising the wider value created when patients receive effective treatment earlier. ACT will seek cross-party support for this pathway. Medicines funding affects families across every community, and patients deserve confidence that progress will continue regardless of changes in government.

Every hospital admission prevented is better for the patient and better for taxpayers. Closing the medicines gap means fewer families being forced to beg for relief, sacrifice their savings, or leave New Zealand for treatment. It means a health system that values modern medicines, keeps people healthier, and gives New Zealanders the same hope that patients across the Tasman already receive.

Closing the medicines gap 26.07.26

<!-- page 3 -->

Costing This policy would increase the medicines budget as a proportion of the health budget by one percentage point each year for seven years reaching 12% in 2033/34. This is estimated to result in the medicines budget reaching $5-6 billion (a growth of just over $3-4 billion from the 2026/27 budget of ~$1.8 billion). On average additional medicines spending per year will be between $500-650 million.

FY
