# Keeping Children Safe

*ACT New Zealand policy document (PDF). Source: <https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/36338/attachments/original/1787114789/Working_With_Children_policy_04.pdf?1787114789> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised. PDF page breaks are marked with HTML comments; tables are reproduced with their original layout.

<!-- page 1 -->

18.08.2026

Keeping Children Safe ACT will introduce a single national Working with Children Card to improve child safety while reducing duplicated bureaucracy for employers and community organisations.

Parents should be able to leave their children with a teacher, coach, afterschool carer, or volunteer knowing the adults around them have been properly checked and remain safe to work with children. The current system does not provide that assurance. Safety checks are carried out by individual employers and generally only rechecked every three years. This provides only a snapshot of a person at one point in time, with no consistent system for identifying risks that emerge between checks. ACT will introduce a single national Working with Children Card that follows the worker, is continuously monitored, considers additional relevant information, and replaces duplicated screening by individual organisations. Queensland has operated a similar system called the Blue Card since 2001. Today, more than one million people hold Blue Cards. In the 2025/26 financial year, 2,438 cards were cancelled or suspended and 6,403 individuals applied and were prevented from obtaining a card, and therefore prevented from working with children. Every Australian state now operates a form of working-with-children clearance.

01

One card

People working with children should not need to undergo the same checks again every time they change jobs or volunteer for another organisation.

ACT will introduce a Working with Children Card that belongs to the individual rather than the employer and is valid for three years. Once issued, the card could be used across eligible jobs, schools, clubs, businesses, and community organisations. Instead of each organisation conducting its own Police check, employers would simply verify that the person holds a valid card. This will reduce duplication, free up Police and Ministry of Justice resources, and make it easier for small organisations to meet their child-safety responsibilities.

Keeping Children Safe 18.08.2026

<!-- page 2 -->

02 One clear standard

04 No card, no start

Whether someone is safe to work with children should not depend on which organisation happens to assess them. ACT will establish a single national standard for determining eligibility for a Working with Children Card. Assessments would consider relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings, and other records relating to children or child-related work. Serious offences against children would result in automatic disqualification. More complex cases would be assessed against clear risk criteria rather than leaving individual employers to interpret records and make difficult judgement calls themselves. The same standard should apply to every applicant, wherever they work.

Children should not be placed at risk while an adult’s safety check is still being completed. ACT will require a person to hold a valid Working with Children Card before they begin child-related work. Queensland provides a useful benchmark. Straightforward applications with no relevant Police or other information can often be processed within five days, while more complex cases can take several weeks. During that assessment period, the applicant would not be permitted to begin working with children. The principle is simple: no card, no start.

03 Continuous safety monitoring A safety check should not become outdated the day after it is completed. ACT will link the Working with Children Card to ongoing information from Police and relevant regulatory bodies. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked and their employer notified. Employers would no longer have to wait for the next three-year check to discover that a worker’s circumstances have changed. The system would also share relevant information with professional regulators, employers and other organisations that work with children. Someone removed from a regulated profession such as teaching because they pose a risk to children should not be able to move into an unregulated role and continue working with them. Eligibility to work with children will be monitored in real time, not checked once every three years.

05 Training before they start Anyone trusted to work with children should understand the basic responsibilities that come with that role. ACT will require every Working with Children Card holder to complete a short, standardised childprotection course before beginning work. Similar to a first-aid course, the training would establish a common baseline of knowledge for people working in child-related roles. It would cover professional boundaries, recognising and responding to concerns, reporting procedures, and relevant obligations under New Zealand law. Training would be refreshed when the card is renewed.

Keeping Children Safe 18.08.2026

<!-- page 3 -->

Costing The estimated cost of the scheme is scaled from Queensland, which has a comparable population and operates a similar system. The estimates assume some existing screening and administrative infrastructure can be reused, reducing establishment and operating costs. Paid workers would pay a modest application fee, often covered by the employer. Volunteers and students undertaking placements would be exempt or pay a discounted rate. Queensland currently charges $108.30 for paid applicants, while checks are free for volunteers and students.

Cost component

Estimated cost (Saving)

One-off establishment cost

$12–20 million

Annual operating cost

~$50 million per year

Revenue recovered through application fees

(~$37.5 million per year)

Net annual cost to taxpayers

~$12.5 million per year

On these estimates, application fees would recover around 75 per cent of annual operating costs, leaving a net ongoing cost to government of approximately $12.5 million a year.

Keeping Children Safe 18.08.2026

# Plenty Is Possible

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/plenty-is-possible> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Hunters and Firearms

## Plenty Is Possible

New Zealand should be one of the best places in the world to fish. Whether you make your living at sea or take the kids out on a Saturday, there should be more fish in the water and a fair chance of bringing something home.

Instead, too many fisheries are managed around scarcity. Local depletion can be hidden inside huge management areas, vulnerable coastlines can be stripped, and blunt rules can punish responsible fishers without stopping the real damage.

ACT believes plenty is possible. We will protect the resource without locking people out of it, rebuild fisheries where they are depleted, and manage important stocks for abundance rather than the bare minimum.

Read our full policy, Unlocking New Zealand’s Fishing Potential, here.

### ACT will:

- Restore abundance in the Hauraki Gulf. Establish a distinct fisheries management area matching the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park, so catch settings reflect what is actually happening within the Gulf instead of averaging it across a much larger area. Existing quota holders would keep their proportional property rights.
- Stop rock pools being stripped. Introduce a nationwide combined recreational daily bag limit of 10 for shellfish and other covered species that do not already have their own limit. Families could still gather a modest feed, but a small number of people could no longer strip an area bare.
- Keep scallop dredges out of closed fisheries. Permanently end dredging in currently closed North Island scallop fisheries and allow selective, lower-impact harvesting if stocks recover.
- Make fishing levies reflect the damage caused. Require Fisheries New Zealand to assess the environmental and economic costs of major harvesting methods, then rebalance existing levies without increasing the overall burden. Higher-impact methods would pay a greater share and lower-impact fishing would pay less.
- Make serious rule-breaking carry serious consequences. Increase and stagger infringement fees so minor breaches are treated differently from deliberate, repeat or large-scale offending.
- Aim for abundance, not survival. Stop treating maximum sustainable yield as the finish line. ACT will progressively manage important fisheries for larger fish populations, giving them room to withstand poor spawning years, changing conditions and mistakes in the science.

### In our team’s words:

ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“Fishing puts food on New Zealand tables whether it is caught off the rocks or picked up with Friday night’s chips. It supports people who make their living at sea and is part of growing up in this country.

“We should not accept decline as normal. A system that aims to leave just enough fish in the water to sustain the maximum possible catch is setting the bar too low. ACT wants real abundance.

“A larger fish population gives us breathing room when spawning is poor or the science gets it wrong. It also means commercial crews spend less time and fuel finding their catch, while families have a better chance of bringing home dinner.

“New Zealanders do not have to choose between fishing and conservation. A healthy marine environment is what makes a successful fishing industry possible. The answer is to target the actual harm, protect vulnerable places and back responsible fishers."

## Economy & Cost of Living

#### Wealth can’t solve all of our problems, but it makes most of them easier. The cost of living crisis is half about high prices, and half about having a low wage economy. We need policies that will make it easier to produce and provide, with more investment in better technology and skills, with more entrepreneurial spirit.

#### The Government cannot create wealth itself, because every dollar the Government has is taxed from someone who created it. What the Government can do is create the conditions and encourage the culture of wealth creation.

#### We believe success spreads, one person’s success can help, inspire, or give the means to invest in another’s. We should celebrate and encourage success instead of practicing tall poppy.

#### ACT backs the person who invests in themselves to upskill, works overtime to save a deposit for a farm or a home, or takes the risk of quitting a regular paycheque to start their own business. You shouldn’t be punished for that with ever-increasing taxes or swaths of red tape.

#### Tax and regulation are needed, but they come at a cost. That’s why we believe Government should be a careful spender, keeping your taxes low, providing only essential services and doing them well. Government should regulate carefully, making rules when there is no other way to solve a problem, and removing red tape when it’s no longer needed.

# Free Speech for Regulated Professionals

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/professional-free-speech> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Democracy & Equal Rights

## Free Speech for Regulated Professionals

Professional regulators exist to protect the public by setting standards for competence, safety and conduct at work. They should not decide which lawful political or personal views a New Zealander is allowed to hold.

Teachers, nurses, real estate agents and other professionals have faced disciplinary action or compulsory ideological training over opinions expressed outside their work. More than 200,000 New Zealanders work in regulated professions. Their ability to earn a living should not depend on agreeing with their regulator's politics.

ACT will legislate to keep regulators focused on professional performance and public safety. Serious misconduct at work would still be punished. Lawful expression in a person's private life would not be a professional offence.

#### ACT will:

- Ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice.
- Require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues.
- Restrict mandatory training to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety.
- Strengthen judicial oversight so courts can rein in regulators that go beyond their legal powers.
- Preserve regulators' ability to act against genuine professional misconduct, harm to clients or patients, and breaches of professional duties.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Public Service spokesperson Todd Stephenson says:

“New Zealanders should not have to choose between their career and their right to free speech. If someone is competent, safe and professional at work, a regulator should not threaten their livelihood because it dislikes a lawful opinion they expressed in their own time.

“More than 200,000 people work in regulated professions. Every one of them should be able to support a political party, sign a petition, attend a peaceful protest or join a public debate without wondering whether their registration is at risk.

“ACT will require regulators to stay politically neutral, keep compulsory training tied to competence and safety, and give the courts stronger ability to stop regulatory overreach. Professionals should be judged on how they do their jobs, not whether their opinions are fashionable.”

# Protect Lawful Hunting

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/protect-lawful-hunting> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Hunters and Firearms

## Protect Lawful Hunting

Hunters acting safely and within the law can be deliberately obstructed by people who step into the line of fire to stop a shot. That creates an obvious danger, but there is no specific infringement offence for it.

Aircraft can also be used to harass game-bird shooters by deliberately scattering or flushing birds. This disturbs the birds and sabotages a lawful activity, with little legal remedy available.

People remain free to oppose hunting. They should not be free to interfere in ways that put others at risk.

Read the full policy here.

#### ACT will:

- Create an infringement offence for deliberately standing in the line of fire of a lawful hunter.
- Create an infringement offence for using drones or helicopters to harass game-bird shooters.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“A hunter acting safely and lawfully should not have someone step into the line of fire to stop a shot. That is not ordinary protest. It creates an immediate risk for everyone there, yet the law has no specific answer.

“Hunters and game-bird shooters are expected to follow strict safety rules, as they should. Those rules cannot work if someone deliberately enters the line of fire. The law needs a clear consequence for that behaviour.”

ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“The same principle applies when activists use drones or helicopters to scatter game birds. It disturbs the birds, disrupts a lawful shoot and can create another hazard in the air and on the ground.

“We would create a specific infringement offence for harassing game-bird shooters with an aircraft. If someone wants to campaign against hunting, they remain free to do so. They should not be free to sabotage a lawful activity in a way that puts people at risk.”

# Keeping Public Spaces Safe

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/public-safety> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Keeping Public Spaces Safe

New Zealanders deserve to feel safe at their local shops and transport hubs, and businesses deserve real tools to stand up for themselves and their communities.

Business owners want protection from trained, uniformed professionals. But Police can’t respond quickly to every call. Security professionals have the potential to fill the gap. New Zealand has twice as many licenced security officers as police officers, but they currently have no more authority than any other citizen.

ACT will give real power – with clear limits – to properly trained security professionals. We’ll introduce a new licence that security professionals can obtain, with training, to gain the authority needed to keep shared spaces and businesses safe.

The Government has already given some guards elevated powers with ad hoc legislation, such as Parliamentary Security. ACT will allow retailers, business associations, shopping strips, and transport operators to access a higher calibre of protection.

Under ACT's plan, licenced Accredited Security Operators would be able to:

- Require a person's name and address on private premises and detain them until Police arrive if they refuse and won't leave.
- Issue conduct-based exclusion notices, enforceable for up to three years across multiple premises – like those of a business association – held on a register under the Privacy Act.
- Remove people who threaten safety, cause damage, or breach a venue's conditions of entry.
- Use reasonable and proportionate force as a last resort, ceasing the moment the person complies or Police arrive.
- Carry out consent-based safety searches, including on the premises, where refusing a search means no entry.

Read the full policy

#### In our team’s words:

"Every licence holder will have to go through specialised advanced training and education. This is not something that any Tom, Dick, or Harry could just pick up. Stringent vetting will ensure only the right people with the right capability will be approved,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

"These powers will apply on private premises, but when combined with citizens’ arrest powers currently going through Parliament, will give licenced professionals real capability to keep the wider community safe.

"ACT’s policy will unlock communities’ potential to protect themselves, without relying solely on the taxpayer or a stretched Police force.”

ACT’s spokesperson for retail crime, Dr Parmjeet Parmar, says:

“Retail crime is still hurting businesses. When people don’t feel safe visiting their local shops, they stay home and shop online. That drains foot traffic and jobs out of town centres.

“Retail NZ’s Crime Report estimates that crime costs the sector $2.6 billion a year. Behind that number are shop owners and workers who have been threatened or harmed, and communities that feel unsafe.

“ACT’s policy means businesses can take real action, sharing the services of highly-effective security professionals. It reflects the reality that, until the Police arrive, communities need real authority to stand up for themselves against thieves and thugs."

documents/put-reside-back-in-resident.md.text:
# Put ‘Reside’ Back in ‘Resident’

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/put-%E2%80%98reside%E2%80%99-back-in-%E2%80%98resident%E2%80%99> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Put ‘Reside’ Back in ‘Resident’

New Zealand should welcome people who want to build a life here. But if someone wants the permanent right to return as a New Zealand resident, it is reasonable to expect them to maintain a real connection to the country.

Right now, someone can hold a Permanent Resident Visa without continuing to live in New Zealand. They can leave and re-enter indefinitely, leaving almost no practical distinction between permanent residence and citizenship.

ACT will put ‘reside’ back in ‘resident’. Residents will receive a five-year travel facility and will need to spend at least 730 days in New Zealand during any rolling five-year period to keep it. The days will not need to be continuous, and sensible exemptions will cover people working or serving New Zealand overseas, accompanying family members, and compelling humanitarian circumstances.

This policy is not retrospective – existing Permanent Resident Visa holders will not be affected. And exemptions for the Active Investor Plus Visa, also known as the Golden Visa, will remain.

#### ACT will:

- Remove the existing Permanent Resident Visa category.
- Give all Resident Visa holders a five-year travel facility, replacing the current two-year initial travel condition.
- Require Resident Visa holders to be physically present in New Zealand for at least 730 days within any rolling five-year period to maintain their travel facility.
- Allow the 730 days to be accumulated across the five years rather than requiring them to be continuous.
- Remove the indefinite, unconditional right to leave and re-enter New Zealand as a resident without maintaining an ongoing connection to the country.
- Provide exemptions for people working overseas for New Zealand employers, accompanying family members, military personnel serving overseas, people with a New Zealand citizen spouse, those with compelling humanitarian reasons, and holders of the Active Investor Plus Visa.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:

"The strangest immigration policy we have is that permanent residents don’t have to be permanently resident.

"New Zealand is, and should be, a welcoming country for migrants, but the privileges of permanent residence must reflect a real and lasting connection to our nation.

"This would also create a clearer answer to the question, what is the difference between permanent residence and citizenship? Right now, the two have nearly identical everyday rights. By introducing standard travel conditions, we create an evident distinction, giving people a reason to graduate to citizenship.

"To unlock New Zealand’s potential, there needs to be a balance between rights and responsibilities. ACT’s plan encourages migrants who choose to make New Zealand their permanent home to continue actively living and contributing here, while also ensuring a fair system for all taxpayers."

# Rural Crime Crackdown

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/rural-crime> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

###### Rural

## Rural Crime Crackdown

Crime in rural New Zealand is growing, and too many rural communities feel like they've been left to fend for themselves. Today, ACT is announcing a new Rural Crime Policy to restore law and order to the countryside.

#### ACT will:

- Fund Police to hire more officers for rural areas with a target of an additional 100,000 extra patrol hours each year, and establish a dedicated rural crime unit.
- Extend eligibility for Text 111 services to people in rural areas with unreliable mobile coverage, ensuring they can contact emergency services via text when a voice call drops out.
- Crack down on armed poachers and livestock rustling with increased penalties and strengthened offences.
- Strengthen the tools used between agencies for rural enforcement coordination.

Federated Farmers' latest Rural Crime Survey found 67% of farmers experienced crime, up from 41% in 2016.

#### In our team’s words:

“Talk to farmers, and you'll hear the same story. Illegal hunters are crossing private land. Livestock stolen or killed. Sheds broken into. Fuel and machinery are disappearing overnight. Meanwhile, police resources have been steadily pulled out of rural communities,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“When people stop reporting crime because they don't believe anything will happen, that's a sign the system isn't working.

“Criminals target rural people because they’re isolated. Our policy takes that out of the equation, with more police presence, connectivity and harsher deterrents.”

ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Mark Cameron says: “When criminals know the nearest police car is miles away, they are emboldened. It is no surprise that nearly half of farmers do not even bother reporting incidents to the police, and of those who do, only 15% see the offender investigated and prosecuted.”

“Farmers deserve the same protection and peace of mind as anyone living in a city. Rural New Zealand helps feed the country and drive our economy. The least the government can do is make sure the people who live and work there feel safe in their own homes and on their own land. ACT will ensure the justice system treats rural crime with the seriousness it deserves, and put police back on the rural beat,” says Mr Hoggard.

"ACT is proud to be rural New Zealand’s authentic voice in parliament. When every other party sold rural New Zealand out with the Zero Carbon Act, ACT stood alone against it and kept campaigning to keep agriculture out of the ETS. We've achieved that in Government, we're making property rights the focus of the RMA, we've gotten rid of Labour's anti-farming policies like the ute tax, winter grazing rules and overzealous freshwater farm plans."

# A Rural Workforce Visa

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/rural-visa> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Rural

###### Immigration

## A Rural Workforce Visa

ACT is announcing its new Rural Workforce Visa (RWV) policy, a dedicated pathway designed to give farmers a reliable, year-round pipeline of workers – without the visa uncertainty that leaves roles unfilled for months at a time.

ACT will:

- Create the Rural Workforce Visa: A standalone, three-year visa specifically for dairy, sheep and beef, and general farm work.
- Implement sector-tying, not geographic borders: The visa is attached to accredited rural employers, not a region. Workers can transfer to any other accredited rural employer without a new application, but cannot move to nonrural sectors. Workers end up in rural communities as a market outcome, not because a bureaucrat drew a line on a map.
- Cut bureaucracy: The visa features an initial three-year term with no renewal required within that period. Before the visa term ends, employers readvertise; if no suitable New Zealander is available, the visa is reissued for a further three years. This removes the repeated annual compliance load on employers.
- Establish a clear residency pathway: ACT will add a new agricultural stream to the Work to Residence Visa. Workers who have held an RWV for 72 cumulative months (six years) with an accredited employer, and who meet standard requirements, will become eligible for residence.

#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand's farms, orchards, and fishing fleets generate $60 billion in exports every year. Right now, they can't find enough capable workers to do the job, held back by a chronic labour shortage that the current immigration system simply isn't equipped to solve," says ACT's Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“Rural New Zealand faces different pressures from urban New Zealand. In many communities, the problem isn't too many people arriving, it's not enough workers being available. Applying an infrastructure levy in those circumstances would make no sense, which is why ACT’s Rural Workforce Visa would be exempt. Federated Farmers’ latest Farm Confidence Survey confirms labour availability remains one of the biggest challenges facing farmers across the country.

“The Government has made progress by introducing the Global Workforce Seasonal Visa and Peak Seasonal Visa. Those pathways help meet seasonal demand, but they do not address the year round roles that keep farms running every day.

“Labour shortages don't just make it harder to run farms. They also make it harder to keep productive land in farming at a time when many rural communities are already under pressure from the expansion of forestry.”

“Immigration should support the industries that drive New Zealand's economy, not leave critical jobs sitting vacant. ACT's Rural Workforce Visa provides certainty and a straightforward pathway for reliable migrant workers to fill genuine workforce shortages. Our immigration settings should support the people who feed the country and drive our economy, not bury them in red tape.” says ACT’s Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar.

Mr Hoggard says the policy respects the basic bargain that New Zealand was built on. People are welcome here if they contribute, respect our democratic values, and help build the country. It is a targeted, pro-market solution that rewards workers who have demonstrated sustained commitment to rural New Zealand.

“ACT’s Rural Workforce Visa reduces regulatory burdens on farmers, removes geographic restrictions, and delivers year-round workforce stability our primary industries need to drive New Zealand’s export economy forward,” says Mr Hoggard.

# ACT’s New Immigration Policy To Put ‘Reside’ Back In ‘Resident’

*ACT New Zealand press release (Scoop mirror). Source: <https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2609/S00003/acts-new-immigration-policy-to-put-reside-back-in-resident.htm> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

Tuesday, 1 September 2026, 8:23 am Press Release: ACT New Zealand

“ACT will bring balance to New Zealand’s immigration system by introducing physical presence requirements for permanent residents, ensuring visa holders have a genuine commitment to our country,” says ACT’s Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar.

“The strangest immigration policy we have is that permanent residents don’t have to be permanently resident.

"New Zealand is, and should be, a welcoming country for migrants, but the privileges of permanent residence must reflect a real and lasting connection to our nation.

“ACT is proposing to change New Zealand’s residence system. Under our policy, the existing Permanent Resident Visa category will be removed, and the existing Resident Visa changed to require all Resident Visa holders to receive a 5 year travel facility, replacing the current 2 year initial travel condition.

“To maintain the travel facility, visa holders would need to be physically present in New Zealand for at least 730 days (2 years) within any rolling five-year period. The 730 days would not need to be continuous, but the indefinite, unconditional right to leave and re-enter the country would be removed. This ensures that those who want the ability to travel to New Zealand as residents must continue to demonstrate a meaningful connection with our country.

“There will be exemptions for individuals working overseas for New Zealand employers, accompanying family members, military personnel serving overseas, and those with a citizen spouse, or other compelling humanitarian reasons.

“The proposed model would better align New Zealand with countries that have comparable immigration systems like Australia, Canada and Singapore, where permanent residence requires an ongoing connection through physical presence or substantial ties.

"This would also create a clearer answer to the question, what is the difference between permanent residence and citizenship? Right now, the two have nearly identical everyday rights. By introducing standard travel conditions, we create an evident distinction, giving people a reason to graduate to citizenship.

"This change ensures that permanent residence reflects a genuine, ongoing commitment to New Zealand.

“To unlock New Zealand’s potential, there needs to be a balance between rights and responsibilities. ACT’s plan encourages migrants who choose to make New Zealand their permanent home to continue actively living and contributing here, while also ensuring a fair system for all taxpayers.”

# Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/scrap-net-zero-cut-the-carbon-tax> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Rural

## Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax

New Zealand should play its part in reducing emissions. But a country responsible for just 0.17 per cent of global emissions needs a sense of proportion. There is no virtue in making petrol, power and food more expensive here while our major trading partners refuse to carry the same costs.

The Zero Carbon Act locks New Zealand into net zero by 2050, whatever our trading partners do. The Emissions Trading Scheme then adds a carbon cost to almost everything New Zealanders buy. At a carbon price of about $55, it costs an average household an estimated $478 a year.

ACT was the only party to vote against the Zero Carbon Act in 2019. We will repeal it, tie our emissions cap to what our trading partners are doing, remove the artificial auction price floor and return the revenue to New Zealanders. If the carbon price rises, the refund rises too.

A climate policy that closes a factory here so the same product can be made overseas has only exported jobs and emissions. Meanwhile, skewed carbon incentives are swallowing productive farms. ACT will give Kiwi industry and farming a fair go and let cleaner technology compete without needless red tape.

Read the full policy, Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax, here.

### ACT will

- Scrap the arbitrary net zero 2050 target and repeal the Zero Carbon Act.
- Tie New Zealand’s emissions cap to a trade-weighted average of our major trading partners.
- Cut the carbon tax by removing the Government’s artificial minimum price for carbon auctions. In 2026, the minimum was $71 while units were trading in the low $50s, contributing to six failed auctions in a row.
- Return 100 per cent of net carbon auction revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund. If the amount becomes too small for individual refunds, it will fund other tax relief.
- Protect Kiwi jobs where overseas competitors face lower or no carbon prices. Industrial carbon assistance will return to its original 90 and 60 per cent rates, with the automatic phase-down stopped while that disadvantage remains. Assistance of up to 100 per cent will be available in exceptional cases.
- Fix the rules that favour converting productive farmland to permanent carbon forests. Permanent forest owners will remain responsible for pest control and for the cost if stored carbon is later released.
- Cut red tape holding back cheaper, cleaner technology and oppose new climate taxes, including a tax on agricultural emissions.
- Renegotiate New Zealand’s commitment under the Paris Agreement. If a fairer arrangement cannot be reached, New Zealand should be prepared to leave.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand’s climate policy is broken and sending the country broke as a result. A small trading nation can’t ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households.

“ACT is the OG No New Taxes party, so we’ll return carbon auction revenue to taxpayers rather than giving politicians another pot of money to spend.”

ACT Climate Change spokesperson Simon Court says:

“If a New Zealand business can produce steel, cement, aluminium or food more efficiently than its overseas competitors, closing that business is an economic own goal and an environmental one too.

“Families are already paying too much at the supermarket and the last thing we should be doing is weakening our ability to grow food by turning productive farms into pine forests.”

# Scrap the Climate Change Commission

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/scrap-the-climate-change-commission> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

###### Rural

## Scrap the Climate Change Commission

While New Zealanders are watching every dollar, Wellington has already spent $100 million on the Climate Change Commission and keeps handing it another $14–15 million a year to produce reports that duplicate work already being done in government or recommend policies that harm the country.

Those recommendations are not harmless paperwork. One proposal to tighten the 2050 emissions target would make the economy 2.2 per cent smaller, costing New Zealanders $2 billion a year by 2035 and $12.5 billion every year by 2050. The Commission has also proposed shrinking New Zealand’s dairy herd, punishing some of the world’s most emissions-efficient farmers and risking production moving to dirtier countries.

ACT will abolish the Commission and transfer its monitoring and reporting duties to the ministry that already measures New Zealand’s emissions and manages the Emissions Trading Scheme. New Zealand does not need two climate bureaucracies charging taxpayers for the same job.

#### ACT will:

- Abolish the Climate Change Commission as an independent Crown entity. The Commission will cease to exist.
- Transfer responsibility for monitoring and reporting on New Zealand’s emissions targets to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport.
- Bring emissions monitoring together with the greenhouse gas inventory and the Emissions Trading Scheme, so one department is responsible for the work.
- End the Commission’s separate role recommending costly new targets and interventions such as shrinking New Zealand’s dairy herd.
- Remove the Commission’s board, executive and corporate overhead, ending the need for taxpayers to support a separate $14–15 million-a-year climate bureaucracy.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:

"The Climate Change Commission has cost taxpayers $100 million since its establishment, and is costing a further $14–15 million every year it continues to exist. Left in place, that's another $42–45 million of taxpayer money gone by the next election spent on writing reports, duplicating work, and proposing ludicrous ideas that will be ignored.

"Their barking mad recommendation to increase our 2050 emissions reduction commitment would have lowered GDP by 2.2%. That’s around $2 billion a year by 2035, rising to about $12.5 billion every year by 2050, wiped from our economy to meet an arbitrary target.

"They put up proposals even Labour and the Greens can’t get behind. In the last term of Government they recommended tighter Emissions Trading Scheme restrictions, but Cabinet rejected it. Commission-linked advice supported a 54% net reduction for the 2030 emissions reduction pledge, but Cabinet opted for a 50% reduction instead. Even the left could recognise a stupid idea.

"We can’t afford to see taxpayer dollars blown on inefficient government agencies and counterproductive climate policies. To unlock New Zealand’s potential and make life more affordable, the waste and duplication need to go. Go sell stupid somewhere else, we’re all full up here."

# Shorter Waits for your GP

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/shorter-waits-for-your-gp> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Health

## Shorter Waits for your GP

When you’re worried about your health or a sick child, the last thing you need is a long wait for a GP. ACT will invest an extra $400 million in general practice over four years to keep experienced doctors here and help them see more patients. We’ll also cut unnecessary red tape for qualified GPs coming from overseas, so you and your family can get care sooner.

#### ACT will:

- Provide an ongoing $100 million annual boost to general practice, on top of normal capitation increases, totalling $400 million over the first four years.
- Keep experienced GPs working and in New Zealand by helping practices offer competitive remuneration and retain staff, making it more attractive for doctors to stay rather than retire early or move overseas.
- Help GPs see more patients by supporting practices to offer extra hours and reward additional appointments, so doctors who want to can see more patients and stay in practice longer.
- Attract qualified doctors from overseas by reforming and streamlining medical regulators so safe, competent professionals can enter the health system sooner.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas says:

“There’s no point promising more free appointments if there aren’t enough doctors to provide them.

“The easiest doctor to recruit is the one you don’t lose. With 35 per cent of GPs intending to retire within five years and 18 per cent considering moving overseas, we need to make it more attractive for them to stay.”

# Stopping Coercion by Animal Abuse

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/stopping-coercion> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Stopping Coercion by Animal Abuse

Victims of family violence should never have to choose between their own safety and the safety of the pet they love.

Family violence isn’t just about physical abuse. Perpetrators use threats against beloved pets as another way to intimidate and trap their victims.

The evidence is confronting. Research found abusive partners were almost 11 times more likely to intentionally harm an animal than partners in non-abusive relationships. More than half of victims said they delayed leaving an abusive relationship because they felt responsible for the safety of their pets.

ACT will strengthen protections for pets used as instruments of coercion and control in family violence by:

- Amending the Crimes Act to make it an offence to use the abuse of a companion animal as a means of coercion or control in a family violence relationship, with a penalty up to seven years in imprisonment.
- Strengthening Protection Orders to ensure offenders cannot withhold, sell, give away, or otherwise dispose of a protected person's companion animal, helping keep pets with the protected person and closing a loophole exploited by family violence offenders.
- Ensuring companion animals are not left with a dangerous abuser when a Protection Order is made, reducing opportunities for offenders to use pets as a tool of coercion or control.
- Requiring Police to record pets on family harm reports to better identify risks and strengthen protections for victims and their animals.
- Giving Police explicit statutory authority and clear operational guidance to remove a companion animal to a place of safety, such as Pet Refuge or the SPCA, where they believe the animal is at risk of harm or is being used as a tool of coercion.

Read the full policy

#### In our team’s words:

"Right now, if Police attend a family violence callout, a victim may escape while the family pet is left behind with the alleged abuser. That gives offenders another way to threaten and manipulate the people they’re abusing,” says ACT’s Family and Sexual Violence spokesperson Karen Chhour.

“ACT will ensure Police have the tools they need to protect victims and remove companion animals from harm when offenders use them as weapons of coercion. New Zealand is falling behind countries that have already recognised the link between animal abuse and family violence.

"In New South Wales, harming or threatening to harm a pet is now a standard condition of every domestic violence protection order because lawmakers recognised exactly how offenders exploit the bond between victims and their animals. More than 40 US states have also strengthened protection orders to include companion animals.

"New Zealand is behind the curve. It's time our laws caught up with the reality of family violence.

"We know pets are often part of the family, and we know abusers deliberately target them. Victims stay longer in dangerous situations because they’re terrified of what will happen if they leave.

“Knowing all of that, doing nothing is not an option. ACT will put victims first, gives Police better tools, strengthen Protection Orders, and make it easier for victims to leave violence without leaving part of their family behind.

“Family violence is about power and control, and ACT won’t let abusers keep using pets to trap their victims.”

---

# Strengthening End of Life Choice

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/strengthening-end-of-life-choice> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Health

## Strengthening End of Life Choice

A terminally ill person suffering unbearably should have the final say over how and when they die.

The End of Life Choice Act has given New Zealanders that option since 2021. The Ministry of Health's first statutory review recommended 25 changes to the law.

ACT MP Todd Stephenson's End of Life Choice Amendment Bill adopts all 25. It would also remove a rule that denies access when a doctor cannot say with certainty that someone has less than six months to live.

#### ACT will:

- Implement all 25 recommendations from the Ministry of Health's statutory review of the End of Life Choice Act.
- Replace the six-month prognosis requirement with a requirement that a person has an advanced, progressive condition expected to cause death.
- Keep the other eligibility tests, including that the person is at least 18, is in an advanced state of irreversible decline, is experiencing unbearable suffering that cannot be tolerably relieved, and is competent to make an informed decision.
- Allow a limited waiver of final consent when a person has been assessed as eligible and chosen the date and time while competent, but loses capacity before that date.
- Require training for practitioners, strengthen the Registrar's oversight, and spell out their duty to check that requests are free from pressure.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“The End of Life Choice Act recognises that a person living with a terminal illness is best placed to decide how their final days should be spent. Almost 1,700 New Zealanders have now chosen an assisted death.

“The latest report also shows the safeguards are working. More than 300 applicants were found ineligible last year, and 42 people withdrew. The checks are real, and the choice remains with the patient right to the end.”

ACT MP Todd Stephenson says:

“My Bill adopts all 25 recommendations from the Ministry of Health's review. It also addresses the six-month prognosis rule, which remains the biggest barrier for terminally ill New Zealanders seeking an assisted death.

“The six-month rule has shut out people who are terminally ill, in irreversible decline, and suffering unbearably because a doctor cannot say their death will occur within six months. Death does not always follow a calendar.

“The Bill replaces that cut-off with a test based on whether a person's condition is advanced, progressive, and expected to cause death. All the other eligibility criteria remain.

“It also allows a limited waiver of final consent when someone has been assessed as eligible and chosen a date while competent, but loses capacity before that date. None of the existing safeguards are being weakened.

“New Zealanders backed the original law by almost two to one. Parliament should now have the chance to consider what we have learned from its first years in operation and make it work better.”

# Real Choice for Students

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/student_services_fee> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Education

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Real Choice for Students

ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.

Every domestic university student currently pays a compulsory Student Services Fee of up to $1,253 a year on top of tuition. Across a three-year degree this can add more than $4,000 to a student’s loan*. Because student loans are subsidised by the taxpayer, the compulsory fee also costs the taxpayer.

#### ACT will:

- ACT will amend the regulations so universities must offer student services as a menu. Students would select the services they want and pay only for those, from fitness facilities to students unions and student media. Services not chosen would still be available on a transparent user-pays basis.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:

“Students should not be forced to fund unions, advocacy or student media they do not support. That is a matter of principle for ACT.

“Right now, student unions are running political campaigns to influence the election. They might even campaign to stop this policy. Students are forced to fund this activism, even if they disagree with it. ACT says unions are free to campaign, but no-one should be forced to fund them.

“Our policy would let students save up to around $4,000 on their student loan over the course of a degree. It would also save the taxpayer money, because student debt is subsidised. We will complete the unfinished business of Voluntary Student Membership and restore genuine choice.”

\*After annual increases to the fee.

# Tougher Penalties for Rubbish Dumping

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/tougher-penalties-for-rubbish-dumping> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Law & Order

## Tougher Penalties for Rubbish Dumping

The people trashing our communities are leaving ratepayers with the bill. ACT will raise fines for illegal rubbish dumping to $1,000, and $2,000 for repeat offenders, to protect roadsides and rivers and make offenders think twice.

#### ACT will:

- Increase the infringement fee for illegal rubbish dumping from $400 to $1,000.
- Set fines of $2,000 for repeat offenders.
- Give courts the power to impose higher penalties for the most serious offences.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard says:

“Illegal dumping is vandalism by another name. It's unfair on ratepayers, damaging to the environment, and shows a complete disregard for people who take pride in their communities.

“The current $400 penalty isn't cutting it. If you're prepared to dump rubbish beside a river, and leave someone else to deal with the mess, a slap on the wrist isn't much of a deterrent.”

# Unlocking Mineral Wealth

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/unlocking-mineral-wealth> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Unlocking Mineral Wealth

New Zealand is sitting on valuable mineral and energy resources while importing more of what a modern economy needs and watching skilled Kiwis leave for mining jobs overseas.

ACT wants New Zealand to build things again. We will make it easier to responsibly develop the resources beneath our feet, bringing investment into our regions, creating high-paying careers at home, strengthening our energy and economic security, and earning royalties for New Zealanders.

Read our full policy, Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth, here.

#### ACT will:

- Keep New Zealand open to responsible mineral exploration and development, with the Critical Minerals List updated as new opportunities emerge.
- Establish clear national rules for mines, quarries and mineral processing, while continuing to protect national parks and Schedule 4 land.
- Keep fast-track consenting available for eligible projects and establish clear deadlines for government decisions.
- Open exploration and extraction on suitable government-owned land outside protected areas under clear and predictable rules.
- Keep onshore and offshore petroleum exploration open where commercially viable opportunities emerge.
- Remove unnecessary barriers to domestic gas production, underground gas storage and reliable thermal generation.
- Cut duplicated approval processes so companies are not forced to prove the same thing repeatedly to different regulators.
- Make regulatory requirements proportionate to the actual scale and risk of a project.
- Protect legitimate investment from arbitrary political reversals and strengthen property rights.
- Require mining and petroleum operators to pay for rehabilitation, decommissioning and ongoing treatment, rather than leaving taxpayers with the cleanup bill.
- Work with industry and training providers so more New Zealanders can build skilled, well-paid careers in the resources sector without moving overseas.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Energy and Resources spokesperson Simon Court says:

“New Zealand has minerals needed for roads, homes, power lines, phones, batteries, and medical technology. We use these products every day, but too often refuse to produce the raw materials ourselves. That does not stop mining globally. It just sends the jobs, investment and environmental responsibility offshore.

“Developing these resources responsibly creates well-paid regional jobs, supports new industries, strengthens domestic supply chains, provides strategic resources to our allies, and generates royalties for the Crown.”

# Unlocking New Zealand's Digital Economy

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/unlocking-new-zealands-digital-economy> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Unlocking New Zealand's Digital Economy

A Kiwi with a good idea should be able to build it here. Instead, our financial rules are still catching up with technology that is already changing how people raise money, invest and get paid.

A fintech start-up can face rules designed for major financial institutions before it has even proved its product. Legitimate digital-finance businesses can struggle to get a bank account. Someone making a small purchase with digital assets can face pointless tax paperwork. That holds New Zealand back.

ACT will modernise the rules so Kiwis can get investment into good ideas, build new financial businesses here and use new ways of moving money, without giving up strong protections against fraud and financial crime.

Read our full policy, Unlocking New Zealand's Digital Economy, here.

#### ACT will:

- Make international payments faster and cheaper. ACT will set clear rules for qualifying payment stablecoins, including strong requirements to protect consumers and the financial system.
- Stop pointless tax paperwork on small purchases. ACT will introduce a sensible exemption for low-value purchases made with digital assets, so Inland Revenue can focus on transactions that actually matter.
- Make it easier for New Zealand businesses to raise money. ACT will create clear legal and tax rules for tokenised assets, allowing ownership in things like businesses, farms, infrastructure and commercial property to be divided and transferred digitally with confidence.
- Give financial start-ups room to prove themselves. Innovative businesses will be able to test new products under supervision before being required to meet the full regulatory regime designed for established financial institutions.
- Give long-term digital investors a clear tax rule. Qualifying personal investments held for more than 12 months will fall outside the new bright-line rule. Professional traders and businesses will continue to be taxed under existing rules.
- Tackle blanket de-banking. ACT will review rules that may be encouraging banks and payment providers to shut legitimate, properly regulated fintech businesses out of essential financial services.

#### In our team's words:

ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“New technology is changing how businesses raise capital, how people invest, and how money moves around the world. Tokenised assets can open up new sources of investment. Stablecoins can make international payments faster and cheaper. New financial technology can create high-value businesses and jobs.

“ACT will cut red tape, set clear rules, and open up investment so Kiwis can raise capital, pay and get paid more easily, and take part in the technologies shaping the future - while keeping strong consumer and financial safeguards".

ACT MP Cameron Luxton says:

“ACT will be unlocking more growth, better jobs, and a future-ready economy that New Zealanders can participate in.

"We will align digital finance policy with a bigger goal, getting capital flowing to good ideas and helping entrepreneurs build globally competitive businesses from New Zealand."

# Welfare as a Hand Up, not a Way of Life

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/welfare> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Economy & Cost of Living

## Welfare as a Hand Up, not a Way of Life

Welfare should unlock potential, not trap it. So why are we paying people to stay at home who could be doing jobs we are currently filling with migrants?

ACT’s welfare policy has two planks:

#### Tightening medical certification for health-related benefits

- All health and disability benefits will be independently issued by an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors.* A person’s usual GP or specialist will still be able to provide medical history, clinical notes, and supporting evidence.
- Assessments will be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion.
- Existing Jobseeker Support – Health Condition or Disability and Supported Living Payment recipients will be reassessed against the new criteria on a phased basis.
- Reassessment will begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic, where much of the recent growth has occurred.
- ACT will allow for long-term arrangements for those with a genuine, enduring disability or health condition so support stays in place for those who truly need it.

\* The Government has already established this as an option, but ACT will make it mandatory.

#### Managed assistance for long-term Jobseeker recipients

- ACT will introduce electronic money management for Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients who remain on a benefit for more than four months.*
- Their benefit will be delivered through an electronic payment card directed to essentials such as groceries, rent, power, transport, health and childcare.
- The card will block spending on alcohol, gambling, tobacco, and cash withdrawals.
- ACT will include carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.

\* New Zealand already has money management as an option in certain circumstances, but ACT will make it mandatory after the four-month threshold.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealanders believe in helping people through tough times. But the deal has to be fair: if you can work, you should be taking real steps toward work, and taxpayer support should go to the essentials it was intended to fund.

“Nobody should be denied support when they genuinely cannot work. But the public deserves confidence that the system is not being gamed, and that people are not being written off when work or greater independence is possible.

“Electronic money management means taxpayer support will not fund purchases that make it harder for people to get their lives back on track. If someone is receiving a benefit funded by working New Zealanders, that support should go to food, housing, power, transport, health, and childcare – not alcohol, gambling, or tobacco.

“Unlocking New Zealand’s potential means unlocking the potential of New Zealanders. That starts with a welfare system that backs people to move forward, rewards effort, protects taxpayers, and refuses to write people off."

# Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

*ACT New Zealand policy page. Source: <https://www.act.org.nz/wind-up-the-waitangi-tribunal> (retrieved 2026-10-23).*

## Full text

> Verbatim text as published; only whitespace and markup have been normalised.

###### Democracy & Equal Rights

## Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

The Waitangi Tribunal has made an important contribution to New Zealand. Its historical work helped identify Crown wrongdoing and created a pathway to resolve past injustices, including the confiscation of land and other breaches of property rights. Most historical claims have now been heard or settled. Those still outstanding should be completed properly.

But the modern Tribunal now passes judgement on day-to-day government policy, proposes alternative policy settings, and seeks to influence decisions that belong to elected Governments and Parliament. It should not operate as a parallel policy institution.

As New Zealand approaches 2040, two hundred years after the signing of the Treaty, it is time to finish the historical settlement process. Every New Zealander should have their rights protected through the same law and courts as we move forward under one law for all with one future together.

Read our full policy 'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal', here.

#### ACT will:

- Complete every eligible historical claim already before the Tribunal. Its jurisdiction will be limited to historical claims lodged by the existing statutory deadline of 1 September 2008, without rushing or cutting off genuine claimants.
- End the Tribunal’s jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, leaving it to focus solely on completing its remaining historical work.
- Strengthen property rights for every New Zealander by adding them to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, so unlawful interference by the Crown can be challenged through the ordinary courts.
- Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed, rather than imposing an arbitrary closure date.

#### In our team’s words:

ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand’s constitutional landscape for more than fifty years. It has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances. But no institution should exist just because it always has,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Every New Zealander deserves strong legal protections and access to the courts, regardless of ancestry. ACT believes those protections should be strengthened for everyone, not maintained through a permanent separate system for one group.

“As 2040 approaches, we should complete the remaining historical settlements, protecting every New Zealander’s right under the same law and courts, and move forward under one law for all with one future together.”
